lessons.plain: Computer architecture is the blueprint of a computer: which major parts it has and how they cooperate to run a program. Think of a kitchen. The processor is the cook following a recipe one step at a time. Main memory is the countertop, small but within easy reach, holding what the cook is using right now. Storage is the pantry, large but slower to reach, keeping things even when the kitchen closes. Input and output devices are the doors where groceries arrive and plates leave. System organization is how these parts are wired together so the work flows smoothly.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your laptop has 16 GB of memory and a 512 GB drive. When you open a large photo, where do you think the photo sits while you edit it, and why not just leave it on the drive?
lessons.teach:
Computer architecture describes a computer's main components and how they communicate. Most computers follow the von Neumann architecture, a design in which program instructions and data live together in the same memory. Its parts are the CPU (central processing unit), which carries out instructions; main memory, or RAM (random-access memory), which is fast but loses its contents when power goes off; storage, such as a solid-state drive, which is slower but keeps data permanently; input/output (I/O) devices like keyboards, screens and network cards; and the bus, the shared set of wires that moves data and addresses between them. Everything is stored in binary, meaning patterns of 0s and 1s.

Inside the CPU, the control unit directs each step, the ALU (arithmetic logic unit) does math and comparisons, and registers are tiny, extremely fast storage slots. The CPU repeats the fetch-decode-execute cycle billions of times per second. Speed comes from the memory hierarchy: small fast layers (registers, then cache, a little memory built into the CPU) keep copies of what is needed soon, so the CPU rarely waits on slower RAM or storage.

Worked example: a program computes 5 + 3. First, the program is copied from storage into RAM. Fetch: the CPU reads the next instruction from the RAM address held in its program counter, a register tracking where it is. Decode: the control unit recognizes this as an add instruction. Execute: the values 5 and 3 are loaded into registers, the ALU adds them, and 8 is written to a register or back to RAM. The program counter moves to the next instruction and the cycle repeats.

A common mistake is treating memory and storage as the same thing. RAM is temporary working space; storage is the permanent record. In a running system, when RAM fills up the computer starts using storage as overflow space, and because storage is far slower, everything slows sharply, even though the drive may still have plenty of free space.

questions.prompt: A smart thermostat runs a small program that checks whether the room temperature (18 degrees) is below the target (21 degrees). The program has already been copied into RAM. Step 1: the CPU reads the next instruction from the RAM address held in its program counter. Step 2: the control unit recognizes it as a compare instruction. Step 3: the values 18 and 21 are loaded into registers. Step 4: ??? Step 5: the result 'true' is written to a register, and the program counter moves to the next instruction. What happens in Step 4?
choices: The cache compares 18 and 21, because it keeps copies of values needed soon.
The control unit compares 18 and 21, because it was the part that recognized the instruction.
The ALU compares 18 and 21 and produces the result.
The bus compares 18 and 21 while it carries them between RAM and the CPU.
questions.why: The ALU (arithmetic logic unit) is the part of the CPU that does math and comparisons, while the control unit only directs the steps.

questions.prompt: What is the defining feature of the von Neumann architecture?
choices: The CPU contains its own permanent storage, so no separate drive is needed.
Data is stored in decimal digits rather than in binary.
Program instructions and data are kept together in the same memory.
Every component has its own private wires instead of sharing a bus.
questions.why: The von Neumann design places program instructions and data together in the same memory.

questions.prompt: A designer's laptop has 16 GB of RAM and a 1 TB solid-state drive with 600 GB free. With a large photo-editing app and 40 browser tabs open, everything becomes very sluggish. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The drive is nearly full, so new files cannot be saved.
The ALU has run out of registers and must stop between instructions.
The program counter has reached the end of RAM and is restarting.
RAM is full, so the computer is using the much slower drive as overflow space.
questions.why: When RAM fills up, the system spills over onto storage, which is far slower, so performance drops sharply even though the drive has plenty of free space.

questions.prompt: An accountant is editing a spreadsheet. She saved it at 2:00 p.m., kept making changes, and at 2:30 p.m. a power cut shuts the computer off. When power returns, what will she find, and why?
choices: All changes up to 2:30 p.m. survive, because the CPU's registers keep their contents.
All changes survive, because cache copies are written back automatically after power returns.
The whole file is gone, because storage is wiped whenever power is lost.
The 2:00 p.m. version is on the drive, but the later changes are lost because they were only in RAM.
questions.why: RAM loses its contents when power goes off, while storage keeps data permanently, so only the saved version survives.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how a CPU, RAM, storage and the bus work together when a program runs, and name one tradeoff that forces computers to use several layers of memory instead of one.
lessons.modelAnswer: When you launch a program, its instructions and data are copied from storage, which is permanent but slow, into RAM, which is fast but erased when power is lost. The CPU then runs the fetch-decode-execute cycle. It fetches an instruction from the RAM address in its program counter, the control unit decodes it, and the ALU executes it using registers, the CPU's tiny fast slots. Then it moves to the next instruction. The bus carries addresses and data between these parts. The tradeoff is speed against size and cost. Fast memory like registers and cache is expensive and small, while large memory like drives is cheap and slow. So computers stack layers, keeping what is needed soon close to the CPU. The limit is that when RAM runs out, the system leans on storage and slows down badly.
rubricPoints: Names the CPU, RAM, storage, I/O and the bus, with each one's role.
Distinguishes RAM as fast and temporary from storage as slow and permanent.
Describes the fetch-decode-execute cycle, including the program counter.
Mentions registers, cache and the ALU inside or near the CPU.
States the speed versus size or cost tradeoff behind the memory hierarchy.
Notes the slowdown when RAM fills and the system falls back on storage.

suggested.rationale: This introductory objective is about forming a correct mental model of how the parts cooperate, and tracing the cycle and memory hierarchy aloud tests that model better than any current hands-on mission.

lessons.plain: An algorithm is a precise, step-by-step recipe for solving a problem. It takes some starting information, follows clear instructions, and always finishes with an answer. Algorithm design means inventing that recipe. Problem-solving strategies are reusable habits for inventing it, such as breaking a big job into smaller jobs, or ruling out half the possibilities at a time. Think of finding a word in a paper dictionary. You could read every page from the start, or you could open near the middle and keep halving. Both work, but one is far faster. Good design means picking a method that is correct and does not waste effort.
lessons.guessPrompt: A friend picks a secret whole number from 1 to 100 and answers each of your guesses with only 'higher', 'lower' or 'correct'. What guessing method would you use, and roughly how many guesses do you think you would need in the worst case?
lessons.teach:
An algorithm is a finite list of unambiguous steps. It takes an input (the information you start with), produces an output (the answer), and always stops. Algorithm design is choosing those steps. Problem-solving strategies are reusable patterns for finding them. Start by stating the problem precisely: what the input is, what the output is, and what counts as correct. Then use decomposition, which means breaking a big problem into smaller ones you can solve separately.

There are three common strategies. Brute force tries every possibility. It is simple and usually correct, but slow when there are many possibilities. Divide and conquer splits the problem into smaller pieces of the same kind, solves those, and combines the results. A greedy strategy takes the best-looking choice at each step and never looks back. It is fast, but it gives the right answer only for some problems.

Strategy matters because the number of steps grows differently as the input grows. Worked example: decide whether 37 is in the sorted list 3, 8, 15, 22, 37, 41, 50. Brute force, called linear search, checks each item from the left: 3, 8, 15, 22, 37. That is five checks. Divide and conquer, called binary search, checks the middle item first, which is 22. Since 37 is larger, discard 22 and everything left of it, leaving 37, 41, 50. Check that middle, 41. Since 37 is smaller, only 37 remains. Check 37: found in three checks. For a million sorted items, linear search may need a million checks, while binary search needs about twenty, because each check halves what remains.

Before trusting an algorithm, trace it by hand on small inputs. Include edge cases: empty input, a single item, a missing target, and duplicates.

A common mistake is writing code before the problem is precisely stated. Another is using a strategy whose assumptions do not hold, such as binary search on an unsorted list, which can wrongly report an item as missing. In a running system, a poor algorithm can pass tests on small data and then become slow or wrong once real data grows.

questions.prompt: A school library keeps its member card numbers in a sorted list: 4, 11, 18, 26, 39, 52, 60. A clerk uses binary search (divide and conquer: check the middle and throw away the half that cannot contain the target) to decide whether card 18 is in the list. Step 1: Check the middle item, 26. Since 18 is smaller, discard 26 and everything to its right, leaving 4, 11, 18. Step 2: ??? Step 3: Check 18. Found, in three checks. Which choice correctly fills in Step 2?
choices: Check the first item, 4. Since 18 is larger, move one place right and check 11 next.
Check the middle item, 11. Since 18 is larger, discard 11 and everything to its left, leaving 18.
Check the middle item, 11. Since 18 is larger, discard 18 and everything to its right, leaving 11.
Check the last item of the whole list, 60. Since 18 is smaller, discard 60 and keep the rest.
questions.why: Binary search checks the middle of what remains (11), and because 18 is larger it keeps only the part to the right of 11, which is 18.

questions.prompt: A courier plans a route. At every stop, the courier drives to whichever unvisited address is nearest right now and never reconsiders earlier choices. Which problem-solving strategy is this, and what is its main risk?
choices: Divide and conquer. It splits the addresses into halves, so it can lose stops when combining.
Decomposition. It breaks the route into pieces, so it cannot finish until every piece is solved.
Greedy. It is fast, but taking the best-looking choice each time does not always give the best overall route.
Brute force. It tries every possible route, so it is slow when there are many addresses.
questions.why: Picking the best-looking option at each step without looking back is the greedy strategy, which is fast but gives the right answer only for some problems.

questions.prompt: A clinic stores about 1,000 patient IDs in a sorted list. Using binary search, where each check halves what remains, roughly how many checks are needed at most to decide whether a given ID is present?
choices: About 100, one tenth of the IDs
About 10, because halving 1,000 about ten times leaves one item
About 1,000, one for each ID
About 500, half of the IDs
questions.why: Each check halves the remaining items, and halving 1,000 roughly ten times (1,000, 500, 250, ... down to 1) leaves a single item, so about ten checks are enough.

questions.prompt: A warehouse program runs binary search on the bin numbers 30, 10, 50, 20, 40 looking for bin 20. It checks the middle, 50, sees 20 is smaller, discards 50 and everything to its right, and continues on 30, 10. It then reports that bin 20 is missing, even though it is in the list. What went wrong?
choices: Binary search always fails when the list has an odd number of items, so an even-length list was needed.
The list was not sorted, so binary search's assumption did not hold and it discarded the half that held the target.
The target was a duplicate, and binary search can only find items that appear exactly once.
The program should have used a greedy strategy, because greedy always finds a target faster than binary search.
questions.why: Binary search assumes a sorted list; on an unsorted list it can throw away the half containing the target and wrongly report the item as missing.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would design an algorithm for a new problem, using linear search versus binary search as your example, and name one limit or tradeoff of the faster strategy.
lessons.modelAnswer: First I pin the problem down: what goes in, what must come out, and what counts as correct. Then I break it into smaller steps and pick a strategy. For searching a list, brute force (linear search) checks items one by one. It works on any list, but it can take as many checks as there are items. Divide and conquer (binary search) checks the middle and throws away the half that cannot contain the target, so a million items take about twenty checks. The tradeoff is that binary search only works if the list is already sorted. On unsorted data it can say an item is missing when it is actually there. Sorting first also costs time, so for a tiny list or a one-off search, linear search may be the simpler and safer choice. Either way, I trace the algorithm by hand on edge cases like an empty list or a missing target before coding it.
rubricPoints: Defines an algorithm as finite, unambiguous steps from input to output that always stop.
States the problem precisely and decomposes it before coding.
Contrasts brute force with divide and conquer using search as the example.
Explains why binary search is faster: each check halves the remaining items.
Names a limit, such as binary search requiring sorted data or greedy not always being correct.
Mentions tracing by hand on edge cases to check correctness.

suggested.rationale: This mission has the learner compare search and sorting approaches and pick the right algorithm, which puts the design-strategy tradeoffs from this lesson into practice.

lessons.plain: A programming language is a set of rules for writing instructions that people can read, such as Python, Java or C. A computer's processor cannot read those words. It only understands machine code, which is long strings of numbers. A compiler is a program that translates your human-readable code into machine code before it runs. It works like a translator who converts a whole book into another language before anyone reads it. An interpreter is the other common approach. It works like a live interpreter at a meeting, translating and carrying out each line as it goes.
lessons.guessPrompt: If you wrote a program on a Windows laptop and a compiler turned it into a ready-to-run file, would you expect that exact file to run on a phone with a different kind of processor? Why or why not?
lessons.teach:
A programming language is a formal notation with exact rules. Its syntax is the grammar, meaning which arrangements of symbols are allowed. Its semantics is the meaning, meaning what those arrangements make the computer do. High-level languages hide hardware details so people can write code faster. Machine code is the set of numeric instructions a specific processor family executes directly. A compiler translates a whole source program (the text you wrote) into another form, usually machine code, before the program runs. An interpreter instead reads the source and carries it out step by step. Many languages mix the two. Java and Python first compile to bytecode, a compact intermediate instruction set, and a virtual machine (a program that acts like a processor) then runs that bytecode.

A compiler works in stages. Lexical analysis splits the text into tokens, the smallest meaningful pieces such as names, numbers and operators. Parsing checks the tokens against the grammar and builds a syntax tree, a structure showing how the pieces nest. Semantic analysis checks meaning, such as whether types match. Optimization rewrites the program to be faster without changing its result. Code generation emits the target instructions.

Here is the statement total = 2 + 3 * y, traced through those stages. The lexer produces seven tokens: total, =, 2, +, 3, *, y. The parser applies precedence, the rule that * binds tighter than +. So the tree puts 3 * y underneath the +. Semantic analysis confirms that y is a declared number. Code generation emits instructions in tree order: load y, multiply by 3, add 2, store the result in total.

A common mistake is believing that code which compiles is correct. A compiler catches syntax and type errors. It cannot catch logic errors, such as writing + where you meant -. In a running system those bugs surface only as wrong output or a crash. A second consequence is that native machine code targets one processor and operating system. A compiled file usually has to be rebuilt for each platform it runs on.

questions.prompt: A shop's inventory program contains the statement area = width * 3 + height * 2. A compiler processes it as follows. Lexical analysis produces nine tokens: area, =, width, *, 3, +, height, *, 2. Parsing applies precedence (* binds tighter than +), so the syntax tree puts width * 3 and height * 2 each underneath the +. Semantic analysis confirms that width and height are declared numbers. Missing step: what instructions does code generation emit, following the tree?
choices: Load area, compare it with width, then multiply by 3 and by 2.
Split the statement into tokens again, then check whether width and height are numbers.
Load width, multiply by 3, load height, multiply by 2, add the two products, store the result in area.
Load width, multiply by 3, add height, multiply that total by 2, store the result in area.
questions.why: Because * binds tighter than +, each product sits lower in the tree and is computed first, and only then are the two products added and stored in area.

questions.prompt: A payroll team's program compiles with no errors. But every paycheck is too high, because a programmer typed + where the tax should have been subtracted with -. What best describes this situation?
choices: It is a logic error. The compiler cannot catch it, so it shows up only as wrong output when the program runs.
It is a syntax error, and the compiler should have refused to build the program.
It is a type error that semantic analysis would have flagged before the program ran.
The optimization stage introduced the bug when it rewrote the program.
questions.why: A compiler checks grammar and types, not intent, so a valid but wrong operator is a logic error that appears only as wrong results at run time.

questions.prompt: A developer writes a statement that tries to add a piece of text to a number. Every symbol is arranged in a grammatically allowed way. The compiler still reports an error saying the types do not match. Which compiler stage caught this?
choices: Code generation, because it emits the target instructions.
Semantic analysis, because it checks meaning, such as whether types match.
Lexical analysis, because it splits the text into tokens.
Optimization, because it rewrites the program to run faster.
questions.why: The grammar was fine, so parsing passed; checking whether the types make sense is the job of semantic analysis.

questions.prompt: A logistics company compiles its Python routing tool once into bytecode and runs that same file on both Windows and Linux servers. A separate tool, written in a language that compiles to native machine code, has to be rebuilt for each server type. Why can the bytecode file be reused?
choices: Bytecode is the numeric instruction set that every processor family executes directly.
Bytecode skips lexical analysis and parsing, so it has no platform details left in it.
Python programs cannot contain errors that depend on the platform, so no rebuild is ever needed.
A virtual machine, which is a program acting like a processor, runs the bytecode on each platform, so the file does not target one specific processor.
questions.why: Bytecode is an intermediate instruction set carried out by a virtual machine on each platform, whereas native machine code targets one processor and operating system and must be rebuilt for each.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how a compiler turns source code into something a processor can run, and name one tradeoff between compiling ahead of time and interpreting.
lessons.modelAnswer: A processor only understands machine code, which is numeric instructions specific to its chip family. A compiler bridges the gap in stages. First it breaks the source text into tokens like names, numbers and operators. Then it parses them against the language's grammar into a syntax tree that captures structure and operator precedence. Next it checks meaning, such as types. Finally it optimizes and generates machine code. An interpreter skips the up-front translation and executes the code piece by piece, often via bytecode on a virtual machine. The tradeoff is this: ahead-of-time compiling gives fast execution and catches syntax and type errors before the program runs, but you must rebuild for each processor and operating system. Interpreting is more portable and quicker to try out, but usually runs slower. Either way, a successful compile does not prove the logic is right.
rubricPoints: States that processors execute only machine code, so high-level code must be translated.
Names the compiler stages: tokenizing, parsing into a syntax tree, semantic checks, and code generation.
Distinguishes a compiler from an interpreter or a bytecode virtual machine.
Gives a real tradeoff such as speed versus portability, or early error detection versus flexibility.
Notes that compiling successfully does not catch logic errors.

suggested.rationale: This objective is conceptual, and the core skill is clearly explaining the translation pipeline and its tradeoffs. None of the listed missions or engines practices compiler stages directly.

lessons.plain: An operating system (OS) is the program that runs the computer for everyone else. It sits between the hardware (processor, memory, disk, network card) and the applications you use, like a browser or a game. Think of it as a building manager: tenants (applications) do not wire their own electricity or fight over the elevator; they ask the manager, who shares out rooms, power and time fairly and keeps one tenant from wrecking another's flat. When you open an app, the OS loads it into memory, gives it a turn on the processor, and handles every request it makes to read a file or draw on the screen.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your laptop has one processor, yet music plays, a download continues and you type in a document all at the same moment. How do you think the computer manages to run all three at once?
lessons.teach:
An operating system is the core software that manages hardware and offers shared services to applications. Its central part, the kernel, runs with full hardware privileges (kernel mode). Applications run in user mode, where they cannot touch hardware directly.

When you launch a program, the OS creates a process: a running instance of that program with its own private memory space, open files and an identity number (process ID). A process may contain several threads, which are separate paths of execution sharing that process's memory. The scheduler is the part of the kernel that decides which thread uses the processor next. It gives each one a short time slice, a few milliseconds, then switches. Saving one thread's state and loading another's is called a context switch. Switching happens so fast that programs appear to run simultaneously.

Because applications cannot reach hardware themselves, they make system calls, which are formal requests to the kernel such as open a file, read bytes, or send data. Virtual memory gives each process the illusion of its own private memory; the OS maps those addresses to real RAM and blocks a process from reading another's memory.

Worked example: a text editor saves a file. First, the editor, in user mode, issues a write system call. Second, the processor switches to kernel mode. Third, the kernel checks the file permissions. Fourth, the kernel passes the data to the disk driver, which is code that speaks to that specific device. Fifth, the kernel returns success and control goes back to the editor in user mode.

A common mistake is thinking a frozen app means the computer is frozen. Usually only that process is stuck; the scheduler keeps running everything else, which is why you can still open a task manager and end it.

In a running system, one process stuck in a tight loop can still consume a whole processor core and slow its neighbours, so engineers watch per-process usage and stop misbehaving processes deliberately.

questions.prompt: A library's self-checkout kiosk runs one program with two threads: one reads barcode scans, the other redraws the screen. The kiosk has a single processor core, and the scheduler gives each thread a 5 ms time slice. Step 1: The scanning thread runs for its 5 ms and stores the scanned book number in the program's memory. Step 2: ??? Step 3: The display thread runs for its 5 ms and reads the book number from that same process memory to show it on screen. Step 4: The cycle repeats every few milliseconds, so to the borrower the scanning and the display seem to happen at the same time. Which choice correctly fills in Step 2?
choices: The scanning thread keeps the processor until all of its scanning work is finished, and only then can the display thread start.
The display thread switches into kernel mode so that it can draw directly on the screen hardware.
The OS creates a new process for the display thread, with its own private memory and process ID.
The scheduler performs a context switch: it saves the scanning thread's state and loads the display thread's state.
questions.why: When a time slice ends, the scheduler saves the running thread's state and loads the next thread's state, which is called a context switch, and the display thread stays inside the same process and shares its memory.

questions.prompt: A photo-editing program is running as one process with three threads: one applies a filter, one saves a backup, and one responds to mouse clicks. Which statement about these threads is correct?
choices: The threads run in kernel mode so that they can reach the disk and mouse directly.
Each thread has its own private memory space and its own process ID.
Only one of the threads can ever run, because a process can hold just one thread at a time.
The threads are separate paths of execution that share the photo editor's process memory.
questions.why: Threads are separate paths of execution inside one process, and they share that process's memory, while the process as a whole has a single private memory space and process ID.

questions.prompt: A budgeting app running in user mode needs to read a settings file stored on the laptop's drive. How does it get the file's contents?
choices: It reads the drive's hardware directly, because it is the program that owns the file.
It waits for the scheduler to give it a longer time slice so that it can reach the disk.
It reads the settings out of another running process's memory, because virtual memory shares memory between apps.
It makes a system call asking the kernel to open and read the file, and the kernel does the hardware work.
questions.why: User-mode applications cannot touch hardware, so they make system calls, which are formal requests to the kernel to do things such as open a file and read bytes.

questions.prompt: On a shared office server, a video-conversion program stops responding, and one processor core shows 100% usage from that program. The other users' programs are slower but still working, and the administrator can still open a task manager. What is the best explanation and response?
choices: The stuck program has switched the processor into kernel mode permanently, so the other programs can no longer make system calls.
The conversion program is reading the other users' memory, so their programs must be closed first.
The whole operating system has frozen, so the only fix is to restart the server.
Only the conversion process is likely stuck, probably in a tight loop. The scheduler is still running everything else, so the administrator should end that one process.
questions.why: A frozen app usually means only that process is stuck, and since the scheduler keeps running other processes, the administrator can deliberately stop the misbehaving process that is using up a core.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how an operating system lets several applications share one computer safely, using the words process, scheduler and system call, and name one cost or limit of this design.
lessons.modelAnswer: The operating system's kernel owns the hardware, and applications run in a restricted user mode. Each running program becomes a process with its own private virtual memory, so one app cannot read or corrupt another's data. The scheduler gives each process's threads short turns on the processor and switches between them quickly, which makes them look simultaneous. When an app needs hardware, for example to write a file or send network data, it makes a system call, and the kernel checks permissions and does the work through a device driver. The tradeoff is overhead: every system call and every context switch costs time, because the processor must change modes and save and restore state. Also, time sharing is not magic capacity. If one process spins in a loop, it still takes real processor time and can slow everyone else.
rubricPoints: The kernel runs privileged while applications run in restricted user mode.
A process is a running program with its own isolated memory.
The scheduler time-slices the processor and context-switches between threads.
Applications reach hardware only through system calls that the kernel checks.
It names a cost, such as switching overhead or one runaway process starving others.

suggested.rationale: Finding and properly stopping a CPU-burning process makes the learner see processes, process IDs and scheduling as they actually behave on a real OS.

lessons.plain: Networking is how computers send messages to each other, and a database is an organized place where a program stores and finds information. Picture a library that answers questions by mail. Your letter needs an address, it may travel in several envelopes that are reassembled on arrival, and the librarian looks the answer up in a well-labeled card catalogue rather than searching every shelf. Networks handle the addressing and delivery. Databases handle the neat storage and quick lookup. Almost every app you use, from a weather app to online banking, combines both: it asks a distant computer a question over a network, and that computer looks up the answer in a database.
lessons.guessPrompt: When you type a website name like example.com into a browser, your computer actually needs a numeric address to reach it. Where do you think it gets that number from?
lessons.teach:
A network is a set of computers connected so they can exchange data. A protocol is an agreed set of rules for that exchange, so both sides understand each other. An IP address (Internet Protocol address) is the numeric label that identifies a machine on a network, much like a street address. Data travels in packets, small chunks that each carry a destination address and may take different routes. TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) numbers the packets, puts them back in order, and asks for any lost ones again, so the receiver gets a complete message. DNS (Domain Name System) is a directory that turns a readable name into an IP address. In the client-server model, a client is the program that asks, and a server is the program that answers.

A database is an organized collection of data managed by software called a DBMS (database management system). A relational database stores data in tables. Each table has columns, which are named fields such as name or email, and rows, which are individual records. A primary key is a column whose value is unique for every row, so each record can be found exactly. SQL (Structured Query Language) is the language used to ask a relational database questions.

Here is a worked example. You open a store's page to view order 42. First, your browser, the client, asks DNS for the store's IP address. Second, it opens a TCP connection to that address and sends the request in packets. Third, the web server receives the request and sends the database the query SELECT * FROM orders WHERE order_id = 42. Fourth, the database uses the primary key to find that one row. Fifth, the server sends the result back in packets, and TCP reassembles them in your browser.

A common mistake is thinking a name like example.com is the address itself. If DNS fails, the server can be running perfectly well and still be unreachable by name. Likewise, a table without a unique primary key can hold duplicate records, and then updates may change the wrong row or miss some rows.

questions.prompt: A clinic's scheduling app on a nurse's tablet needs today's appointment list from a server named clinic-schedule.org. Step 1: The app, acting as the client, asks DNS for the server's IP address and gets back 10.4.8.21. Step 2: The app opens a TCP connection to 10.4.8.21 and sends its request in packets. Step 3: The server queries the appointments table for the row whose primary key, appt_id, is 3107. Step 4: The server sends the result back split into 6 packets. Packets 2, 1, 4, 6 and 5 arrive in that order, and packet 3 is lost along the way. Step 5: ______. Step 6: The tablet shows the complete appointment record in the right order. What belongs in Step 5?
choices: The app shows the five packets that arrived, because each one already carries its own destination address.
The server looks up the tablet's name in DNS again so that it can resend the whole message by a new route.
DNS sees that packet 3 is missing and sends it again, then hands the packets to the app.
TCP puts the received packets back in number order and asks for the missing packet 3 to be sent again.
questions.why: TCP is the protocol that numbers packets, reorders them on arrival, and requests any lost ones again, so the receiver ends up with a complete message.

questions.prompt: A city library keeps a relational database table called members with these columns: member_id, last_name, home_branch and join_year. Two members can share a last name, many members use the same branch, and many joined in the same year. Each member_id is assigned once and never reused. Which column should be the primary key?
choices: last_name, because it identifies each person by name
join_year, because the values are numbers and can be sorted
member_id, because its value is different for every row
home_branch, because every member has one
questions.why: A primary key must hold a unique value in every row so each record can be found exactly, and only member_id guarantees that.

questions.prompt: Members of a gym can't load the booking site by typing gymbook.net into their browsers. A technician confirms that the web server is running normally. When she types the server's numeric IP address directly into a browser, the site loads fine. What is the most likely cause?
choices: TCP is reassembling the packets out of order
The database table is missing a primary key
DNS is failing to turn the name gymbook.net into the IP address
The web server has crashed and has to be restarted
questions.why: The server can be reached by its IP address but not by its name, so the failing step is DNS, the directory that translates names into IP addresses.

questions.prompt: A warehouse keeps an inventory table with no unique primary key. By accident, it now holds two rows that both have item_id 88. One row says 40 units and the other says 12 units. A worker sends an update to set the quantity for item_id 88 to 30. What problem can this cause?
choices: The update may change the wrong row or both rows, so the stock count can no longer be trusted
The database will refuse to store any new rows until the network is restarted
DNS will translate item_id 88 into the wrong IP address
Nothing goes wrong, because the database automatically merges rows that share an item_id
questions.why: Without a unique primary key, duplicate records can exist, and an update can then change the wrong row or affect more rows than intended.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what happens, step by step, when an app on a phone shows a user their account balance, covering both the network side and the database side. Name one limit or tradeoff, such as what breaks if one piece fails.
lessons.modelAnswer: The phone app is the client. It first uses DNS to turn the bank server's name into an IP address. It then opens a TCP connection and sends its request as packets. TCP keeps the packets in order and resends any that get lost. The server receives the request and runs an SQL query against a relational database, something like asking the accounts table for the row whose primary key matches this user's account number. Because the primary key is unique, the database returns exactly one row. The server sends the balance back over the same connection. The tradeoff is that every step is a separate dependency. If DNS fails, the app cannot find the server even though the server is healthy. TCP's reliability also costs time, because waiting for resent packets adds delay on a poor network.
rubricPoints: Identifies the client and the server and what each one does.
Explains that DNS turns a name into an IP address.
Describes data moving as packets, with TCP keeping them ordered and complete.
Describes a relational table with rows and columns, queried with SQL.
Explains that a primary key uniquely identifies a row.
Names a limit, such as DNS being a point of failure or TCP's reliability adding delay.

suggested.rationale: Tracing one request end to end, from the name lookup through the packets to the database query, is the kind of situation an intro exam asks you to reason through, and it ties the two halves of this objective together.

lessons.plain: Computing ethics is about doing the right thing when you build or use computer systems. It covers three big questions. Who owns digital work, such as code, music or designs? That is intellectual property. Who gets to see and use information about people? That is privacy. Which uses of computers are actually illegal, such as breaking into systems or stealing data? That is computer crime. Think of a shared apartment building. You don't take a neighbor's things just because they are in the hallway. You don't read their mail. You don't enter their unit because the door was left unlocked. The same manners and laws apply online.
lessons.guessPrompt: You find a useful piece of code on a public website with no copyright notice anywhere on the page. Do you think you are automatically free to copy it into your own project? Why or why not?
lessons.teach:
Computing ethics is the study of right and wrong conduct when building and using computer systems. Three areas matter most.

Intellectual property (IP) is legal ownership of creations of the mind. Copyright protects a specific expression, such as source code or a song, and applies automatically once the work is created. A patent protects an invention or method for a limited time, but it must be applied for. A trademark protects a brand name or logo. A trade secret is valuable information a company deliberately keeps private. A license is the owner's written permission stating how others may use a work. Open-source licenses grant broad rights but still attach conditions, such as keeping the author's notice.

Privacy is a person's reasonable control over information about them. Personal data is anything that identifies someone, such as a name, location or email address. Good practice starts with consent, meaning people knowingly agree. It also includes data minimization, meaning you collect only what you need, and protecting whatever you keep.

Computer crime is illegal use of, or attack on, computers. Examples include unauthorized access (entering a system without permission), malware (software built to cause harm), phishing (tricking people into revealing secrets) and data theft.

These rules work because they create shared expectations. Creators keep a reason to create, and users can trust systems with their data. Permission becomes the clear line between legitimate use and intrusion.

Worked example: you want a sorting function from a public code site for a class project. Step 1: it is someone's written expression, so copyright applies even without a notice. Step 2: look for a license file. Step 3: it says MIT license, which allows reuse if you keep the copyright notice. Step 4: copy it, keep the notice, and cite it as your course policy requires. If there were no license, you would have no permission to copy it.

A common mistake is treating publicly reachable as free to take or enter. An unprotected server is not an invitation to log in.

In a running system, careless logging of personal data, such as full card numbers in a log file, turns a small breach into exposure of customers' private information.

questions.prompt: A small bakery chain is adding a loyalty sign-up form to its phone app. The only purpose is to give customers a free pastry after every ten purchases. The developer's draft form asks for name, email, birth date, home address and phone number. Here is the developer's privacy review, with one step missing. Step 1: All five fields are personal data, because each one can identify a specific customer. Step 2: [missing]. Step 3: Add a clear sign-up screen that explains what is collected and why, so customers knowingly agree before anything is saved. Step 4: Store the remaining fields protected, not in plain text that anyone with server access can read. Which choice correctly fills Step 2?
choices: Remove the home address and the birth date, because counting purchases toward a reward does not need them.
Publish the form's source code under an open-source license, so customers can see how their data is handled.
Keep every field, because customers chose to type the data in, so collecting it is automatically fine.
Add a trademark notice to the form so the bakery's brand is protected before data collection begins.
questions.why: Data minimization means collecting only the data the purpose actually needs, and a purchase-count reward does not need a home address or a birth date.

questions.prompt: A game studio has a secret formula for tuning enemy difficulty. It has never published or registered the formula, and only three employees know it. Which form of intellectual property best describes how the studio is protecting it?
choices: Trade secret, because it is valuable information the company deliberately keeps private.
Trademark, because the formula is closely tied to the studio's well-known game titles.
Patent, because any method of doing something is a protected invention once it has been written down.
Copyright, because the formula was protected automatically when the studio created it.
questions.why: A trade secret is valuable information a company keeps private on purpose. A patent would have to be applied for, and a trademark only covers brand names and logos.

questions.prompt: While browsing, a student finds that a city parking office's admin dashboard loads with no password and shows driver records. What is the ethical and legal way to treat this?
choices: Log in briefly to confirm the problem, since a system with no password counts as public.
Do not enter or use the dashboard, and report the exposure, since being reachable does not give permission.
Explore the dashboard freely, because unauthorized access only applies to systems that use passwords.
Download a few records as proof, because the data was already exposed by the city's mistake.
questions.why: Permission is the line between legitimate use and intrusion, so an unprotected system is not an invitation to log in or take data.

questions.prompt: An online pharmacy's developers write each customer's full name, home address and prescription details into a debug log file to make troubleshooting easier. Later, an attacker steals just that log file. What is the most likely consequence?
choices: The theft is not a computer crime, because the attacker took a log file and not the main database.
A small breach becomes exposure of many customers' private information, because personal data was logged carelessly.
Little harm results, because log files hold only technical messages and are not personal data.
The pharmacy's copyright on its code is lost, because the log file was taken without a license.
questions.why: Careless logging of personal data turns the theft of a single file into exposure of customers' private information, and data theft is a computer crime whatever file is taken.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how intellectual property, privacy and computer crime each shape what you may do with code and data you find or collect. Name at least one tradeoff or limit, such as the cost of collecting less data or the limits of what an open-source license allows.
lessons.modelAnswer: Intellectual property means someone usually owns the code or content we find. Copyright applies automatically, so we check for a license before copying anything. Even an open-source license like MIT has conditions, such as keeping the author's notice. Privacy means personal data, like names, emails or locations, belongs to the people it describes. We get consent, collect only what we need, and protect what we store. That means we avoid writing sensitive data into logs. Computer crime covers things like unauthorized access, malware and phishing. Finding an open server does not give us permission to enter it. The tradeoff is that data minimization can limit features or analytics we might want later. License conditions also limit how freely we can reuse or redistribute code. We accept those limits because breaking them risks legal trouble and loss of user trust.
rubricPoints: Defines intellectual property and notes that copyright applies without a notice, so a license is needed to reuse code.
Defines privacy and personal data and mentions consent or data minimization.
Defines computer crime with at least one example such as unauthorized access, malware or phishing.
States that publicly reachable does not mean permitted to use or enter.
Names a real tradeoff or limit, such as lost features from collecting less data or conditions on open-source reuse.

suggested.rationale: This objective is about judging and justifying conduct, so explaining the rules and their tradeoffs in your own words is the core skill to practice.

lessons.plain: A function is a rule that takes an input and gives back exactly one output, like a vending machine where pressing B4 always drops the same snack. A graph is a picture of that rule: every input across the bottom, its output plotted above it. Some functions grow by repeated multiplying (exponential), like money doubling. Others ask the reverse question, how many doublings got us here (logarithmic). Inverse trig functions also run a rule backwards: given a sine value, find the angle that produced it. Running a rule backwards only works cleanly when each output came from just one input.
lessons.guessPrompt: If a population doubles every year starting from 1, it is 8 after some number of years. How many years, and what question are you really asking when you work that out?
lessons.teach:
A function is a rule assigning each input exactly one output. Its domain is the set of allowed inputs; its range is the set of outputs it actually produces. Its graph is all points (x, f(x)). An exponential function has the form f(x) = b^x with base b > 0 and b not equal to 1; its domain is all real numbers, its range is positive numbers only, and when b > 1 it rises faster and faster. The inverse of a function, written f^-1, undoes it: if f(a) = c, then f^-1(c) = a. An inverse exists only when the function is one-to-one, meaning no two inputs share an output. Graphically, an inverse is the original reflected across the line y = x, so domain and range swap.

The logarithm log_b(x) is the inverse of b^x: it answers which exponent turns b into x. Because exponentials only output positives, logarithms only accept positive inputs. Sine is not one-to-one (it repeats), so to build arcsin we restrict sine to angles from -π/2 to π/2, where it is one-to-one. Arcsin therefore returns only angles in that window, called the principal value. Arccos uses 0 to π; arctan uses the open interval -π/2 to π/2.

Worked example: find arcsin(sin(5π/6)). Step 1: sin(5π/6) = 1/2. Step 2: arcsin(1/2) asks which angle between -π/2 and π/2 has sine 1/2. Step 3: that angle is π/6. So the answer is π/6, not 5π/6, because 5π/6 lies outside the restricted window.

Common mistake: assuming arcsin(sin x) = x for every x, or that log(a + b) = log a + log b (the true rule is log(ab) = log a + log b). In running software, math libraries follow these exact rules: an inverse sine call returns only principal values, and taking the log of zero or a negative number yields an error or NaN that can quietly corrupt later results.

questions.prompt: A robotics team's controller computes arccos(cos(-π/3)) to recover a joint angle. You may use these facts: cos(-π/3) = 1/2, cos(π/3) = 1/2, and cos(2π/3) = -1/2. Arccos returns only principal values, which are angles from 0 to π. Step 1: cos(-π/3) = 1/2. Step 2: arccos(1/2) asks which angle between 0 and π has cosine 1/2. Step 3 is missing: which angle does arccos return, and so what is the final answer?
choices: -π/3, because arccos undoes cosine and gives back the original input
2π/3, because arccos shifts the answer into the second quarter of the circle
π/3, because it is the only angle from 0 to π whose cosine is 1/2
5π/3, because that angle also has cosine 1/2 and is positive
questions.why: Arccos only returns angles in the window 0 to π, and π/3 is the one angle in that window with cosine 1/2. The original input -π/3 lies outside the window, so arccos cannot return it.

questions.prompt: A data analyst models growth with h(x) = log_2(x - 3). Which inputs x are in the domain of h, meaning the set of allowed inputs?
choices: All x greater than or equal to 3
All x greater than 3
All x greater than 0
All real numbers
questions.why: A logarithm accepts only positive inputs, so x - 3 must be greater than 0. That means x > 3. At x = 3 the input to the log is 0, which is not allowed.

questions.prompt: The point (2, 9) lies on the graph of g(x) = 3^x. The graph of g^-1, the inverse of g, is g reflected across the line y = x. Which point must lie on the graph of g^-1?
questions.why: An inverse undoes the function. Since g(2) = 9, it follows that g^-1(9) = 2. Reflecting across y = x swaps the coordinates, which gives the point (9, 2).

questions.prompt: A warehouse dashboard takes the natural log of each day's shipment count before averaging the results. On one holiday the count is 0. Following standard math library rules, what is the most likely outcome?
choices: The library automatically skips the 0 and averages the other days
The library treats log(0) as 0, so the average is barely affected
The log call raises an error or returns NaN, and the bad value can quietly corrupt the average
The library returns the smallest positive number, so the average stays accurate
questions.why: Logarithms accept only positive inputs, so log(0) is undefined. Math libraries respond with an error or NaN (not a number), and a NaN carried into an average quietly spoils the result.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how logarithms and inverse trig functions are both inverses, and name the limit that forces us to restrict domains or inputs.
lessons.modelAnswer: Both are functions run backwards. An exponential b^x takes an exponent and gives a result; the logarithm log_b takes that result and gives the exponent back. Sine takes an angle and gives a ratio; arcsin takes the ratio and returns an angle. Graphically, each inverse is the original mirrored across y = x, so inputs and outputs swap roles. The limit is that undoing only works if each output came from a single input. Exponentials already pass that test, but they only produce positive numbers, so a logarithm accepts only positive inputs. Sine repeats, so we restrict it to -π/2 to π/2 before inverting, meaning arcsin always returns an angle in that window. The tradeoff: arcsin(sin x) gives back x only when x is in that window; otherwise you get a different angle with the same sine.
rubricPoints: States that an inverse undoes a function, swapping inputs and outputs.
Links logarithm to exponential as finding the exponent.
Notes an inverse needs a one-to-one function.
Explains sine's domain is restricted to make arcsin, giving principal values.
Mentions logarithms accept only positive inputs.
Describes the inverse graph as a reflection across y = x.

suggested.rationale: No mission or planned engine practices calculus function analysis, and putting inverse relationships and domain restrictions into your own words is the skill that later limits and derivatives rely on.

lessons.plain: A limit asks: as you slide an input closer and closer to some target number, what output value are you heading toward? It cares about the approach, not about what happens exactly at the target. Think of walking toward a door in a hallway: even if the door is locked and you never step through, everyone can see which door you are heading for. Continuity is the friendly case where nothing surprising happens at the target. The function is defined there, the approach settles on one value, and the actual value matches it. You could draw the graph through that point without lifting your pencil.
lessons.guessPrompt: The function f(x) = (x² − 4)/(x − 2) cannot be evaluated at x = 2 because you would divide by zero. If you plug in 1.9, 1.99, 2.01 and 2.1, what single number do the outputs seem to be closing in on?
lessons.teach:
The limit of f(x) as x approaches a, written lim x→a f(x) = L, means f(x) can be made as close to L as you like by taking x close enough to a, but not equal to a. The value f(a) itself plays no part. A one-sided limit looks at the approach from only one direction: from the left (x slightly less than a) or from the right (x slightly greater than a). The ordinary two-sided limit exists only when both one-sided limits exist and are equal.

A function is continuous at a when three things hold. First, f(a) is defined. Second, the limit as x→a exists. Third, that limit equals f(a). If any of the three fails, there is a discontinuity at a. A removable discontinuity is a hole that could be patched by defining or redefining one point. A jump discontinuity is where the left and right limits disagree.

Worked example: take f(x) = (x² − 4)/(x − 2) as x→2. Step 1: substitute directly. You get 0/0, which is called an indeterminate form. It tells you nothing yet. Step 2: factor the top, x² − 4 = (x − 2)(x + 2). Step 3: for x ≠ 2, cancel the common factor, which leaves x + 2. Cancelling is legal because the limit never uses x = 2 itself. Step 4: substitute into x + 2 to get 4. So the limit is 4, but f(2) is undefined. Condition one fails, so f has a removable discontinuity at 2.

A common mistake is to read 0/0 as "the limit does not exist." In fact, 0/0 is a signal to simplify. A related mistake is assuming the limit must equal f(a), which is only true where the function is continuous.

This matters in software too. Code that evaluates a formula exactly at a hole will divide by zero or return a not-a-number value, even though nearby inputs behave perfectly well. Simplifying the expression first avoids that failure.

questions.prompt: A sensor-calibration script uses g(x) = (x² − 25)/(x − 5) for every x ≠ 5. The programmer separately set g(5) = 7. Is g continuous at x = 5? Step 1: substituting x = 5 into the formula gives 0/0, an indeterminate form. Step 2: factor the top as (x − 5)(x + 5). Step 3: for x ≠ 5, cancel the common factor to leave x + 5. Step 4: substitute 5 into x + 5, so the limit as x→5 is 10. Step 5 (missing): compare the limit with g(5) to decide about continuity. Which choice correctly completes Step 5?
choices: The limit must equal the function's value, so the limit is really 7, and g is continuous at 5.
Because g(5) = 7 is defined, all three continuity conditions hold, so g is continuous at 5.
The left and right limits must disagree because the values differ, so g has a jump discontinuity at 5.
g(5) = 7 is defined and the limit 10 exists, but 10 ≠ 7, so condition three fails: a removable discontinuity at 5.
questions.why: Continuity requires the limit to equal the function's value, and here the limit is 10 while g(5) is 7, so g has a removable discontinuity at 5: redefining that one point as 10 would patch it.

questions.prompt: For a function p, the limit as x approaches 4 from the left is 3, and the limit as x approaches 4 from the right is also 3. The programmer also set p(4) = 5. What is the two-sided limit of p(x) as x→4?
choices: It does not exist, because p(4) differs from 3
4, the average of the one-sided limits and p(4)
5, because the limit is the function's value at 4
3, because both one-sided limits exist and equal 3
questions.why: The two-sided limit exists when both one-sided limits exist and agree, and the value p(4) plays no part in the limit.

questions.prompt: A shipping-cost function c(x) approaches 2 as x approaches 1 from the left, and approaches 6 as x approaches 1 from the right. Also, c(1) = 6. Which statement is correct?
choices: c has a removable discontinuity at 1 that can be fixed by redefining c(1) as 2.
The two-sided limit at 1 does not exist, and c has a jump discontinuity at 1.
c is continuous at 1, because c(1) is defined.
The two-sided limit at 1 is 6, because it matches c(1).
questions.why: When the left and right limits disagree, the two-sided limit does not exist, and that kind of break is called a jump discontinuity.

questions.prompt: A pricing service computes h(x) = (x² − 1)/(x − 1), and it returns a not-a-number error when the input is exactly x = 1, even though inputs like 0.999 and 1.001 work fine. What is the correct reading of the situation?
choices: The 0/0 is a signal to simplify: h equals x + 1 for x ≠ 1, so the limit at 1 is 2, and simplifying first avoids the error.
The limit as x→1 must be 0, because the top of the fraction becomes 0 at x = 1.
The 0/0 shows the limit as x→1 does not exist, so the service should reject any input near 1.
Nothing can be learned at x = 1, because a limit always requires the function to be defined at that point.
questions.why: Factoring the top as (x − 1)(x + 1) and cancelling for x ≠ 1 leaves x + 1, so the limit is 2. Using the simplified form avoids dividing by zero at the hole.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what a limit is and what makes a function continuous at a point, using the (x² − 4)/(x − 2) example. Include one limitation of finding a limit just by plugging in numbers close to the target.
lessons.modelAnswer: A limit is the value a function's outputs approach as the input gets close to a target, ignoring what happens exactly at the target. For (x² − 4)/(x − 2) at x = 2, direct substitution gives 0/0. That is indeterminate, not a final answer. Factoring the top as (x − 2)(x + 2) and cancelling, which is fine because we never use x = 2 itself, leaves x + 2. That approaches 4. A function is continuous at a point when it is defined there, the limit exists, and the two match. Here f(2) is undefined, so there is a removable discontinuity, a hole. Plugging in nearby numbers is a useful hint, but it is not proof. It can miss left and right sides that disagree, and rounding errors can mislead you. Algebraic simplification gives the real answer.
rubricPoints: Defines a limit as the value approached near the target, independent of the value at the target.
States the three conditions for continuity.
Treats 0/0 as indeterminate and simplifies by factoring and cancelling.
Concludes the limit is 4 and identifies a removable discontinuity at x = 2.
Names a limitation, such as numeric guessing missing one-sided disagreement or suffering from rounding.

suggested.rationale: No mission or planned engine covers calculus, and limits are mastered by reasoning through exam-style problems like holes, jumps and 0/0 forms, then explaining each step.

lessons.plain: A derivative measures how fast something is changing at one exact moment. Picture a car's speedometer: the trip average tells you distance divided by time, but the speedometer tells you your speed right now. A derivative is that 'right now' rate for any function. On a graph, it is the steepness, or slope, of the curve at a single point. You find it by measuring the slope over a tiny gap and shrinking the gap toward nothing. Because doing that by hand every time is slow, mathematicians proved shortcut rules that give the same answer much faster.
lessons.guessPrompt: The curve y = x² is flat at x = 0 and gets steeper as x grows. Without any formulas, guess: is the curve steeper at x = 3 than at x = 1, and roughly how many times steeper?
lessons.teach:
The derivative of a function f at an input x, written f'(x), is the instantaneous rate of change of f there. On a graph it is the slope of the tangent line, the line that just touches the curve at that point. The formal definition is f'(x) = the limit, as h approaches 0, of [f(x+h) − f(x)] / h. Here h is a small step in the input. The fraction is the difference quotient, which is the slope of a secant line, a line through two nearby points on the curve. A limit is the value an expression settles toward as h shrinks, without h ever equaling zero.

This works because a secant slope is an average over a gap. Shrinking the gap turns that average into the rate at a single point.

Worked example for f(x) = x². Step 1: f(x+h) = x² + 2xh + h². Step 2: subtract f(x) to get 2xh + h². Step 3: divide by h to get 2x + h, which is allowed because h is not zero. Step 4: let h approach 0, which gives 2x. So the slope at x = 3 is 6, and at x = 1 it is 2.

Shortcut rules, each provable from the definition. Constant rule: a constant has derivative 0. Power rule: x^n has derivative n·x^(n−1). Constant multiple rule: (c·f)' = c·f'. Sum rule: (f+g)' = f' + g'. Product rule: (fg)' = f'g + fg'. Quotient rule: (f/g)' = (f'g − fg')/g². Chain rule, for one function inside another, f(g(x)): the derivative is f'(g(x))·g'(x). Standard results: e^x has derivative e^x, ln x has derivative 1/x, sin x has derivative cos x, and cos x has derivative −sin x.

Rules example: y = (3x²+1)^5. The outer function is a fifth power and the inner function is 3x²+1. By the chain rule, y' = 5(3x²+1)^4 · 6x = 30x(3x²+1)^4.

A common mistake is treating the derivative of a product as the product of the derivatives. For x·x = x², that gives 1·1 = 1, but the true derivative is 2x. Another mistake is substituting h = 0 before simplifying, which produces 0/0, an undefined expression.

questions.prompt: A learner finds the derivative of f(x) = x³ straight from the formal definition, f'(x) = the limit as h approaches 0 of [f(x+h) − f(x)] / h. Step 1: expand f(x+h) = x³ + 3x²h + 3xh² + h³. Step 2: subtract f(x) to get 3x²h + 3xh² + h³. Step 3: ??? Step 4: let h approach 0, which leaves 3x², so the slope at x = 2 is 12. Which expression correctly completes Step 3?
choices: Set h = 0 now, giving 0/0, so the derivative is 0
Divide by h to get 3x² + 3xh + h³
Divide by h to get 3x² + 3xh + h², which is allowed because h is not zero
Divide by h to get 3x² + 3xh² + h³
questions.why: Every term of 3x²h + 3xh² + h³ contains h, so dividing each by the nonzero h gives 3x² + 3xh + h², and letting h approach 0 then leaves 3x².

questions.prompt: In the formal definition of the derivative, what does the difference quotient [f(x+h) − f(x)] / h measure before any limit is taken?
choices: Only the change in output, with no division
The slope of a secant line through two nearby points
The exact slope of the tangent line at x
The area under the curve from x to x+h
questions.why: Before h shrinks, the fraction is the rise over the run between the points at x and x+h, which is the slope of a secant line, an average rate over that gap.

questions.prompt: Find the derivative of y = x⁴·cos x.
choices: −4x³ sin x
4x³ sin x
4x³ cos x + x⁴ sin x
4x³ cos x − x⁴ sin x
questions.why: By the product rule, (fg)' = f'g + fg' = 4x³·cos x + x⁴·(−sin x), because the derivative of cos x is −sin x.

questions.prompt: A student wants the slope of f(x) = 5x² at x = 1. They write the difference quotient [5(1+h)² − 5] / h and immediately set h = 0 without simplifying. What happens?
choices: They get 0/0, an undefined expression, so no slope comes out
They get 5, the coefficient of x²
They get 0, because the top becomes zero
They correctly get the slope, 10
questions.why: Setting h = 0 before simplifying makes both the top and the bottom zero, giving the undefined 0/0. The h must be divided out first, which gives 10 + 5h, and only then is h allowed to approach 0, which gives 10.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what the limit definition of the derivative actually computes, why we still need it when shortcut rules exist, and name one limit or tradeoff of relying only on the rules.
lessons.modelAnswer: The derivative is the slope of a curve at a single point, its instantaneous rate of change. The definition takes the slope between x and a nearby point x+h, which is [f(x+h) − f(x)]/h, then lets h shrink toward zero without reaching it. For x², that slope simplifies to 2x + h, which settles to 2x. The rules, such as power, product, quotient and chain, are shortcuts proven from that definition. They are much faster, so we use them day to day. The tradeoff is that the rules are only as trustworthy as your memory of them. A misremembered rule, like assuming a product's derivative is just the product of derivatives, silently gives a wrong answer. The definition is slower, but it is what you fall back on to check a result. It is also what you need when no rule fits, for example at a corner of a graph where the limit doesn't exist.
rubricPoints: States that the derivative is the instantaneous rate of change, or the tangent slope at a point.
Describes the difference quotient with h shrinking toward zero but never equal to it.
Explains that the shortcut rules are derived from the definition and are faster.
Names a tradeoff, such as misapplied rules giving wrong answers or the limit failing to exist.
Uses at least one correct example or rule, such as the product or chain rule.

suggested.rationale: No mission or planned engine practices calculus, and explaining how the limit definition connects to the shortcut rules is the understanding this objective depends on.

lessons.plain: A derivative measures how fast something is changing at one instant, like a car's speedometer reading rather than its average speed for the trip. Applications of derivatives turn that reading into answers. Is a quantity rising or falling? Where does it peak or bottom out? What is the best possible design under some limit? L'Hopital's Rule is one special tool in this kit. Some limits look like a dead end, such as zero divided by zero. The rule settles them by comparing how fast the top and the bottom are changing instead of their raw values. It is like judging a race by the runners' speeds when both are still at the start line.
lessons.guessPrompt: As n gets enormous, which way does the ratio ln(n) / n head: toward 0, toward 1, or upward without limit? Go with your gut about which part grows faster.
lessons.teach:
Applications of derivatives means using the derivative to answer practical questions. The derivative is the instantaneous rate of change of a function, which is also the slope of its graph at a point. A first calculus course leans on three uses.

First, the sign gives the direction. Where f'(x) > 0 the function is increasing, and where f'(x) < 0 it is decreasing.

Second, a critical point is an x where f'(x) = 0 or where f' does not exist. A local maximum (the highest value nearby) or a local minimum (the lowest value nearby) can only happen at a critical point or at an endpoint of the interval. Optimization means finding the best value. You do it by setting the derivative to zero and checking each candidate.

Third, L'Hopital's Rule handles limits of a ratio f(x)/g(x) that land on an indeterminate form. An indeterminate form is a result such as 0/0 or ∞/∞ that tells you nothing by itself. The rule says that in those cases the limit equals the limit of f'(x)/g'(x), as long as that new limit exists. It works because, close to the point, each function behaves like its tangent line. So the ratio of the functions approaches the ratio of their slopes.

Worked example: the limit of ln(n)/n as n grows without bound. Step 1, check the form. ln n goes to ∞ and n goes to ∞, so this is ∞/∞ and the rule applies. Step 2, differentiate the top and the bottom separately. The derivative of ln n is 1/n, and the derivative of n is 1. Step 3, take the new limit: (1/n)/1 = 1/n, which goes to 0. So ln(n)/n goes to 0, meaning n grows far faster than ln n.

A common mistake is applying the quotient rule to f/g. The rule differentiates the numerator and the denominator separately. Another mistake is using the rule when the form is not indeterminate. For (x+1)/x as x goes to 1, direct substitution gives 2, but blindly applying the rule gives 1, which is wrong.

This matters for running systems because it is how growth rates are compared. Since ln(n)/n goes to 0, a logarithmic-cost search eventually beats a linear scan on large enough inputs.

questions.prompt: A student wants the limit of (x^2 - 9)/(x - 3) as x approaches 3. Step 1, check the form: the top gives 9 - 9 = 0 and the bottom gives 3 - 3 = 0, so the form is 0/0 and L'Hopital's Rule applies. Step 2 is missing. Step 3, take the new limit by substituting x = 3 into the new ratio, which gives 6. Which choice correctly completes Step 2?
choices: Differentiate the numerator and the denominator separately: the top becomes 2x and the bottom becomes 1, giving the new ratio 2x/1.
Conclude that 0/0 equals 0, so the limit is 0 and no further work is needed.
Differentiate only the numerator to get 2x, and keep the denominator x - 3 as it is.
Apply the quotient rule to the whole fraction (x^2 - 9)/(x - 3) and use that result as the new expression.
questions.why: L'Hopital's Rule replaces f/g with f'/g', where each part is differentiated on its own, giving 2x/1, which equals 6 at x = 3.

questions.prompt: A function f has derivative f'(x) = 2x - 8. On which set of x-values is f decreasing?
choices: Only at x = 4
questions.why: A function decreases where its derivative is negative, and 2x - 8 < 0 exactly when x < 4.

questions.prompt: A bakery estimates its daily profit as P(x) = -x^2 + 40x - 100 dollars, where x is the number of cakes baked. Its derivative is P'(x) = -2x + 40. Using the critical-point method, how many cakes give the maximum profit?
choices: 40 cakes
20 cakes
300 cakes
10 cakes
questions.why: Setting P'(x) = -2x + 40 equal to 0 gives x = 20, and since the derivative is positive before 20 and negative after, the profit peaks there.

questions.prompt: A learner evaluates the limit of (x + 4)/(x + 2) as x approaches 0. Which statement is correct?
choices: Applying L'Hopital's Rule gives 1/1 = 1, and that is the correct limit.
Direct substitution gives 4/2 = 2, so the form is not indeterminate and the limit is 2; L'Hopital's Rule does not apply.
The form is 0/0, so L'Hopital's Rule must be used, giving 1.
The quotient rule should be applied to the fraction before taking the limit.
questions.why: L'Hopital's Rule only applies to indeterminate forms like 0/0 or ∞/∞, and here substitution gives the definite value 2, so using the rule would wrongly give 1.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how L'Hopital's Rule decides a limit like ln(n)/n, and name one situation where using the rule gives a wrong answer.
lessons.modelAnswer: Some limits of a ratio collapse into 0/0 or ∞/∞. Those forms are indeterminate: the top and bottom are both vanishing or both exploding, so the raw values tell you nothing. L'Hopital's Rule says to look at their rates of change instead. You take the derivative of the top and of the bottom separately, then find the limit of that new ratio. For ln(n)/n, both parts go to infinity. Their derivatives are 1/n and 1, so the new ratio is 1/n, which goes to 0. That means n outgrows ln n. The limit is that the rule only applies to indeterminate forms. Try it on (x+1)/x as x goes to 1 and you get 1, but plugging in directly gives the true answer, 2. Also, you must not use the quotient rule, and if the new limit does not exist, the rule settles nothing.
rubricPoints: Defines an indeterminate form as 0/0 or ∞/∞.
States that the top and bottom are differentiated separately, not with the quotient rule.
Traces an example such as ln(n)/n reaching 0.
Names the limit that the rule only applies to indeterminate forms, with a failing example.
Connects derivatives to rates of change or comparing growth.

suggested.rationale: No mission or planned engine makes the learner do calculus, so working exam-style limit and optimization problems, then reasoning about which step applies, builds the skill best.

lessons.plain: An integral adds up lots of tiny pieces to get a total. Picture a car whose speed changes from moment to moment. If you know its speed at every instant, how far did it travel? You could chop the trip into many short time slices, treat the speed as nearly constant in each slice, multiply speed by time for each, and add the results. Making the slices thinner and thinner gives the exact distance. That exact total is the integral. On a graph, it is the area between the curve and the horizontal axis over a stretch of inputs. Integration undoes differentiation, the way subtraction undoes addition.
lessons.guessPrompt: A tap fills a tank at a steady 4 liters per minute for 5 minutes. How much water went in, and what shape on a graph of 'rate versus time' does that amount match?
lessons.teach:
A definite integral of a function f from a to b, written as the integral from a to b of f(x) dx, is the signed area between the graph of f and the x-axis from x = a to x = b. Signed means area above the axis counts as positive and area below counts as negative. The dx marks x as the variable being sliced.

Why it works: a Riemann sum approximates that area by splitting [a, b] into n strips of width Δx = (b − a)/n, building a rectangle on each strip whose height is f at some point in the strip, and adding the rectangle areas. As n grows, the strips get thinner, the rectangles hug the curve, and the sum approaches one exact number, the definite integral.

An antiderivative of f is any function F whose derivative is f. The indefinite integral, written with no limits, means the whole family F(x) + C, where C is an arbitrary constant, because constants vanish when differentiated. The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus links the two ideas: if F is an antiderivative of a continuous f, then the integral from a to b of f(x) dx equals F(b) − F(a).

Worked example: the integral of 2x from 0 to 3. First estimate. Split into 3 strips of width 1 and use right endpoints: heights 2, 4, 6, so the sum is 12, an overestimate because 2x rises. Now go exact. An antiderivative of 2x is x², since the derivative of x² is 2x. Evaluate 3² − 0² = 9. Check with geometry: the region is a triangle with base 3 and height 6, so its area is 9.

A common mistake is treating the integral as total area when the function dips below the axis. The integral of x from −1 to 1 is 0, because the negative and positive pieces cancel, even though the shaded region is not empty. Another frequent slip is dropping + C from an indefinite integral.

In practice, integrating a rate gives a total. Integrating requests per second over an hour gives total requests, and integrating velocity gives displacement.

questions.prompt: A student is finding the exact value of the integral of 3x² from x = 1 to x = 2 using the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus. Step 1: Recognize that we need an antiderivative F, meaning a function whose derivative is 3x². Step 2: ______. Step 3: Evaluate F(2) − F(1) = 8 − 1 = 7. Which choice correctly fills in Step 2?
choices: Take F(x) = x³, because the derivative of x³ is 3x²
Take F(x) = 3x³, because raising the power by one gives the antiderivative
Take F(x) = 6x, because 6x is what you get from 3x² when you differentiate it
Take F(x) = x³ + C and keep C, so the final answer is 7 + C
questions.why: The derivative of x³ is 3x², so x³ is an antiderivative, and x³ gives F(2) − F(1) = 8 − 1 = 7, which matches Step 3.

questions.prompt: The function f(x) = −2 is a horizontal line lying below the x-axis. What is the definite integral of f from x = 0 to x = 4?
choices: 0, because a flat line encloses no area
−8, because area below the axis counts as negative
−2, because that is the height of the function
8, because the shaded rectangle has area 4 times 2
questions.why: The integral is signed area, and the rectangle with width 4 and height 2 lies below the axis, so it counts as −8.

questions.prompt: Water flows into a tank at a rate of r(t) = 3t² liters per minute, where t is in minutes. Using the idea that integrating a rate gives a total, how much water enters between t = 0 and t = 2?
choices: 12 liters, the flow rate at t = 2
4 liters, from t² evaluated as 2² − 0²
24 liters, from 6t evaluated at t = 2 and doubled
8 liters, from t³ evaluated as 2³ − 0³
questions.why: An antiderivative of 3t² is t³, so the total is 2³ − 0³ = 8 liters.

questions.prompt: You estimate the integral of f(x) = x² from 0 to 2 with a Riemann sum. You use 2 strips and take each rectangle's height from the right endpoint of its strip. What is the sum, and is it an overestimate or an underestimate of the true integral?
choices: 2.5, an overestimate, because each strip has width 0.5
5, an overestimate, because x² rises across [0, 2]
5, an underestimate, because the rectangles stay under the curve
1, an underestimate, because the heights are 0 and 1
