questions.prompt: A warehouse system follows the rule: 'If a package weighs more than 30 kg, then it is sent to the heavy-goods dock.' Treating this rule as a conditional statement, which observation shows the rule was broken (the conditional is false)?
choices: A 12 kg package is sent to the regular dock.
A 45 kg package is sent to the heavy-goods dock.
A 45 kg package is sent to the regular dock instead of the heavy-goods dock.
A 12 kg package is sent to the heavy-goods dock.
questions.why: A conditional is false only when the hypothesis is true and the conclusion is false: here the package weighs more than 30 kg but is not sent to the heavy-goods dock.

questions.prompt: A city traffic system uses the rule: 'If the river gauge reads above 6 meters, then the riverside road is closed.' Which statement is guaranteed to have the same truth value as this rule?
choices: The river gauge reads above 6 meters and the riverside road is closed.
If the riverside road is not closed, then the river gauge does not read above 6 meters.
If the riverside road is closed, then the river gauge reads above 6 meters.
If the river gauge does not read above 6 meters, then the riverside road is open.
questions.why: This is the contrapositive ('if not Q then not P'), which always has the same truth value as the original conditional, unlike the converse in the first choice.

questions.prompt: A developer claims: 'For every positive integer n, the number n squared + n + 11 is prime.' She tests n = 1, 2, 3 and 4, gets 13, 17, 23 and 31 (all prime), and writes 'proved' in her notes. Which assessment is correct?
choices: This is a valid proof, because four consecutive cases rule out any pattern breaking later.
This is a proof by contrapositive, because she checked that non-prime results never appeared.
This is not a proof: examples can only disprove an 'every' claim, so she still needs a general argument or a counterexample.
This is a proof by contradiction, because she assumed the claim and found no impossibility.
questions.why: Checking a handful of cases never proves a universal claim; only a general argument can prove it, while a single failing case (a counterexample) would disprove it.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how a direct proof, a proof by contrapositive, and a proof by contradiction differ, and why testing several examples is not a proof. Name one limit or tradeoff of these techniques.
lessons.modelAnswer: A proof shows a claim is true in every case by chaining justified steps. For 'if P then Q,' a direct proof assumes P and works forward until Q appears. A proof by contrapositive instead assumes Q is false and shows P must be false; that works because 'if not Q then not P' always has the same truth value as the original. A proof by contradiction assumes the whole claim is false and reasons to something impossible, so the assumption must be wrong. Testing examples only shows the claim holds for those cases; there could be an untested case that fails, though a single failing case, a counterexample, does disprove an 'every' claim. The tradeoff is that the technique you pick changes how easy the proof is, and none of them tells you which one will work; you often try several. Also, the converse is never proved for free.
rubricPoints: Defines a proof as justified steps covering every case, not sample cases.
Describes direct proof as assuming the hypothesis and deriving the conclusion.
Explains contrapositive is equivalent to the original but the converse is not.
Describes proof by contradiction as assuming the claim false and reaching an impossibility.
Notes a single counterexample disproves a universal claim while examples cannot prove one.
Names a limit, such as choosing a technique being trial and error.

suggested.rationale: No mission or planned engine exercises formal proofs, and the core skill is articulating why each reasoning step is valid, which explaining it back trains directly.

lessons.plain: A set is simply a collection of distinct things, where only membership matters: order does not count and duplicates do not count. Think of a guest list. Writing a name twice does not add a second guest, and shuffling the list does not change who is invited. Set theory is the vocabulary for comparing and combining such collections. It covers who is on both lists, who is on either list, and who is on one list but not the other. Nearly all later mathematics and computer science, including databases, logic and probability, is described in this language, so it is the first thing a discrete math course builds.
lessons.guessPrompt: Club A has members {Ana, Ben, Cy} and Club B has members {Ben, Cy, Dee}. How many different people belong to at least one of the two clubs, and how many belong to both?
lessons.teach:
A set is an unordered collection of distinct objects called elements. We write it with braces, so {1, 2, 3} equals {3, 1, 2} and also {1, 1, 2, 3}. Writing x ∈ A means x is an element of A, and x ∉ A means it is not. The empty set, written ∅ or {}, has no elements. The universal set U is every object under discussion. The cardinality |A| is the number of elements in A.

A is a subset of B, written A ⊆ B, when every element of A is also in B. Two sets are equal exactly when each is a subset of the other. The power set P(A) is the set of all subsets of A. If |A| = n, then |P(A)| = 2^n, because each element is either in or out of a subset.

There are four main operations. The union A ∪ B holds elements in A or B or both. The intersection A ∩ B holds elements in both. The difference A − B holds elements in A but not B. The complement of A holds elements of U not in A. The Cartesian product A × B is the set of all ordered pairs (a, b) with a in A and b in B.

Worked example: let U = {1,…,6}, A = {1,2,3,4} and B = {3,4,5}. Step 1: A ∪ B = {1,2,3,4,5}. Step 2: A ∩ B = {3,4}. Step 3: A − B = {1,2}. Step 4: the complement of A is {5,6}. Step 5: check the counting rule |A ∪ B| = |A| + |B| − |A ∩ B|. That gives 4 + 3 − 2 = 5, which matches step 1. You subtract the overlap because those elements were counted twice.

A common mistake is confusing ∈ with ⊆, or ∅ with {∅}. The number 3 is an element of {3}, but {3} is a subset of it. The set ∅ has zero elements, while {∅} has one element. Mixing these up costs points on proofs and leads to wrong counts. In code it also produces bugs, such as treating a list holding an empty list as if it were empty.

questions.prompt: A school tracks two clubs. Chess club C = {Ana, Ben, Cal, Dee, Eli}, so |C| = 5. Robotics club R = {Cal, Dee, Fay}, so |R| = 3. Step 1: the union C ∪ R, meaning students in either club or both, is {Ana, Ben, Cal, Dee, Eli, Fay}, so |C ∪ R| = 6. Step 2: the intersection C ∩ R, meaning students in both clubs, is ____. Step 3: check with the counting rule |C ∪ R| = |C| + |R| − |C ∩ R|, which gives 5 + 3 − 2 = 6. This matches Step 1. Which set belongs in Step 2?
choices: {Ana, Ben, Cal, Dee, Eli, Fay}
{Fay}
{Ana, Ben, Eli}
{Cal, Dee}
questions.why: Cal and Dee are the only students who appear in both C and R, which gives the overlap of 2 used in Step 3.

questions.prompt: A set S has 5 elements. How many elements does its power set P(S) have? The power set is the set of all subsets of S.
questions.why: Each of the 5 elements is either in or out of a given subset, so there are 2^5 = 32 subsets.

questions.prompt: Which statement about the empty set ∅ and the set {∅} is true? The empty set is the set with no elements.
choices: |∅| = 1, because ∅ counts as one element
{∅} = ∅, because both of them describe nothing
|{∅}| = 0, because the set contains only an empty set
questions.why: {∅} is a set with exactly one element, and that element is ∅. So ∅ is an element of {∅}, and the cardinality of {∅} is 1.

questions.prompt: Let X = {p, q} and Y = {1, 2, 3}. The Cartesian product X × Y is the set of all ordered pairs (x, y) with x in X and y in Y. Which statement is true?
choices: {p, 1} is an element of X × Y
questions.why: In the pair (q, 3), the first entry q is in X and the second entry 3 is in Y. That is exactly the form an element of X × Y must have.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what a set is and how union, intersection, difference and subset differ. Then explain why |A ∪ B| is not simply |A| + |B|, and name one limit of describing data as a set.
lessons.modelAnswer: A set is a collection of distinct elements where order and repetition are ignored. You only ask whether something is in it or not. The union gathers everything in either set. The intersection keeps only what both share. The difference A − B keeps what is in A but not in B. A is a subset of B if everything in A also appears in B. A subset is a relationship between two sets, which is different from one object being an element of a set. You cannot just add |A| and |B| to count the union, because elements in both sets would be counted twice. So you subtract |A ∩ B| once. One limit is that sets throw away order and duplicates. If you care about sequence or how many times something happened, like repeated log entries, a set loses that information. You would need a list or a count instead.
rubricPoints: Defines a set as an unordered collection of distinct elements.
Correctly distinguishes union, intersection and difference.
Distinguishes being an element (∈) from being a subset (⊆).
Explains subtracting the intersection to avoid double counting in a union.
Names a limit such as sets losing order and duplicate information.

suggested.rationale: Set theory is mastered by working exam-style problems that combine operations, counting and the element-versus-subset distinction, and no current mission or planned engine drills those directly.

lessons.plain: Boolean algebra is the arithmetic of true and false. Instead of numbers like 7 or 42, every variable can only be 1 (true, on) or 0 (false, off). Instead of plus and times, you combine them with AND (both must be true), OR (at least one is true), and NOT (flip it). Think of light switches wired to a lamp: two switches in a row means both must be on, side by side means either one works. Boolean algebra gives you rules for rewriting these combinations into simpler, equivalent forms, which is exactly what computer chips and program conditions depend on.
lessons.guessPrompt: A door unlocks if you have a badge OR a key. In plain words, what does 'NOT (badge OR key)' mean, and is it the same as 'no badge AND no key' or 'no badge OR no key'?
lessons.teach:
Boolean algebra is a system where variables take only the values 0 (false) and 1 (true), combined by three operations. AND, written xy or x·y, gives 1 only when both inputs are 1. OR, written x + y, gives 1 when at least one input is 1. NOT, the complement, written x', flips 0 to 1 and 1 to 0. A truth table lists the output for every combination of inputs; two expressions are equivalent when their truth tables match.

It works because a handful of laws always hold, so you can rewrite expressions the way you rearrange ordinary algebra. Identity: x + 0 = x and x·1 = x. Complement: x + x' = 1 and x·x' = 0. Idempotent: x + x = x. Distributive: x(y + z) = xy + xz. Absorption: x + xy = x. De Morgan's laws: (x + y)' = x'y' and (xy)' = x' + y'.

Worked example: simplify xy + xy'. Step 1, factor out x using the distributive law: x(y + y'). Step 2, the complement law says y + y' = 1, giving x·1. Step 3, the identity law gives x. Check with a truth table: when x = 1 the expression is 1 whichever value y has, and when x = 0 it is 0. The y variable never mattered.

A common mistake is pushing NOT through a product without flipping the operation, writing (xy)' = x'y'. Test x = 1, y = 0: xy = 0, so (xy)' = 1, but x'y' = 0·1 = 0. De Morgan says the AND must become OR: x' + y'. Another slip is treating 1 + 1 as 2; in Boolean algebra 1 + 1 = 1.

The consequence in a running system is real. Each operation corresponds to a logic gate in a circuit, so a simpler expression means fewer gates, less power and less delay. In software, a wrongly negated condition such as a mis-applied De Morgan in an if statement silently lets the wrong users through or blocks the right ones.

questions.prompt: A warehouse door controller unlocks when signal U = m + mn + m·m' is 1. Here m means a manager badge was scanned and n means it is night shift. An engineer simplifies U in three steps. Step 1: by the absorption law, m + mn = m, so U = m + m·m'. Step 2: ???. Step 3: by the identity law, m + 0 = m, so U = m. Which statement correctly fills in Step 2?
choices: By De Morgan's law, m·m' = m' + m, so U = m + m' + m.
By the complement law, m·m' = 1, so U = m + 1.
By the complement law, m·m' = 0, so U = m + 0.
By the idempotent law, m·m' = m, so U = m + m.
questions.why: The complement law says a variable ANDed with its own complement is always 0, which gives m + 0, the form Step 3 needs.

questions.prompt: A sprinkler system's alarm output is (x + y)·z'. Here x = 1 (smoke detected), y = 1 (heat detected) and z = 0 (manual override off). What is the output?
choices: It cannot be determined without a truth table
questions.why: Boolean OR gives x + y = 1 + 1 = 1, not 2. NOT flips z = 0 to z' = 1, and 1·1 = 1.

questions.prompt: A library app shows a warning when the condition NOT (isMember OR hasGuestPass) is true. A developer wants to rewrite it without the outer NOT. Which version is equivalent?
choices: isMember AND hasGuestPass
(NOT isMember) OR (NOT hasGuestPass)
isMember OR hasGuestPass
(NOT isMember) AND (NOT hasGuestPass)
questions.why: De Morgan's law says (x + y)' = x'y', so pushing NOT through an OR turns each term into its complement and turns the OR into an AND.

questions.prompt: A student claims that (a + b)' = a' + b'. Which single input assignment proves the claim wrong?
choices: None, because the two expressions are equivalent
questions.why: With a = 1 and b = 0, a + b = 1, so (a + b)' = 0, but a' + b' = 0 + 1 = 1. The two outputs differ, so the expressions are not equivalent.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what Boolean algebra is and how you would simplify an expression like xy + xy', then name one limit or tradeoff of simplifying by hand with algebraic laws.
lessons.modelAnswer: Boolean algebra works on values that are only 0 or 1, using AND (both true), OR (at least one true) and NOT (flip). It has laws like identity, complement, distributive, absorption and De Morgan that let you replace an expression with a simpler one that has the same truth table. For xy + xy', I factor out x to get x(y + y'). Since y + y' is always 1, that becomes x·1, which is just x, so y was irrelevant. I can confirm by checking the truth table. The tradeoff is that hand simplification depends on spotting the right law in the right order, and it gets error-prone with many variables. A truth table is a reliable check, but it doubles in size with each added variable. The classic trap is De Morgan: NOT of an AND becomes an OR of the NOTs, not an AND.
rubricPoints: States that Boolean variables take only the values 0 and 1.
Defines AND, OR and NOT correctly.
Simplifies xy + xy' to x using the distributive, complement and identity laws.
Mentions verifying equivalence with a truth table.
Applies or warns about De Morgan's law correctly, flipping AND and OR under negation.
Names a limit, such as hand simplification getting error-prone or truth tables growing exponentially with more variables.

suggested.rationale: Simplifying expressions and checking them against truth tables is best practiced by reasoning through exam-style problems, and no listed mission or planned engine drills Boolean simplification directly.

lessons.plain: A function is a rule that takes each input from one collection and gives back exactly one output. Think of a coat check: every coat handed in gets one ticket, never two, and never none. A sequence is just a function whose inputs are the counting numbers 0, 1, 2, 3 and so on, so it produces an ordered list like 1, 3, 5, 7. A relation is looser. It simply records which pairs of things are connected, such as "is a sibling of" or "is less than or equal to," and one item may be connected to many others or to none.
lessons.guessPrompt: A coat check hands out numbered tickets. If two different coats were accidentally given the same ticket number, what problem would appear when people come back to collect their coats?
lessons.teach:
A function f from a set A to a set B assigns every element of A exactly one element of B. A is the domain (allowed inputs), B is the codomain (where outputs are allowed to land), and the range is the set of outputs actually produced. A function is one-to-one (injective) if different inputs always give different outputs. It is onto (surjective) if every element of the codomain is hit by some input. It is a bijection if it is both, which means it can be reversed perfectly.

Worked example: f(x) = 2x + 1 from the integers to the integers. Is it one-to-one? If 2a + 1 = 2b + 1, subtract 1 and divide by 2 to get a = b, so yes. Is it onto? Try to reach 4: 2x + 1 = 4 gives x = 1.5, which is not an integer. Every output is odd, so even numbers are never hit. Not onto, so not a bijection.

A sequence is a function whose domain is the natural numbers; we write a_n for the nth term. It can be given by a closed form, like a_n = 2n + 1, or by a recurrence, which defines each term from earlier ones: a_0 = 1, a_n = a_(n-1) + 2. Tracing the recurrence: a_1 = 3, a_2 = 5, a_3 = 7, matching 2(3) + 1 = 7.

A relation from A to B is any set of ordered pairs (a, b), meaning a is related to b. A relation on one set is reflexive if every element relates to itself, symmetric if (a, b) always implies (b, a), and transitive if (a, b) and (b, c) imply (a, c). One that has all three is an equivalence relation. The relation ≤ on numbers is reflexive and transitive but not symmetric, since 2 ≤ 5 but 5 is not ≤ 2.

A common mistake is confusing codomain with range and calling a function onto just because every output it produces lands somewhere sensible. In software, a lookup that is not one-to-one, such as two user IDs mapping to one account, causes collisions and lost data.

questions.prompt: A warehouse labels shelf positions with integers and uses the function g(x) = x - 7 from the integers to the integers to convert old labels to new ones. We want to show that g is a bijection, meaning it is both one-to-one and onto. Step 1 shows g is one-to-one. If g(a) = g(b), then a - 7 = b - 7. Adding 7 to both sides gives a = b, so different inputs always give different outputs. Step 2 shows g is onto. [MISSING STEP] Step 3 concludes that g is both one-to-one and onto, so g is a bijection and every new label can be traced back to exactly one old label. Which choice correctly fills in Step 2?
choices: Take any integer y in the codomain and choose x = y + 7, which is also an integer. Then g(x) = y, so every y is hit.
Solve x - 7 = y to get x = y - 7, which is an integer, so every y is hit.
Check that g(0) = -7 is an integer, so every output lands in the integers and g is onto.
Since g is one-to-one, it must also be onto, so there is nothing more to check.
questions.why: Onto means every element of the codomain is reached. For any integer y, the input y + 7 is an integer and g(y + 7) = (y + 7) - 7 = y, so every y is hit.

questions.prompt: On the set {1, 2, 3}, consider the relation R = {(1,1), (2,2), (3,3), (1,2), (2,1)}. Which description is correct?
choices: R is reflexive, symmetric, and transitive, so it is an equivalence relation.
R is symmetric and transitive but not reflexive.
R is reflexive and symmetric but not transitive.
R is reflexive and transitive but not symmetric.
questions.why: Every element relates to itself, so R is reflexive. The pairs (1,2) and (2,1) both appear, so R is symmetric. Chaining pairs, (1,2) with (2,1) gives (1,1), and (2,1) with (1,2) gives (2,2); both are in R, so R is transitive. Having all three properties makes it an equivalence relation.

questions.prompt: A bacteria-count model uses a recurrence, which defines each term from the one before it: b_0 = 2 and b_n = 3 times b_(n-1). What is b_3?
questions.why: Tracing the recurrence from the start: b_1 = 3 times 2 = 6, then b_2 = 3 times 6 = 18, then b_3 = 3 times 18 = 54.

questions.prompt: A school assigns lockers using a function h from the students {Ana, Ben, Cai} to the lockers {1, 2, 3, 4}. The assignments are h(Ana) = 1, h(Ben) = 2, and h(Cai) = 2. Which statement is true?
choices: h is one-to-one but not onto, because lockers 3 and 4 are unused.
h is not a function, because two students share a locker.
h is onto, because every student gets a locker that exists in the codomain.
h is neither one-to-one nor onto, and its range is {1, 2}.
questions.why: Ben and Cai, two different inputs, give the same output, so h is not one-to-one. Lockers 3 and 4 are never hit, so h is not onto. The outputs actually produced are {1, 2}, so that is the range. Sharing an output does not stop h from being a function, because each student still gets exactly one locker.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate the difference between a function and a relation, and how you would check whether a function is one-to-one and onto. Name one limit, such as why some functions cannot be reversed.
lessons.modelAnswer: A relation is any set of ordered pairs saying which things are connected; one input can link to many outputs or to none. A function is a special relation where every input in the domain gets exactly one output. To check one-to-one, I assume two inputs give the same output and see whether that forces the inputs to be equal; for 2x + 1 it does. To check onto, I pick an arbitrary element of the codomain and try to solve for an input that reaches it; for 2x + 1 on the integers, even numbers can't be reached, so it is not onto. The limit is that only a bijection can be reversed: if two inputs share an output, you can't tell which one you started from, and if some codomain values are missed, the reverse has nothing to send them back to. A sequence is just a function on the natural numbers.
rubricPoints: A function gives each domain element exactly one output, while a relation is any set of ordered pairs.
Distinguishes codomain from range.
Describes how to test one-to-one by assuming equal outputs and deriving equal inputs.
Describes how to test onto by trying to reach an arbitrary codomain element.
States that only a bijection has a perfect reverse, which is the limit or tradeoff.
Identifies a sequence as a function on the natural numbers, given by closed form or recurrence.

suggested.rationale: No listed mission or planned engine exercises these definitions directly, and being able to state and apply the definitions of one-to-one, onto, and relation properties in your own words is the core skill tested in the course.

lessons.plain: A matrix is a rectangular grid of numbers arranged in rows and columns, like a spreadsheet with no labels. Matrices let you store and transform many related numbers at once: a table of distances between cities, or which people know which other people. Algorithmic thinking means writing down a procedure so precise that someone, or a computer, could follow it without guessing, and then asking how much work it takes. Multiplying two matrices is a good first example: it follows a fixed recipe, and counting the steps shows why large grids get expensive quickly.
lessons.guessPrompt: If one grid of numbers has 2 rows and 3 columns, and another has 3 rows and 2 columns, how many rows and columns do you think their product has, and why might the order you multiply them in matter?
lessons.teach:
A matrix is a rectangular array of numbers. Its size, or dimensions, is written rows by columns, so a 2x3 matrix has 2 rows and 3 columns. Each number is an entry, named by its row and column: the entry in row i, column j. Two matrices of the same size are added entry by entry.

Matrix multiplication works differently. To multiply A (m x k) by B (k x n), the number of columns of A must equal the number of rows of B. The result is m x n. Each entry in row i, column j is found by pairing row i of A with column j of B, multiplying matching numbers, and adding the products. This rule is useful because it chains transformations: applying B and then A to data equals applying the single matrix AB.

Worked example: A has rows (1, 2) and (3, 4); B has rows (5, 6) and (7, 8). Row 1 of A with column 1 of B: 1x5 + 2x7 = 19. Row 1 with column 2: 1x6 + 2x8 = 22. Row 2 with column 1: 3x5 + 4x7 = 43. Row 2 with column 2: 3x6 + 4x8 = 50. So AB has rows (19, 22) and (43, 50).

Algorithmic thinking turns this into a precise procedure: for each row i, for each column j, start a sum at zero, and for each position p add A[i][p] times B[p][j]. Three nested loops. For two n x n matrices that is n times n times n, or n cubed, multiplications. Counting steps like this is how you judge an algorithm's cost before running it.

A common mistake is assuming AB equals BA. Try it: BA starts with 5x1 + 6x3 = 23, not 19. Order matters, and sometimes only one order is even allowed by the dimensions. Another mistake is multiplying entry by entry instead of row by column.

In a running program, the cubic cost matters: a 1,000 x 1,000 product needs about a billion multiplications, so doubling the size multiplies the work by eight.

questions.prompt: A small shop tracks two price tables. Matrix C has rows (2, 0) and (1, 3). Matrix D has rows (4, 1) and (2, 5). Both are 2x2, so CD is allowed, and the result is 2x2. Here is the row-by-column work so far. Row 1 of C with column 1 of D: 2x4 + 0x2 = 8. Row 1 of C with column 2 of D: 2x1 + 0x5 = 2. Row 2 of C with column 1 of D: 1x4 + 3x2 = 10. Missing step: row 2 of C with column 2 of D. Which value completes it, so that CD has rows (8, 2) and (10, ?)
choices: 16, from 1x1 + 3x5
17, from pairing row 2 of C with row 2 of D: 1x2 + 3x5
15, because the entry in row 2, column 2 is C's 3 times D's 5
8, from adding the matching entries 3 + 5
questions.why: Row 2 of C is (1, 3) and column 2 of D is (1, 5), so you multiply the matching numbers and add: 1x1 + 3x5 = 16.

questions.prompt: A data team multiplies matrix P, which is 3x4 (3 rows, 4 columns), by matrix Q, which is 4x2. What happens?
choices: The product PQ is 4x4
The product PQ is 2x3
The product PQ is 3x2
The product is not allowed because the two matrices are different sizes
questions.why: P has 4 columns and Q has 4 rows, so PQ is allowed, and the result takes P's row count and Q's column count: 3x2.

questions.prompt: A program multiplies two 200x200 matrices with the three-nested-loop method and takes about 2 seconds. Roughly how long should the same method take for two 400x400 matrices?
choices: About 4 seconds, because the size doubled
About 6 seconds, because there are three loops
About 8 seconds, because the work grows with n squared
About 16 seconds, because the work grows with n cubed
questions.why: The method does n x n x n multiplications, so doubling n multiplies the work by 2 x 2 x 2 = 8, turning 2 seconds into about 16.

questions.prompt: A student has matrix R, which is 2x3, and matrix S, which is 3x2. They compute RS and then say SR must give the same answer. What is actually true?
choices: SR has the same size as RS but may have different entries
SR is 3x3 while RS is 2x2, so they cannot be equal
SR equals RS because multiplication of numbers works in any order
SR is not allowed because the dimensions do not match
questions.why: RS uses R's 2 rows and S's 2 columns to give a 2x2 result, while SR uses S's 3 rows and R's 3 columns to give a 3x3 result, so order matters and the two products cannot be equal.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how to multiply two matrices, why the order of multiplication matters, and what the step count tells you about using this method on very large matrices.
lessons.modelAnswer: A matrix is a grid of numbers described as rows by columns. You can only multiply A times B if A's column count equals B's row count, and the answer takes A's rows and B's columns. Each answer entry comes from one row of A and one column of B: multiply the matching numbers and add them up. For example, row (1, 2) with column (5, 7) gives 1x5 + 2x7 = 19. Order matters: AB and BA usually differ, and one of them may not even be defined. As an algorithm it is three nested loops, so two n x n matrices take about n cubed multiplications. That is the tradeoff: the method is simple and exact, but the work grows fast. Doubling the size makes it roughly eight times slower, so for huge matrices you have to think about cost before you run it.
rubricPoints: Defines a matrix and its dimensions as rows by columns.
States the dimension rule: inner sizes must match and the result takes the outer sizes.
Describes each product entry as a row of the first times a column of the second, summed.
Notes that matrix multiplication is not commutative, so AB generally differs from BA.
Counts the work as about n cubed multiplications for n x n matrices and names that growth as the limit.

suggested.rationale: Counting how work grows with nested loops is the core algorithmic-thinking skill behind the n-cubed cost of matrix multiplication, and this mission makes the learner practise exactly that.

lessons.plain: Mathematical induction is a way to prove that something is true for every whole number without checking each one. You show it works for the first number, then show that whenever it works for one number it must also work for the next. Picture a long line of dominoes: if the first falls and each falling domino knocks over the next, every domino falls. Combinatorics is the math of counting, such as how many ways things can be arranged or chosen, without writing out every possibility. Together they let you reason with confidence about patterns that go on forever.
lessons.guessPrompt: Five people meet and every person shakes hands once with every other person. Without drawing it out, how many handshakes happen in total? Try to find a shortcut rather than counting one by one.
lessons.teach:
Mathematical induction is a proof method for showing that a statement holds for every whole number n from some starting value onward. It has two parts. The base case checks the statement for the first value, usually n = 1. The inductive step assumes the statement is true for some arbitrary n = k, and uses that assumption to prove it for n = k + 1. The assumption is called the inductive hypothesis. It works like dominoes. The base case knocks over the first one. The step guarantees that each falling domino knocks over the next, so none are left standing.

Worked example: prove 1 + 2 + ... + n = n(n+1)/2. Base case: when n = 1, the left side is 1 and the right side is 1·2/2 = 1. They are equal. Inductive step: assume 1 + ... + k = k(k+1)/2. Add (k+1) to both sides. The left side becomes 1 + ... + (k+1). The right side becomes k(k+1)/2 + (k+1) = (k+1)(k+2)/2, which is the formula with n = k+1. The proof is complete.

Combinatorics is the mathematics of counting outcomes without listing them. The product rule says that if one choice has a options and a separate second choice has b options, there are a·b combined outcomes. A permutation is an ordered arrangement. The number of ways to order n distinct items is n!, read "n factorial," which means n·(n−1)·...·1. A combination is an unordered selection. The number of ways to choose k items from n is C(n,k) = n!/(k!(n−k)!). Example: choosing 2 of 4 servers to pair up gives 4!/(2!·2!) = 24/4 = 6. In general, C(n,2) = n(n−1)/2 pairs.

Common mistakes: in induction, skipping the base case, or quietly using the k+1 statement while trying to prove it. In counting, using permutations when order does not matter, which overcounts by a factor of k!.

Counting also predicts how a system grows. If each of n services talks directly to every other service, there are n(n−1)/2 links. With 10 services that is 45 links, and with 100 services it is 4,950, which is why such designs quickly become hard to operate.

questions.prompt: A tutor proves by induction that the sum of the first n odd numbers is n squared: 1 + 3 + 5 + ... + (2n − 1) = n², for every n ≥ 1. Base case: when n = 1, the left side is 1 and the right side is 1² = 1, so they match. Inductive step: assume 1 + 3 + ... + (2k − 1) = k² (the inductive hypothesis). MISSING STEP: add the next odd number to both sides. Then the right side becomes k² + 2k + 1 = (k + 1)², which is the formula for n = k + 1, so the proof is complete. Which term must be added to both sides in the missing step?
choices: (k + 1)², because that is the right side we want to reach
2k − 1, because it is the last term already in the sum
k + 1, because the step moves from k to k + 1
2k + 1, the next odd number after 2k − 1
questions.why: The next term in the pattern is 2(k + 1) − 1 = 2k + 1, and adding it gives k² + 2k + 1 = (k + 1)², the statement for n = k + 1.

questions.prompt: A hospital IT team must pick 3 of its 6 technicians to form a review committee. Every committee member has the same role, so the order of picking does not matter. How many different committees are possible?
questions.why: Order does not matter, so this is a combination: C(6,3) = 6!/(3!·3!) = 720/36 = 20, while 120 is the ordered count that overcounts by 3! = 6.

questions.prompt: A student wants to prove a formula holds for all n ≥ 1. They show correctly that if it is true for n = k, it is also true for n = k + 1. They never test n = 1, and it turns out the formula is false at n = 1. What is the status of the proof?
choices: It is valid, as long as the formula is checked at n = k + 1
It is invalid, because without a true base case nothing starts the chain
It only needs the step repeated once more for n = k + 2
It is valid, because the inductive step is the part that covers all values
questions.why: Induction needs both parts: the step only passes truth along, so if the first case is false, no value is ever proven, like dominoes with none knocked over first.

questions.prompt: A logistics company has 30 regional warehouses, and each warehouse keeps a direct network link to every other warehouse. How many direct links are there in total?
questions.why: Each link joins an unordered pair, so the count is C(30,2) = 30·29/2 = 435, while 870 counts each link twice by treating the pair as ordered.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how a proof by induction works and how to tell whether a counting problem needs permutations or combinations. Name one limit or pitfall of each.
lessons.modelAnswer:
Induction proves a statement for all whole numbers in two steps. First, the base case shows it is true for the starting value, like n = 1. Second, the inductive step assumes it is true for some k and uses that assumption to prove it for k + 1. Like dominoes, the first one falls and each one knocks over the next, so the statement holds for every n. One limit is that without the base case the proof proves nothing. Induction also only covers values from the base case onward.

For counting, ask whether order matters. If it does, as with ranking or scheduling, use permutations, for example n! orderings. If it doesn't, as with picking a team, use combinations, C(n,k) = n!/(k!(n−k)!). For example, there are C(4,2) = 6 pairs of 4 servers. The pitfall is using permutations for an unordered choice. That overcounts by k!.
rubricPoints: States that induction needs a base case and an inductive step.
Explains that the inductive step assumes the statement for k and proves it for k + 1.
Notes a limit, such as the proof failing without a base case or only covering values from the base case onward.
Distinguishes permutations (order matters) from combinations (order does not matter).
Gives or applies a correct counting formula, such as n! or C(n,k).
Identifies the overcounting pitfall of using permutations for unordered choices.

suggested.rationale: Writing an induction proof and justifying a choice of counting rule are reasoning skills you build by explaining them step by step, and no listed mission or engine has you practise them directly.

lessons.plain: Long before Greek proofs or algebra, people in Egypt and Mesopotamia (the region of ancient Babylon, in modern Iraq) built practical mathematics for taxes, land measurement, building, trade and astronomy. The core idea is how they wrote numbers. Egyptians used a tally-like system: one symbol each for one, ten, a hundred and so on, repeated and added up, like paying with stacks of coins. Babylonians used place value, as our digits do, so a symbol's position changes its worth. But they counted in sixties instead of tens. That base-sixty habit survives in 60-minute hours and 360-degree circles.
lessons.guessPrompt: If you could only write numbers by repeating a symbol for 1, a symbol for 10 and a symbol for 100, how many symbols would you need to write 999, and why might that become a problem for very large numbers?
lessons.teach:
A number system is a set of symbols plus rules for combining them into values. The base is the size of the group you count in. We use base ten. An additive system gives each symbol a fixed value, and you sum whatever symbols appear. A positional, or place-value, system gives a symbol a value that depends on where it sits.

Egyptian hieroglyphic numerals were additive and base ten. There were separate signs for 1 (a stroke), 10 (a heel-bone shape) and 100 (a coil of rope), and further signs for higher powers of ten. Order did not change the value. For fractions, Egyptians mostly used unit fractions, meaning fractions with numerator 1. They wrote 2/5 as 1/3 + 1/15. The Rhind papyrus, a scribe's teaching scroll from around 1550 BCE, is full of such problems.

Babylonian cuneiform numerals were wedge marks pressed into clay. They were positional and sexagesimal, which means base sixty. They used only two marks: a vertical wedge for 1 and a corner wedge for 10. These built up the digits 1 to 59.

Here is a worked example. Take the Babylonian digits 2 and 15, written side by side. The left digit sits in the sixties place. Step 1: 2 × 60 = 120. Step 2: add the units, 120 + 15 = 135. An Egyptian would write the same 135 additively as one coil, three heel-bones and five strokes, which makes nine symbols.

A common mistake is assuming the Babylonians had a full zero and a point like our decimal point. For most of their history they had neither. Later a placeholder sign marked an empty middle position, but nothing marked where the whole part ended. So the digits 2 and 15 could mean 135, or 2 + 15/60, or 2 × 3600 + 15 × 60. Readers had to judge the scale from context. Place value is powerful and compact, but it depends on a zero and a clear position marker to be unambiguous. This is the same lesson behind binary and hexadecimal in computing.

questions.prompt: A clay tablet shows three Babylonian digits side by side: 3, 20 and 5. Read them as a whole number, with the rightmost digit in the units place. The places from right to left are units, sixties and 3600s (since 60 × 60 = 3600). Step 1: the leftmost digit sits in the 3600s place, so 3 × 3600 = 10800. Step 2: ______. Step 3: add everything to the units digit, 10800 + 1200 + 5 = 12005. Which choice correctly fills in Step 2?
choices: 20 × 3600 = 72000, because the middle digit sits in the 3600s place
20 × 10 = 200, because each place is worth ten times the one to its right
20 + 60 = 80, because the symbols are simply summed
20 × 60 = 1200, because the middle digit sits in the sixties place
questions.why: In a base-sixty positional system the middle of three places is the sixties place, so the digit 20 is worth 20 × 60 = 1200, which matches the total in Step 3.

questions.prompt: An Egyptian scribe records a delivery of 342 jars using hieroglyphic numerals. These are additive and base ten, with a coil of rope for 100, a heel-bone for 10 and a stroke for 1. How would the scribe write 342?
choices: Three symbols, one each for the digits 3, 4 and 2
Two coils, fourteen heel-bones and two strokes
342 separate strokes, one for each jar
Three coils, four heel-bones and two strokes, nine symbols in all
questions.why: In an additive system each symbol has a fixed value and you add them up, so 342 needs three 100-signs, four 10-signs and two 1-signs.

questions.prompt: Egyptian scribes mostly wrote fractions as sums of unit fractions, meaning fractions whose numerator is 1. Which of these is a correct unit-fraction way to write 3/4?
choices: 3/4 written as a single fraction
questions.why: Both 1/2 and 1/4 have numerator 1, and they add to 3/4. The choice 1/2 + 2/8 uses a non-unit fraction, and 1/3 + 1/4 sums to only 7/12.

questions.prompt: A Babylonian tablet shows the digits 1 and 30 side by side. There is no mark showing where the whole-number part ends. Which of these is NOT a possible reading of those digits?
choices: 31, found by adding the two digits together
questions.why: The system is positional, so the left digit is always worth sixty times the right one. Without a point the overall scale is unclear, but simply adding the digits, as an additive system would, is never a valid reading.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how Egyptian and Babylonian numerals differed, and name one real weakness of the Babylonian place-value system.
lessons.modelAnswer: Egyptian numerals were additive and base ten. Each sign had a fixed value: a stroke for 1, a heel-bone for 10, a coil for 100. You just added up the signs. That is easy to read but gets long, so 135 needs nine symbols. Egyptians also wrote fractions as sums of unit fractions, like 1/3 + 1/15 for 2/5. Babylonians were positional and base sixty. They built digits 1 to 59 from two wedge marks, and a digit's position set its worth, so the digits 2 and 15 mean 2 × 60 + 15 = 135. That is far more compact and handles fractions neatly. The weakness is that they had no true zero for most of their history and no point separating whole numbers from fractions. The same digits could mean 135, 2.25 or 8100, so readers relied on context.
rubricPoints: Defines additive versus positional (place-value) notation.
States that Egyptian numerals were base ten and Babylonian numerals were base sixty.
Mentions Egyptian unit fractions or the Rhind papyrus as typical practice.
Shows or describes how a Babylonian digit's position multiplies its value by a power of sixty.
Names the tradeoff: Babylonian notation was compact but ambiguous without a full zero or a point separating whole and fractional parts.

suggested.rationale: This is a history-of-ideas objective with no matching mission, and contrasting additive and positional systems in your own words is the core skill the course will assess.

lessons.plain: Greek geometry is the ancient Greek habit of proving facts about shapes instead of just measuring them. Earlier cultures knew useful rules that worked; the Greeks asked why they must always work. Pythagoras and his followers tied number to shape. Euclid gathered geometry into one book, the Elements, where every result follows from a few starting assumptions. Archimedes pushed those methods to curved shapes like circles and spheres. Think of it like a recipe book where every dish is built only from a handful of basic ingredients and allowed steps, so you can trust each result because you can trace exactly how it was made.
lessons.guessPrompt: If you draw a six-sided shape inside a circle so its corners touch the circle, is the shape's perimeter longer or shorter than the circle's circumference? What might that tell you about the value of pi?
lessons.teach:
Greek geometry (roughly 600 to 200 BCE) changed mathematics from collecting rules into proving them. A proof is a chain of reasoning where each step follows from earlier ones. This style is called deductive: you start from accepted statements and derive new ones.

Pythagoras (around 570 to 495 BCE) led a school that saw numbers in shapes. The Pythagorean theorem says that in a right triangle the squares of the two shorter sides add up to the square of the longest side, the hypotenuse. A common mistake is thinking Pythagoras discovered this relationship; Babylonian tablets list such triples over a thousand years earlier. What the Greek tradition added was a general proof, and even the credit for that proof to Pythagoras himself is uncertain.

Euclid (around 300 BCE) wrote the Elements, thirteen books organizing geometry and number theory. It starts from definitions, axioms (common notions accepted as obvious) and postulates (geometric starting assumptions, such as being able to draw a line between two points). Every theorem, a proven statement, is built only from these and earlier theorems. This axiomatic method became the model for mathematics ever since.

Archimedes (around 287 to 212 BCE) extended these methods to curves using the method of exhaustion: trapping an unknown quantity between shapes you can measure, then tightening the trap. Trace his bound on pi with a circle of radius 1, whose circumference is 2 times pi. Step one: a regular hexagon inside the circle has six sides of length 1, perimeter 6. Since it lies inside, 6 is less than 2 pi, so pi exceeds 3. Step two: a hexagon drawn outside, touching the circle, has perimeter about 6.93, so pi is below about 3.46. Step three: doubling the sides repeatedly up to 96 squeezes the gap until 223/71 is less than pi and pi is less than 22/7. This squeezing idea foreshadows the limits used much later in calculus.

questions.prompt: A student uses Archimedes' squeezing idea with squares instead of hexagons, on a circle of radius 5. That circle's circumference is 10 times pi. Step one: a square drawn inside the circle has a perimeter of about 28.28. Because it lies inside the circle, 28.28 is less than 10 pi, so pi exceeds about 2.83. Step two: a square drawn outside the circle, touching it, has sides of length 10, so its perimeter is 40. What is the correct conclusion for step two?
choices: Because the outer square lies outside the circle, 40 is greater than 10 pi, so pi is less than 4.
Averaging 28.28 and 40 gives the exact circumference, so pi equals about 3.41.
Because 40 is less than 10 pi, pi must be greater than 4.
Because the perimeter is 40 and the circumference is 2 times pi, pi equals 20.
questions.why: A shape drawn outside the circle has a longer boundary than the circle, so 10 pi is less than 40 and pi must be below 4, which is an upper bound to pair with the lower bound from step one.

questions.prompt: A modern logic textbook opens with a short list of starting assumptions. It then proves every later result using only those assumptions and results it has already proved. Which Greek approach does this book follow?
choices: Archimedes' method of exhaustion
The Babylonian practice of listing number triples
The Pythagorean school's habit of seeing numbers in shapes
Euclid's axiomatic method in the Elements
questions.why: Building everything from stated definitions, axioms and postulates plus earlier theorems is the axiomatic method that Euclid's Elements made the model for mathematics.

questions.prompt: A classmate presenting on the triangle with sides 5, 12 and 13 says, "Pythagoras was the first person to discover that the squares of the short sides add up to the square of the hypotenuse." What is the best correction?
choices: The relationship holds only for the 3, 4, 5 triangle, so the claim is wrong about 5, 12, 13.
Babylonian tablets listed such triples over a thousand years earlier; the Greek contribution was a general proof, and even crediting that proof to Pythagoras is uncertain.
Archimedes discovered it while bounding pi with polygons.
Euclid discovered the relationship, and Pythagoras later copied it.
questions.why: The relationship was known in Babylon long before Pythagoras. What the Greek tradition added was a general proof, and it is not certain that Pythagoras himself produced it.

questions.prompt: A geometry student starts from Euclid's postulates and some results already proved. Using only these, she shows that the two base angles of any isosceles triangle are equal. In Euclid's system, what is this newly established statement called?
choices: A definition, because it describes what an isosceles triangle is
An axiom, because it is a common notion accepted as obvious
A theorem, because it is a statement proven from the starting assumptions and earlier theorems
A postulate, because it is a geometric starting assumption
questions.why: A theorem is a statement that is proven, built only from definitions, axioms, postulates and earlier theorems, and this statement was derived rather than assumed.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what made Greek geometry different from earlier mathematics, using Euclid, Pythagoras and Archimedes as examples, and name one limit of the Greek approach or one common misconception about it.
lessons.modelAnswer: Earlier cultures like the Babylonians knew rules that worked, such as right-triangle relationships, but the Greeks insisted on proof: deductive reasoning from accepted starting points. Pythagoras's school linked numbers and shapes, and the right-triangle theorem carries his name, though the relationship was known long before him and even the first proof may not be his. Euclid's Elements organized geometry axiomatically: from a few definitions, axioms and postulates, every theorem is derived step by step, which became the template for mathematics. Archimedes applied the method of exhaustion to curves, for example trapping pi between the perimeters of inscribed and circumscribed polygons until it lay between 223/71 and 22/7. A limit is that exhaustion gives bounds for one problem at a time rather than a general technique; that general machinery waited for calculus, centuries later.
rubricPoints: Greek mathematics emphasized deductive proof rather than just working rules.
Euclid's Elements built theorems from definitions, axioms and postulates.
The Pythagorean relationship was known earlier; Greek credit lies in general proof, and attribution to Pythagoras is uncertain.
Archimedes used the method of exhaustion, such as bounding pi with polygons.
Names a limit, such as exhaustion being case-by-case rather than a general method like calculus.

suggested.rationale: This is a history-of-ideas objective with no matching mission or engine, and explaining why proof and the axiomatic method mattered is the core skill a history-of-mathematics course assesses.

lessons.plain: Algebra is the part of math that works with unknown quantities and the rules for finding them. Its history is largely the story of how people learned to write problems down. For centuries, equations were written entirely in words, like a long recipe. Slowly, writers began using abbreviations, and eventually full symbols such as letters for unknowns and signs for equals and plus. Think of how directions changed from 'walk past the old mill, then turn toward the river' to a map with a dot and an arrow. The math underneath stayed the same, but the shorter notation made it far easier to see patterns and solve harder problems.
lessons.guessPrompt: Before symbols like x and = existed, how do you think a mathematician would have written down 'some number squared plus ten times that number equals thirty-nine', and what would make that harder to work with?
lessons.teach:
Historians usually describe three stages of algebraic notation. Rhetorical algebra writes everything in ordinary words. Syncopated algebra uses abbreviations or shorthand for some quantities and operations, but still leans on words. Symbolic algebra uses dedicated symbols for unknowns, known values, operations and relations.

The Greek writer Diophantus (around the third century CE) is the classic syncopated example: he used shorthand for an unknown and its powers. Around 820 CE in Baghdad, al-Khwarizmi wrote a book whose title contains 'al-jabr', the source of the word algebra. Al-jabr meant moving a subtracted term to the other side so it becomes added; al-muqabala meant cancelling equal terms on both sides. His work was rhetorical, with no symbols, and he justified methods with geometric pictures. Later, Renaissance writers added signs: Robert Recorde introduced the equals sign in 1557. François Viète (late 1500s) used letters for both unknowns and known values, letting one formula cover a whole family of problems. René Descartes (1637) set the habit of x, y, z for unknowns, a, b, c for knowns, and raised numbers for powers.

Worked example. Al-Khwarizmi's problem reads: a square and ten roots equal thirty-nine. Step 1: in modern symbols, x² + 10x = 39. Step 2: take half of ten, which is 5, and square it to get 25. Step 3: add 25 to both sides: x² + 10x + 25 = 64. Step 4: the left side is (x + 5)², so x + 5 = 8. Step 5: x = 3. He pictured step 3 as literally completing a square drawing, and he accepted only the positive answer.

A common mistake is assuming algebra began with symbols. The ideas and methods came first; notation arrived centuries later. The consequence of better notation was real: general formulas, easier manipulation, and the groundwork for analytic geometry and later mathematics.

questions.prompt: A student solves 'a square and six roots equal sixteen' with al-Khwarizmi's completing-the-square method. Step 1: in modern symbols, x² + 6x = 16. Step 2: half of six is 3, and 3 squared is 9. Step 3: ??? Step 4: the left side is (x + 3)², so x + 3 = 5. Step 5: x = 2, the positive answer. Which choice correctly fills in Step 3?
choices: Add 9 to both sides: x² + 6x + 9 = 25
Add 9 to the left side only: x² + 6x + 9 = 16
Add 3 to both sides: x² + 6x + 3 = 19
Add 36 to both sides: x² + 6x + 36 = 52
questions.why: Completing the square adds the square of half the root coefficient (9) to both sides, which gives (x + 3)² = 25, so x + 3 = 5.

questions.prompt: An old merchant's manual writes a problem as 'cos. p. 5 aeq. 12'. Here 'cos.' is a shorthand for the unknown, 'p.' is short for 'plus', and 'aeq.' is short for 'equals'. The rest of the book's explanations are in full sentences. Which stage of algebraic notation does this represent?
choices: Rhetorical algebra, because the problem is still built from words
Symbolic algebra, because the unknown has a dedicated label
Syncopated algebra, because abbreviations stand in for some quantities and operations while words remain
Geometric algebra, because no numbers are raised to powers
questions.why: Shorthand abbreviations mixed with ordinary words is the definition of syncopated algebra. It is not fully rhetorical, and it does not yet use dedicated symbols.

questions.prompt: In al-Khwarizmi's method, al-jabr means moving a subtracted term to the other side so that it becomes added. Applying al-jabr to 3x² = 15x − 6 gives which equation?
choices: x² = 5x − 2
3x² = 15x
questions.why: The subtracted 6 moves to the other side and becomes added, giving 3x² + 6 = 15x. The other choices either move an added term, divide through, or simply drop the 6.

questions.prompt: A classmate says: 'Al-Khwarizmi wrote everything in words and used no symbols, so what he did wasn't really algebra. Algebra started when symbols like the equals sign appeared.' What is the best response?
choices: The claim is correct: algebra only began when Descartes introduced x, y and z in 1637.
The claim is mistaken because al-Khwarizmi actually used letters for unknowns and known values.
The claim is mistaken: algebraic ideas and methods, like completing the square, came first, and symbolic notation arrived centuries later.
The claim is correct: algebra only began with Recorde's equals sign in 1557.
questions.why: Al-Khwarizmi's methods were genuine algebra written rhetorically. Assuming algebra began with symbols is the common mistake, and he did not use letters at all.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how algebraic notation moved from words to symbols, naming at least two key figures, and describe one tradeoff or limit of the older word-based approach compared with symbols.
lessons.modelAnswer: Algebra's methods existed long before its symbols. Historians split the development into rhetorical algebra, written fully in words; syncopated algebra, with shorthand like Diophantus used; and symbolic algebra. Al-Khwarizmi, around 820 CE, gave us the word algebra through al-jabr, moving subtracted terms across an equation, but he wrote everything in words and proved steps with geometric pictures, such as completing a square to solve 'a square and ten roots equal thirty-nine', giving 3. Later Recorde introduced the equals sign, Viète used letters for knowns as well as unknowns, and Descartes fixed x, y, z for unknowns. The tradeoff is that word-based algebra is readable sentence by sentence but hard to manipulate, hides general patterns, and ties each solution to one specific problem. Symbols are compact and general, though they are less self-explanatory to a newcomer.
rubricPoints: Names the rhetorical, syncopated and symbolic stages and what distinguishes them.
Credits al-Khwarizmi with al-jabr methods while noting his work used words, not symbols.
Mentions at least one later contributor to symbols, such as Recorde, Viète or Descartes.
States that methods came before notation.
Identifies a limit of word-based algebra, such as difficulty manipulating or generalizing.

suggested.rationale: This is a historical narrative with no hands-on mission, so retelling the stages and key figures in your own words is the best way to retain it for a history-of-mathematics course.

lessons.plain: Calculus is the mathematics of change and accumulation. It answers two linked questions: how fast is something changing right now, and how much has built up over time? In the late 1600s, Isaac Newton in England and Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz in Germany each turned scattered earlier tricks into one general method. Each also saw that the two questions undo each other. Picture a car's speedometer and its odometer. One tells you the speed at this instant, the other the total distance travelled. Calculus is the rulebook for converting either reading into the other. A bitter argument later followed over who got there first.
lessons.guessPrompt: Two people working in different countries, who rarely wrote to each other, both invent the same powerful method within about ten years of each other. Why might that happen, and what would you expect them to argue about afterwards?
lessons.teach:
Calculus is a general method for finding rates of change, called derivatives, and accumulated totals, called integrals. A derivative is the instantaneous rate at which one quantity changes as another changes, such as speed at a single moment. An integral is the total built up from many tiny pieces, such as the area under a curve.

Earlier mathematicians, including Fermat, Cavalieri, Wallis and Barrow (Newton's teacher), had already solved particular tangent and area problems. Newton and Leibniz each made three advances. They found general rules that work for many curves. They used the fundamental theorem of calculus, the insight that differentiation and integration are inverse operations. And they wrote down a systematic notation.

Newton worked around 1665 to 1666 and called his method fluxions. A fluxion is the rate at which a flowing quantity changes, and he wrote it with a dot over the letter. He published little of it until much later. Leibniz worked around 1673 to 1676 and published first, in 1684 and 1686. He used infinitesimals, meaning quantities smaller than any positive number but not zero. He wrote them as dx, and he invented the elongated S, ∫, from the Latin summa, meaning sum.

Here is a worked example in the style of Newton, finding the rate of change of y = x². First, let x grow by a tiny amount o. Then y becomes (x + o)² = x² + 2xo + o². Subtract the original value: the change is 2xo + o². Divide by o to get 2x + o. Finally, drop o because it is vanishingly small. The rate is 2x. In Leibniz's notation the same result is written dy/dx = 2x.

A common mistake is to assume one man simply copied the other. Historians now agree they worked independently. Even so, a 1712 Royal Society report, largely written by Newton himself, accused Leibniz of plagiarism.

The priority dispute had lasting effects. British mathematicians loyally kept Newton's awkward dot notation. Continental mathematicians adopted Leibniz's flexible dx and ∫ and advanced faster. Another weak point was logical: neither man rigorously justified dropping the vanishing o, and critics such as Bishop Berkeley attacked exactly that step.

questions.prompt: A student copies Newton's style to find the rate of change of a cube, y = x³. Step 1: let x grow by a tiny amount o, so y becomes (x + o)³ = x³ + 3x²o + 3xo² + o³. Step 2: subtract the original value; the change is 3x²o + 3xo² + o³. Step 3: [missing]. Step 4: drop every term that still contains o because o is vanishingly small, leaving the rate 3x². What is the result of Step 3?
choices: Drop o first, giving 3x²
Divide by o², giving 3x²/o + 3x + o
Divide by o, giving 3x² + 3xo + o²
Divide only the first term by o, giving 3x² + 3xo² + o³
questions.why: Dividing the whole change by o leaves 3x² + 3xo + o². Only after that can the remaining o terms be dropped to give 3x².

questions.prompt: In an old Cambridge notebook from the 1700s, a tutor writes a letter with a small dot above it to stand for how fast a quantity is changing. Which method and term does this belong to?
choices: Barrow's tangent method, where the dot marks a single point on a curve
Leibniz's infinitesimals, where the dot marks a quantity smaller than any positive number
Newton's fluxions, where the dot marks the rate at which a flowing quantity changes
Leibniz's integral sign, where the dot marks a sum of many tiny pieces
questions.why: Newton called his method fluxions and wrote a fluxion, the rate of change of a flowing quantity, with a dot over the letter. British mathematicians loyally kept that notation.

questions.prompt: A teacher shows a class that the rate of change of y = 4x² is 8x. She lets x grow by o, expands the expression, subtracts the original, divides by o to get 8x + 4o, and then discards the 4o. A skeptic in the style of Bishop Berkeley objects to one step as not logically justified. Which step?
choices: Letting x grow by a tiny amount o
Subtracting the original value of y
Expanding (x + o)² correctly
Discarding the leftover o term as if it were zero after dividing by it
questions.why: Neither Newton nor Leibniz rigorously justified dropping the vanishing o. If o could be divided by, it was not zero, so throwing it away looked inconsistent. Berkeley attacked exactly that step.

questions.prompt: A classmate argues: "Newton worked on calculus about a decade before Leibniz, and a Royal Society report accused Leibniz of plagiarism, so Leibniz must have copied Newton." Which response best fits what historians now conclude?
choices: Historians agree Leibniz copied Newton, which is why Continental mathematicians fell behind
Historians agree Newton copied Leibniz, because Leibniz published first in 1684
Historians agree both copied Barrow, so neither made any new advance
Historians agree the two worked independently, and the 1712 report was largely written by Newton himself
questions.why: Working earlier does not prove copying. Historians conclude the two men developed calculus independently, and the report accusing Leibniz was not neutral, since Newton largely wrote it.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what Newton and Leibniz each actually contributed to calculus, why it is fair to credit both, and name one weakness or tradeoff in what they produced.
lessons.modelAnswer:
Calculus handles two problems: instantaneous rates of change, called derivatives, and accumulated totals, called integrals. People like Fermat and Barrow had already solved special cases. Newton and Leibniz each turned those cases into a general method, and each recognised the fundamental theorem, that differentiating and integrating undo each other.

Newton got there first, around 1665, with his fluxions, but he published late. Leibniz worked independently in the 1670s and published first, in the 1680s. His dx and ∫ notation proved far more usable.

It is fair to credit both, because historians agree they worked independently. Even so, the Royal Society report that Newton steered accused Leibniz of plagiarism.

There are two weaknesses to name. First, neither man rigorously justified treating a tiny increment as nonzero and then discarding it, which Berkeley criticised. Second, Britain's loyalty to Newton's notation slowed its mathematics compared with the Continent.
rubricPoints: Defines calculus in terms of derivatives (rates of change) and integrals (accumulated totals).
States that both men saw differentiation and integration as inverse operations, the fundamental theorem.
Notes that Newton developed fluxions first but published late, while Leibniz published first with dx and ∫ notation.
Says they worked independently despite the priority dispute and the 1712 Royal Society report.
Names a limitation, such as the lack of rigour around infinitesimals or the cost to Britain of Newton's notation.

suggested.rationale: This is a history topic with no matching mission or engine, and the core skill is explaining who contributed what, and why the dispute mattered, in your own words.

lessons.plain: For about two thousand years, mathematicians treated Euclid's geometry as the one true description of space. One of his starting assumptions, the parallel postulate, always felt less obvious than the others. It says that through a point off a line, exactly one line runs parallel to it. In the 1800s, people tried replacing that rule with a different one and found the resulting geometry was perfectly consistent. Think of a board game where changing one rule still gives a playable game, just a different one. That discovery showed that geometry is a choice of assumptions, not a fixed fact about the world.
lessons.guessPrompt: On the surface of a globe, if you draw a triangle using the shortest paths between three cities, do you think its angles add up to exactly 180 degrees, more, or less? Why?
lessons.teach:
Non-Euclidean geometry is any consistent geometry that keeps Euclid's other basic assumptions but changes the parallel postulate. An axiom, or postulate, is a statement accepted without proof as a starting point. Consistent means no contradiction can be derived from the axioms. Euclid's fifth postulate, in its common modern form, says that through a point not on a given line there is exactly one parallel. Two lines are parallel when they never meet.

For centuries, mathematicians tried to prove the fifth postulate from the other four. In the 1820s and 1830s, Nikolai Lobachevsky and János Bolyai, working separately, assumed instead that many parallels pass through the point. They kept deriving theorems and never hit a contradiction. This became hyperbolic geometry, where triangle angles sum to less than 180 degrees. Carl Friedrich Gauss had reached similar ideas privately but did not publish them. Later, Bernhard Riemann described elliptic, or spherical-type, geometry, where no parallels exist and triangle angles sum to more than 180 degrees. Riemann also introduced the idea of curvature varying from place to place, which Einstein's general relativity used decades later. Eugenio Beltrami and Felix Klein built models, which are concrete settings inside ordinary mathematics where the new axioms hold. These models showed hyperbolic geometry is as consistent as Euclid's.

Here is a worked example on a sphere, where "lines" are great circles, the largest circles around the ball. Start at the North Pole. Walk down to the equator. Turn 90 degrees and walk a quarter of the way around the equator. Turn 90 degrees and walk back to the pole. The two turns at the equator give 90 plus 90 degrees, and the angle at the pole is 90 degrees, so the total is 270 degrees, well over 180.

A common mistake is to think non-Euclidean geometry proved Euclid wrong. It did not. It proved that the parallel postulate is independent, which means it cannot be derived from the other axioms. This shifted 19th-century mathematics toward studying axiom systems themselves and toward greater rigor.

questions.prompt: A pilot flies a triangle on a globe, where the 'lines' are great circles. She starts at the North Pole and flies straight down a meridian to the equator. She turns 90 degrees and flies one eighth of the way around the equator. She turns 90 degrees again and flies straight back to the pole. The angle she measures at the pole is 45 degrees. Step 1: The two turns at the equator give 90 + 90 = 180 degrees. Step 2: Adding the pole angle gives 180 + 45 = 225 degrees. Step 3: (missing) What does this total tell us about the geometry of her flight path?
choices: The sum should really be 180 degrees, so her instruments must be wrong, because every triangle in any geometry sums to 180.
The sum is less than 180 degrees, so the path follows hyperbolic geometry, the system of Lobachevsky and Bolyai.
The sum shows that Euclid's geometry has been proved false, because a triangle broke his 180-degree rule.
The sum is more than 180 degrees, which fits elliptic (spherical-type) geometry, the kind Riemann described, where no parallels exist.
questions.why: A triangle whose angles add to more than 180 degrees is the signature of elliptic geometry, where great circles always meet and so no parallels exist.

questions.prompt: A student works inside an axiom system that keeps all of Euclid's other basic assumptions. In this system, through a point not on a given line, infinitely many lines pass that never meet the given line. She draws a triangle and measures its angles at 60, 50 and 55 degrees, a total of 165. Which geometry is she working in?
choices: Euclidean geometry
A geometry that must contain a contradiction
Hyperbolic geometry
Elliptic geometry
questions.why: Many parallels through a point, together with triangle angles that add to less than 180 degrees, are exactly what defines hyperbolic geometry.

questions.prompt: In a study group, a classmate says: "Once Lobachevsky and Bolyai built a geometry with many parallels, Euclid's geometry was shown to be wrong." Which response best corrects this?
choices: Incorrect, because Lobachevsky and Bolyai later found a contradiction in their own system.
Incorrect. It showed the parallel postulate is independent: it cannot be derived from the other axioms, so different choices for it give different consistent geometries.
Partly correct. Euclid was wrong only about triangles, not about parallel lines.
Correct. Hyperbolic geometry replaced Euclid's geometry, which mathematicians stopped using after the 1830s.
questions.why: Non-Euclidean geometry did not refute Euclid. It showed that the parallel postulate cannot be proved from the other axioms, so Euclidean and non-Euclidean systems can both be consistent.

questions.prompt: A logician invents a new set of axioms and worries that it might secretly contain a contradiction. She then builds a concrete setting inside ordinary, well-accepted mathematics in which every one of her axioms holds. This is the same strategy Beltrami and Klein used for hyperbolic geometry. What does her construction show?
choices: Her axioms are true statements about physical space.
Her axioms can all be derived from Euclid's five postulates.
Her new system is as consistent as the ordinary mathematics she built the setting in.
Her system must be identical to Euclidean geometry.
questions.why: A model, meaning a concrete setting inside accepted mathematics where the axioms hold, shows the new system is just as consistent as the mathematics used to build it. This is how hyperbolic geometry was shown to be as consistent as Euclid's.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate in your own words why the discovery of non-Euclidean geometry mattered, and name one limit on what it showed, for example what it did not prove about Euclid.
lessons.modelAnswer: Euclid built geometry on a handful of axioms. The parallel postulate says exactly one parallel passes through a point off a line, and people spent centuries trying to prove it from the others. In the early 1800s, Lobachevsky and Bolyai replaced it with "many parallels" and got hyperbolic geometry, where triangle angles sum to less than 180 degrees. Riemann's approach gave geometries with no parallels, like a sphere, where the sums exceed 180 degrees. Models by Beltrami and Klein showed these systems are as consistent as Euclid's. So the parallel postulate is independent of the other axioms. The limit is that this does not make Euclid wrong. Euclidean geometry is still consistent and works well at everyday scales. The real lesson is that axioms are choices, and which geometry fits physical space is a question for observation, not pure logic.
rubricPoints: States that non-Euclidean geometry changes only the parallel postulate.
Distinguishes hyperbolic (angle sum under 180) from elliptic or spherical (over 180).
Names key figures such as Lobachevsky, Bolyai, Gauss, or Riemann.
Explains that models proved consistency and the postulate's independence.
Notes the limit: Euclid was not disproved; axioms became choices.

suggested.rationale: No mission or engine covers geometry history, and putting the independence idea and its limits into your own words is the core skill here.

lessons.plain: Set theory is the study of collections of things, called sets, and it became the common foundation that most of modern mathematics is built on. In the late 1800s Georg Cantor used sets to compare the sizes of infinite collections and found that some infinities are bigger than others. Contradictions then turned up, and mathematicians responded by writing careful ground rules, called axioms. Think of it as rewriting the building code after a few houses cracked. Every later floor of mathematics now rests on that agreed foundation.
lessons.guessPrompt: Are there more whole counting numbers (1, 2, 3, ...) than even numbers (2, 4, 6, ...), or the same amount? Guess, and say why.
lessons.teach:
A set is a collection of distinct objects, called its elements. Two sets have the same size, or cardinality, when you can pair every element of one with exactly one element of the other with nothing left over. Such a pairing is called a one-to-one correspondence, or bijection. Georg Cantor, working from the 1870s, took this pairing idea seriously for infinite sets, and that is why his results surprised people.

Here is a worked example. Pair each counting number n with the even number 2n. So 1 goes with 2, 2 goes with 4, and 3 goes with 6. Every counting number gets exactly one partner. Every even number k is reached once, from k/2. Nothing is left over on either side, so the two sets have the same cardinality, even though the evens look like half. A set that can be paired with the counting numbers is called countable.

Cantor then showed that the real numbers are uncountable, meaning strictly bigger. His tool was the diagonal argument. Suppose someone hands you a complete list of decimals. Build a new decimal that differs from the first number in its first digit, from the second number in its second digit, and so on down the diagonal. This new number differs from every entry, so it is missing from the list, and therefore no list can be complete. So there are different sizes of infinity.

A common mistake is to assume that a set which contains another set must be bigger. That holds for finite sets but fails for infinite ones, as the evens show.

Around 1901 Bertrand Russell found a paradox. Consider the set of all sets that do not contain themselves. That set contains itself exactly when it does not, which is a contradiction. The lesson was that 'any collection you can describe is a set' is too loose a rule. Ernst Zermelo and Abraham Fraenkel replaced it with precise axioms, called ZF, or ZFC when the axiom of choice is added. ZFC became the standard foundation. David Hilbert hoped to prove such a system complete and consistent. In 1931 Kurt Gödel showed this cannot fully succeed: any consistent system strong enough for arithmetic has true statements it cannot prove. Diagonal reasoning later underpinned Alan Turing's proof that no program can decide, for every program, whether it halts.

questions.prompt: A puzzle club wants to show that the counting numbers {1, 2, 3, ...} and the set {11, 12, 13, ...} (every whole number from 11 upward) have the same cardinality, meaning the same size. They use this pairing, a one-to-one correspondence (bijection): each counting number n goes with n + 10. Step 1: 1 goes with 11, 2 goes with 12, 3 goes with 13. Step 2: every counting number gets exactly one partner, because n + 10 is a single, definite number. Step 3: [missing]. Step 4: nothing is left over on either side, so the two sets have the same cardinality. Which statement correctly fills Step 3?
choices: Every number k from 11 upward is reached once, from the counting number k + 10.
The set {11, 12, 13, ...} sits inside the counting numbers, so it must be smaller.
Every number k from 11 upward is reached exactly once, from the counting number k − 10.
The first ten counting numbers have no partner, so the counting numbers are bigger.
questions.why: To finish the bijection you must show every element of the second set is hit exactly once, and k is reached only from k − 10, which is a counting number whenever k is 11 or more.

questions.prompt: A student claims: "The multiples of 5 (5, 10, 15, ...) are only some of the counting numbers, so there must be fewer of them." Using Cantor's idea of cardinality, which response is correct?
choices: The claim is right: a set that sits inside another set always has smaller cardinality.
The claim is wrong: the multiples of 5 are actually bigger, because each one is five times a counting number.
The claim is right: the multiples of 5 are uncountable, so they cannot be compared with the counting numbers.
The claim is wrong: pairing each counting number n with 5n matches the two sets with nothing left over, so they have the same cardinality.
questions.why: Cardinality is decided by whether a one-to-one pairing exists, and n with 5n pairs every counting number with exactly one multiple of 5, so the finite-set intuition about subsets being smaller fails here.

questions.prompt: Someone claims this is a complete list of decimals between 0 and 1. Its first three entries begin 0.512..., 0.348..., and 0.976.... Applying Cantor's diagonal argument (build a number whose first digit differs from the first entry's first digit, whose second digit differs from the second entry's second digit, and so on), which new number's first three digits are consistent with the method?
questions.why: The diagonal digits are 5, 4 and 6, and 0.657... differs at every one of those positions (6 vs 5, 5 vs 4, 7 vs 6), while each other choice matches at least one diagonal digit.

questions.prompt: A research team builds a formal system of axioms that is consistent and strong enough to handle ordinary arithmetic. They announce that, with enough effort, it will prove every true statement about arithmetic. According to the history of modern foundations, what is the right assessment?
choices: It cannot succeed, because Russell's paradox shows any such system contradicts itself.
It cannot succeed, because Gödel showed in 1931 that such a system has true statements it cannot prove.
It can succeed, because ZFC was designed to be complete and consistent, fulfilling Hilbert's hope.
