It can succeed only if the system adds the axiom of choice, turning ZF into ZFC.
questions.why: Gödel's 1931 result says any consistent system strong enough for arithmetic has true statements it cannot prove, so the team's promise of proving every truth is impossible.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate, in your own words, how Cantor compared infinite sets and why Russell's paradox pushed mathematicians toward axioms. Name one limit that Gödel showed any such foundation must have.
lessons.modelAnswer: Cantor said two sets are the same size if you can pair their elements one-to-one with nothing left over. With that rule, the counting numbers and the even numbers match: n pairs with 2n. So a part of an infinite set can be as big as the whole. His diagonal argument shows the real numbers cannot be listed at all. Any proposed list misses a number built to differ from each entry at one digit, so some infinities really are larger. Russell then showed that 'every describable collection is a set' leads to contradiction, through the set of all sets that do not contain themselves. That led to careful axioms, ZFC, which now underlie most of mathematics. The limit is Gödel's result. A consistent system strong enough for arithmetic will always contain true statements it cannot prove, so no foundation is both complete and provably airtight from inside. The same diagonal trick gives Turing's halting problem in computer science.
rubricPoints: Defines equal size of sets by one-to-one pairing.
Gives an example such as counting numbers matched with even numbers.
Explains the diagonal argument showing the reals are uncountable.
Describes Russell's paradox and why it motivated axioms like ZFC.
Names Gödel's incompleteness as a limit on any such foundation.

suggested.rationale: This is a conceptual history topic with no matching mission or engine, so explaining Cantor's arguments and their consequences back in your own words is the core skill.

lessons.plain: A vector space is a collection of objects, called vectors, that you can add together and stretch by numbers without ever leaving the collection. Arrows on a flat sheet of paper are the classic example: add two arrows tip to tail, or double one, and you still have an arrow on the sheet. A subspace is a smaller collection sitting inside a bigger vector space that is itself a complete vector space. Think of a straight road through the origin on a map: walking along it or adding two trips along it keeps you on the road. A road that misses the origin fails.
lessons.guessPrompt: Picture all the points on a straight line drawn on graph paper that does not pass through the origin (0,0). If you add two points from that line, like adding their coordinates, do you expect the result to stay on the same line? Why or why not?
lessons.teach:
A vector space is a set of objects called vectors, together with two operations: vector addition and scalar multiplication. A scalar is an ordinary number, here a real number. The set must obey familiar arithmetic rules, such as order of addition not mattering. Most importantly, it must be closed under both operations. Closed means the result of the operation always lands back inside the set. It must also contain a zero vector, the vector that changes nothing when added. Examples include R^2 and R^3, the sets of pairs and triples of real numbers. Others are all polynomials of degree at most 2, and all 2-by-2 matrices.

A subspace is a subset of a vector space that is a vector space in its own right, using the same operations. You do not need to recheck every rule, because the arithmetic rules are inherited from the larger space. The subspace test needs only three checks. First, the zero vector is in the subset. Second, the subset is closed under addition. Third, it is closed under scalar multiplication.

Worked example: let W be all (x, y, z) in R^3 with x + y + z = 0. Zero check: 0 + 0 + 0 = 0, so (0,0,0) is in W. Addition: take two vectors in W, (a,b,c) and (d,e,f). Their sum has coordinates adding to (a+b+c) + (d+e+f) = 0 + 0 = 0, so the sum is in W. Scaling: for any scalar k, the coordinates of k(a,b,c) add to k(a+b+c) = k times 0 = 0. All three pass, so W is a subspace, a plane through the origin. Now try x + y + z = 1. The zero vector gives 0, not 1, so it fails immediately.

A common mistake is checking only that the set looks like a line or plane, forgetting it must pass through the origin. Another is testing closure with one specific pair of vectors instead of arbitrary ones. One example can disprove closure but never proves it. This matters later because the solution set of a system with all right-hand sides equal to zero always forms a subspace.

questions.prompt: Let V be the set of all pairs (x, y) in R^2 with y = 4x. We use the subspace test. Zero check: (0, 0) satisfies 0 = 4 times 0, so the zero vector is in V. Addition: take any two vectors in V, written (a, 4a) and (b, 4b). Their sum is (a + b, 4a + 4b) = (a + b, 4(a + b)), which has the form (t, 4t), so the sum is in V. Scaling: [missing step]. All three checks pass, so V is a subspace, a line through the origin. Which choice correctly fills in the missing scaling step?
choices: For any scalar k, k(a, 4a) = (ka, 4ka) = (ka, 4(ka)), which has the form (t, 4t), so it is in V.
For any scalar k, k(a, 4a) = (ka, 4a), so the second coordinate does not match and V fails the test.
Take k = 2 and the vector (1, 4). Then 2(1, 4) = (2, 8), and 8 = 4 times 2, so scaling always stays in V.
No scaling check is needed, because addition passed and the arithmetic rules are inherited from R^2.
questions.why: It scales an arbitrary vector of V by an arbitrary scalar and shows the result still has the form (t, 4t), which proves closure under scalar multiplication.

questions.prompt: In plain terms, what does it mean for a set of vectors to be closed under scalar multiplication?
choices: Multiplying any vector in the set by any real number gives a result that is still in the set.
Multiplying any two vectors in the set together gives another vector in the set.
Multiplying a vector by a scalar never changes it, just as adding the zero vector does not.
At least one vector in the set, when multiplied by some number, stays in the set.
questions.why: Closure means the operation always lands back inside the set, so every vector times every scalar must remain in the set.

questions.prompt: Let L be the set of all (x, y) in R^2 with y = 2x + 5. Its graph is a straight line. Is L a subspace of R^2, and why?
choices: Yes, because any straight line in R^2 is a subspace.
No, because it passes the zero check but fails closure under addition only.
Yes, because scaling a point on the line by 1 keeps it on the line.
No, because (0, 0) is not in L: plugging in x = 0 gives y = 5, not 0.
questions.why: A subspace must contain the zero vector, and this line misses the origin, so it fails the test immediately even though it looks like a line.

questions.prompt: Let Q be the set of all (x, y) in R^2 with x ≥ 0 and y ≥ 0. A student notes that (0, 0) is in Q, checks that (1, 2) + (3, 4) = (4, 6) is in Q, and concludes Q is a subspace. What is the correct verdict?
choices: Q is not a subspace, because the zero vector (0, 0) is not in Q.
Q is a subspace, because one checked example is enough to prove closure under each operation.
Q is a subspace: it contains zero, and the student's addition example shows closure under addition.
Q is not a subspace: scaling (1, 2) by -1 gives (-1, -2), which is outside Q, so closure under scalar multiplication fails.
questions.why: One specific example can never prove closure, but one counterexample can disprove it, and multiplying by -1 pushes a vector of Q outside Q.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how to decide whether a subset of R^3 is a subspace, using one example that passes and one that fails. Also name a limit of the shortcut test: what it lets you skip, and what kind of checking it does not let you get away with.
lessons.modelAnswer: A subspace is a subset of a vector space that is itself a vector space under the same addition and scaling. Because it inherits the arithmetic rules from the big space, I only check three things. It must contain the zero vector, and it must be closed under addition and under scalar multiplication, meaning results stay inside the set. For example, the plane x + y + z = 0 passes. Zero satisfies it, and sums and multiples of solutions still add to zero. The plane x + y + z = 1 fails at once, because zero isn't on it. The shortcut lets me skip the rules like commutativity. The limit is that closure must be shown for arbitrary vectors and scalars using algebra. Trying a couple of specific vectors can expose a failure, but it can never prove the set is a subspace.
rubricPoints: Defines a vector space as a set closed under addition and scalar multiplication, with a zero vector.
States that a subspace is a subset that is a vector space using the same operations.
Gives the three-part test: contains zero, closed under addition, closed under scaling.
Shows one passing and one failing example, such as planes through and not through the origin.
Notes the tradeoff: the inherited rules can be skipped, but closure must be proven for arbitrary vectors, not checked with samples.

suggested.rationale: Mastering subspaces means justifying the three-part test in your own words for arbitrary vectors, which explaining it back trains directly; no OpsForge mission or planned engine covers abstract linear algebra.

lessons.plain: A system of linear equations is a set of equations that must all be true at the same time, where each unknown appears only multiplied by a number and added up, with no squares or products of unknowns. Solving the system means finding values for the unknowns that satisfy every equation at once. Gaussian elimination is a step-by-step recipe for doing that: you tidy the equations so each one has fewer unknowns than the one above, like peeling an onion layer by layer, until the last equation names one value outright. Then you work back up, filling in the rest.
lessons.guessPrompt: Suppose x + y = 10 and x − y = 4. Without guessing numbers, what happens if you add the two equations together, and how does that help you find x and then y?
lessons.teach:
A linear equation is one where each unknown (variable) is multiplied by a constant and the terms are summed, such as 2x + 3y − z = 5. A system is several such equations sharing the same unknowns. A solution is a set of values that makes every equation true at once. A system is consistent if it has at least one solution and inconsistent if it has none.

We write the system as an augmented matrix: a grid where each row holds one equation's coefficients, with the right-hand constants in a final column. Three elementary row operations never change the solution set: swap two rows, multiply a row by a nonzero number, or add a multiple of one row to another. They work because each is reversible and keeps every equation true for exactly the same values.

Gaussian elimination uses these operations to reach row echelon form: each row's first nonzero entry, called the pivot, sits to the right of the pivot above it, and everything below a pivot is zero. Then back substitution solves from the bottom row upward.

Worked example: x + y + z = 6, 2x + 3y + z = 11, x + 2y + 3z = 14. Replace row 2 with row 2 minus 2 times row 1, giving y − z = −1. Replace row 3 with row 3 minus row 1, giving y + 2z = 8. Replace row 3 with row 3 minus the new row 2, giving 3z = 9, so z = 3. Back substitute: y − 3 = −1, so y = 2. Then x + 2 + 3 = 6, so x = 1.

If elimination produces a row like 0 = 5, the system is inconsistent. If a column has no pivot, its variable is free and there are infinitely many solutions.

A common mistake is applying an operation to the coefficients but forgetting the constant column, which silently gives a wrong answer. In computer implementations, dividing by a tiny pivot magnifies rounding error, so software swaps rows to use the largest available pivot (partial pivoting). Elimination costs roughly n³ operations for n equations.

questions.prompt:
A coffee roaster mixes three blends and records this system for the unknowns x, y and z: x + 2y + z = 9, 2x + 5y + 3z = 22, 3x + 7y + 5z = 32. It solves the system with Gaussian elimination as follows.

Step 1: Replace row 2 with row 2 minus 2 times row 1, giving y + z = 4.
Step 2: Replace row 3 with row 3 minus 3 times row 1. [MISSING]
Step 3: Replace row 3 with row 3 minus the new row 2, giving z = 1.
Step 4: Back substitute: y + 1 = 4, so y = 3. Then x + 6 + 1 = 9, so x = 2.

Which equation should Step 2 produce?
questions.why: Subtracting 3 times row 1 from row 3 gives (3−3)x + (7−6)y + (5−3)z = 32 − 27. That is y + 2z = 5, and z = 1 from Step 3 together with y = 3 confirms it.

questions.prompt: A student is solving a system with three unknowns, x, y and z. After several elementary row operations, one row of the augmented matrix reads [0 0 0 | 4]. What does this tell the student?
choices: The system is inconsistent and has no solution, because that row says 0 = 4.
The row can be deleted and the student should continue with back substitution.
The variable z is free, so there are infinitely many solutions.
z = 4, and the student should back substitute that value upward.
questions.why: Every coefficient in the row is zero, so the row stands for the equation 0 = 4. No values of the unknowns can make that true, so the system is inconsistent.

questions.prompt: A logistics team models shipments with three unknowns, a, b and c. After Gaussian elimination, the augmented matrix in row echelon form is [1 2 −1 | 3] and [0 1 4 | 2], plus a final row of all zeros, [0 0 0 | 0]. How many solutions does the system have?
choices: None, because the last row is all zeros.
Exactly one, because two rows contain pivots.
Infinitely many, because the c column has no pivot, so c is a free variable.
Exactly two, one for each nonzero row.
questions.why: The row 0 = 0 is always true, so the system is consistent. Only the a and b columns contain pivots, so c is free, and each choice of c gives a different solution.

questions.prompt: A program runs Gaussian elimination on a computer. At the current column, the entry in the pivot position is 0.0002, and a row below it has 7 in the same column. With partial pivoting, what does the software do, and why?
choices: It multiplies the pivot row by zero to clear the small entry before continuing.
It stops and reports that the system is inconsistent, because the pivot is close to zero.
It divides by 0.0002 anyway, because a nonzero pivot is always mathematically valid.
It swaps the two rows so that 7 becomes the pivot, because dividing by a tiny pivot magnifies rounding error.
questions.why: Partial pivoting swaps rows so the largest available entry becomes the pivot. Swapping rows is an elementary row operation, so the solution set does not change, and avoiding division by a tiny number limits rounding error.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how Gaussian elimination solves a system of linear equations, why the row operations are allowed, and name one limitation or risk of the method.
lessons.modelAnswer: Gaussian elimination turns a system of linear equations into an easier one with the same solutions. I write the equations as an augmented matrix, then use three row operations: swapping rows, scaling a row by a nonzero number, and adding a multiple of one row to another. These are safe because each can be undone, so no solutions are gained or lost. I use them to create zeros below each pivot until the matrix is in row echelon form, a staircase shape. Then I solve the bottom equation and back substitute upward. If I get a row saying 0 equals a nonzero number, there is no solution; a variable without a pivot is free, giving infinitely many solutions. One limitation is that on a computer, dividing by a very small pivot amplifies rounding error, so we swap in a larger pivot. It also costs about n³ operations, which grows fast for big systems.
rubricPoints: Defines a system of linear equations and what a solution is.
Describes the three elementary row operations and why they preserve solutions.
Explains reaching row echelon form and then back substitution.
Recognizes inconsistent systems (0 = nonzero) and free variables.
Names a limitation such as rounding error with small pivots or roughly n³ cost.

suggested.rationale: No current mission or planned engine exercises linear algebra, so reasoning through exam-style systems by hand, including inconsistent and free-variable cases, builds the skill best.

lessons.plain: A matrix is a rectangular grid of numbers arranged in rows and columns, like a spreadsheet with no labels. Matrix algebra is the set of rules for combining these grids: adding them, scaling them, flipping them, and multiplying them. Think of a matrix as a recipe card that turns ingredient amounts into dish amounts. Multiplying two matrices is like feeding one recipe's output into another. Because order matters in a kitchen, it matters here too. Doing step A then step B can give a different result from doing B then A. These rules are the everyday toolkit for the rest of linear algebra and for numerical computing.
lessons.guessPrompt: If you multiply a grid with 2 rows and 3 columns by a grid with 3 rows and 4 columns, how many rows and columns do you think the result has? Could you multiply them in the opposite order?
lessons.teach:
A matrix is a rectangular array of numbers. An m×n matrix has m rows and n columns. The number in row i, column j is called the (i,j) entry.

Addition works only for two matrices of the same size, and you add them entry by entry. Scalar multiplication multiplies every entry by one ordinary number, called a scalar. The transpose, written A^T, turns each row into a column, so an m×n matrix becomes n×m.

Matrix multiplication follows a different rule. The product AB exists only when the number of columns of A equals the number of rows of B. An m×n matrix times an n×p matrix gives an m×p matrix. Entry (i,j) of AB is the dot product of row i of A with column j of B: multiply the matching pairs of numbers and add them up. The rule is built this way because a matrix stands for a combining rule, and multiplying two matrices chains those rules together.

Worked example: let A = [[1,2],[3,4]] and B = [[0,1],[1,0]].
Entry (1,1) of AB: (1,2)·(0,1) = 0+2 = 2.
Entry (1,2): (1,2)·(1,0) = 1.
Entry (2,1): (3,4)·(0,1) = 4.
Entry (2,2): (3,4)·(1,0) = 3.
So AB = [[2,1],[4,3]], which is A with its columns swapped. Working out BA the same way gives [[3,4],[1,2]], which is A with its rows swapped. So AB ≠ BA.

The identity matrix I is square, with 1s on the main diagonal and 0s everywhere else. For any matching A, AI = IA = A. An inverse A^-1, when it exists, satisfies AA^-1 = A^-1A = I. Only square matrices can have one, and not every square matrix does.

A common mistake is to assume multiplication commutes (that AB always equals BA), or to multiply entry by entry. In numerical code, swapping the order of two square matrices produces wrong numbers with no error message. Swapping non-square matrices usually triggers a shape-mismatch error instead.

questions.prompt: A game studio's graphics code multiplies two 2×2 matrices, C = [[2,0],[1,3]] and D = [[1,4],[2,1]], to get CD. Each entry (i,j) of CD is the dot product of row i of C with column j of D. Entry (1,1) is (2,0)·(1,2) = 2+0 = 2. Entry (1,2) is (2,0)·(4,1) = 8+0 = 8. Entry (2,1) is (1,3)·(1,2) = 1+6 = 7. What is entry (2,2) of CD?
choices: 3, because 3 × 1 = 3 (multiplying the matching (2,2) entries)
4, because 1 × 4 = 4
questions.why: Entry (2,2) is the dot product of row 2 of C, (1,3), with column 2 of D, (4,1), giving 1×4 + 3×1 = 7.

questions.prompt: A data team stores a matrix A that is 4×3 and a matrix B that is 3×5. Which statement about the products AB and BA is correct?
choices: AB and BA both exist and are both 4×5
AB does not exist, but BA is 3×3
AB is 4×5, and BA does not exist
AB is 3×3, and BA does not exist
questions.why: AB needs A's columns (3) to equal B's rows (3), giving a 4×5 result, while BA would need B's 5 columns to match A's 4 rows, so BA is undefined.

questions.prompt: A logistics app has a matrix P that is 2×3 and a matrix Q that is 3×2. Which of these sums can actually be computed?
choices: Q + P^T, because transposing P makes it 2×3
P + Q^T, because transposing Q makes it 2×3
P + Q, because both matrices hold six numbers
P + Q, because addition does not depend on shape
questions.why: Addition needs two matrices of the same size, and the transpose turns the 3×2 matrix Q into a 2×3 matrix that matches P.

questions.prompt: In a simulation program, an engineer meant to compute XY for two 3×3 matrices X and Y but typed YX instead. What is the most likely result when the code runs?
choices: It stops with a shape-mismatch error, because the order was swapped
It runs without an error but usually produces wrong numbers, because matrix multiplication does not generally commute
It produces the transpose of the intended answer, so the result can be fixed by transposing
It produces the same answer, because two square matrices of the same size always commute
questions.why: Both orders are valid for two 3×3 matrices, so no error appears, but AB and BA are generally different, so the output is silently wrong.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how matrix multiplication works and when it is allowed, and name one way it behaves differently from multiplying ordinary numbers.
lessons.modelAnswer: A matrix is a grid of numbers with some count of rows and columns. Adding two matrices or multiplying one by a scalar happens entry by entry, and addition only works for matrices of the same size. Multiplication is different. AB is defined only when A's column count equals B's row count, and an m×n times an n×p gives an m×p result. To get entry (i,j), you take row i of A and column j of B, multiply the matching pairs, and add them. The big difference from ordinary numbers is that order matters. AB usually does not equal BA, and sometimes only one of the two orders is even defined. Also, not every square matrix has an inverse. The tradeoff to keep in mind is that in code, the wrong order with square matrices gives silently wrong answers rather than an error.
rubricPoints: Defines a matrix as a grid with rows and columns, and notes that addition requires equal sizes.
States the compatibility rule: columns of the first must equal rows of the second, and m×n times n×p gives m×p.
Describes each product entry as a row-times-column dot product.
Notes that matrix multiplication is not commutative.
Mentions the identity matrix or that inverses do not always exist.
Names a practical consequence, such as silent wrong results or shape errors in code.

suggested.rationale: No current mission or planned engine drills matrix arithmetic, so working exam-style problems by hand, such as checking dimensions and computing small products in both orders, builds the skill best.

lessons.plain: A linear transformation is a rule that moves vectors (arrows with a length and a direction) to new vectors while keeping straight lines straight and keeping the origin fixed in place. Picture a sheet of graph paper you can stretch, rotate, flip or squash. The grid lines stay evenly spaced and parallel, and the center point never moves. Because the rule is so well behaved, you only need to know what it does to a few starting arrows. Everything else follows from those, which is why such rules can be written compactly as a table of numbers called a matrix.
lessons.guessPrompt: A rule acting on arrows in the flat plane sends the arrow (1, 0) to (2, 0) and the arrow (0, 1) to (0, 2). If the rule treats sums and stretches fairly, where would you guess it sends the arrow (3, 5)?
lessons.teach:
A linear transformation is a function T that takes vectors from one vector space V to another vector space W and obeys two rules. A vector space is a set of vectors that you can add together and scale. The first rule is T(u + v) = T(u) + T(v) for any vectors u and v. The second is T(cu) = cT(u) for any scalar c, where a scalar is an ordinary number. Together these rules say that T respects adding and scaling. One consequence follows straight away: T(0) = 0, because T(0) = T(0·u) = 0·T(u) = 0.

This matters because every vector in R^n is a combination of the standard basis vectors e1, ..., en. A basis is a smallest set of vectors whose combinations reach every vector in the space. By linearity, T(x1 e1 + ... + xn en) = x1 T(e1) + ... + xn T(en). So once you know where T sends each basis vector, you know T everywhere. Place those images side by side as columns and you get the standard matrix A, with T(x) = Ax.

Worked example: let T(x, y) = (2x + y, x − y). Each output entry is a plain sum of number-times-input, so both rules hold. First, T(e1) = T(1, 0) = (2, 1). Next, T(e2) = T(0, 1) = (1, −1). That makes A the matrix with rows [2 1] and [1 −1]. Test it on (3, 4). Computing directly gives (6 + 4, 3 − 4) = (10, −1). Using the columns gives 3·(2, 1) + 4·(1, −1) = (10, −1). The two answers match.

Two sets describe any T. The kernel is every input sent to zero. The range is every output T can actually produce. In the example above, only (0, 0) maps to zero, so T loses no information.

A common mistake is calling a shift such as T(x) = x + (1, 0) linear because it looks like a straight-line move. It sends 0 to (1, 0), so it fails the test. Such maps are called affine, and they have no plain matrix form on their own. In numerical code, treating a non-linear step as a matrix multiply produces silently wrong answers.

questions.prompt: A graphics team uses the map T(x, y) = (x + 3y, 4x) and wants its standard matrix A. Each output entry is a plain sum of number-times-input, so T is linear. Step 1: T(e1) = T(1, 0) = (1 + 0, 4·1) = (1, 4). Step 2: [missing]. Step 3: Place the images side by side as columns, so A has rows [1 3] and [4 0]. Step 4: Check on (2, 5). Directly, T(2, 5) = (2 + 15, 8) = (17, 8). Using the columns, 2·(1, 4) + 5·(3, 0) = (17, 8). The answers match. What is the missing Step 2?
questions.why: Plugging x = 0 and y = 1 into T gives (3, 0), and that result becomes the second column of A, matching the check in Step 4.

questions.prompt: Which of these maps from R^2 to R^2 is a linear transformation?
choices: T(x, y) = (x², y)
T(x, y) = (3y, x − y)
T(x, y) = (x·y, x)
questions.why: Each entry of (3y, x − y) is a plain sum of number-times-input, so T respects adding and scaling. The shift sends 0 to (2, 0), and the product and square terms break the scaling rule: doubling the input does not double the output.

questions.prompt: The kernel of a linear transformation is the set of every input it sends to zero. For T(x, y) = (x − y, 2x − 2y), which input is in the kernel?
questions.why: T(1, 1) = (1 − 1, 2 − 2) = (0, 0). Each of the other inputs produces a nonzero output.

questions.prompt: A linear transformation T on R^2 sends e1 = (1, 0) to (5, −2) and e2 = (0, 1) to (1, 3). What is T(2, −1)?

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what makes a transformation linear and why that lets you replace it with a matrix. Name one kind of map that looks simple but is not linear, and say what that costs you.
lessons.modelAnswer: A transformation T is linear if it respects the two vector operations. Transforming a sum gives the sum of the transforms, and transforming a scaled vector gives the scaled transform. That means you never need a formula for every input. Any vector is a combination of basis vectors, so T of that vector is the same combination of T applied to each basis vector. Write those basis images as the columns of a matrix A, and applying T is just computing Ax. A quick sanity check is that T must send zero to zero. A shift like x plus a fixed vector fails that check, so it is affine, not linear. That is the tradeoff: shifts are useful, but you lose the direct matrix form. You have to handle the shift separately, for example with an extra coordinate, or your matrix-based calculations will be wrong.
rubricPoints: States both rules: T(u+v)=T(u)+T(v) and T(cu)=cT(u).
Notes that a linear map must send the zero vector to zero.
Explains that the images of the basis vectors determine T completely.
Says the standard matrix has those images as its columns, so T(x)=Ax.
Identifies a translation (shift) as non-linear and names the loss of a plain matrix form.

suggested.rationale: No current mission or planned engine exercises linear algebra, and the core skill is explaining why linearity reduces a map to its matrix and where that breaks down.

lessons.plain: Most of the time, multiplying a vector by a matrix both stretches it and turns it to point somewhere new. A few special directions are not turned at all. They only get stretched, shrunk, or flipped. An arrow pointing in one of those directions is an eigenvector. The amount it gets stretched is its eigenvalue. Think of kneading dough on a board. Most specks of flour swirl around, but a speck lying along the exact line you push stays on that line and only moves farther out. Those special lines show what the matrix really does.
lessons.guessPrompt: A matrix doubles every vector that lies on the x-axis, keeping it on the x-axis. What stretch factor would you guess goes with that direction, and would the vector (0, 0) count as a special direction?
lessons.teach:
An eigenvector of a square matrix A is a nonzero vector v that A only rescales, so that A·v = λ·v. The number λ (lambda) is the eigenvalue that belongs to v. If λ is 3, v is tripled. If λ is 1/2, v is halved. If λ is negative, v is flipped to point the opposite way.

To find eigenvalues, rewrite A·v = λ·v as (A − λI)·v = 0. Here I is the identity matrix, which has 1s on the diagonal and 0s elsewhere. We need a nonzero v that solves this equation. That happens only when A − λI is singular, meaning it squashes some direction down to zero. A matrix is singular exactly when its determinant is zero. The determinant is a single number computed from a square matrix; for the 2×2 matrix [[a,b],[c,d]] it equals ad − bc. Setting det(A − λI) = 0 gives the characteristic polynomial. Its roots are the eigenvalues.

Worked example: take A = [[2,1],[1,2]].
First, A − λI = [[2−λ, 1],[1, 2−λ]].
Its determinant is (2−λ)² − 1 = λ² − 4λ + 3 = (λ−1)(λ−3), so λ = 3 or λ = 1.
For λ = 3, A − 3I = [[−1,1],[1,−1]], which forces x = y, so v = (1,1). Check: A·(1,1) = (3,3) = 3·(1,1).
For λ = 1, A − I = [[1,1],[1,1]], which forces y = −x, so v = (1,−1). Check: A·(1,−1) = (1,−1).

Common mistake: forgetting that any nonzero multiple of an eigenvector is also an eigenvector, so (2,2) is just as correct as (1,1). A related error is counting the zero vector, which satisfies the equation for every λ and so is excluded by definition. Another slip is computing det(A) − λ instead of det(A − λI).

Why it matters later: in Numerical Methods, repeatedly multiplying by a matrix makes vectors line up with the eigenvector of largest absolute eigenvalue. That is the idea behind the power method. Eigenvalues above 1 in absolute value make a repeated process blow up, and eigenvalues below 1 make it settle down.

questions.prompt:
A warehouse robot's motion model uses the matrix A = [[4,1],[2,3]]. We want its eigenvalues and eigenvectors.

Step 1: A − λI = [[4−λ, 1],[2, 3−λ]].
Step 2: MISSING. Compute the determinant of A − λI and factor it.
Step 3: The roots are λ = 5 and λ = 2.
Step 4: For λ = 5, A − 5I = [[−1,1],[2,−2]], which forces x = y, so v = (1,1). Check: A·(1,1) = (5,5) = 5·(1,1).
Step 5: For λ = 2, A − 2I = [[2,1],[2,1]], which forces y = −2x, so v = (1,−2). Check: A·(1,−2) = (2,−4) = 2·(1,−2).

Which line correctly fills in Step 2?
choices: (4−λ)(3−λ) = 0, so the diagonal entries give the roots
questions.why: Using ad − bc on A − λI gives (4−λ)(3−λ) − (1)(2) = λ² − 7λ + 10, whose roots 2 and 5 match Steps 3 to 5.

questions.prompt: For the matrix A = [[1,3],[3,1]] and the vector v = (1,−1), you compute A·v = (−2, 2). What does this tell you?
choices: v is an eigenvector with eigenvalue 2, because the entries of A·v are twice the size of v's entries
v is an eigenvector with eigenvalue −1/2, so A halves v and flips it
v is an eigenvector with eigenvalue −2, so A doubles v's length and flips it to point the opposite way
v is not an eigenvector, because A·v points in a different direction than v
questions.why: (−2, 2) = −2·(1, −1), so A·v = λ·v with λ = −2. A negative eigenvalue flips the vector, and an absolute value of 2 doubles its length.

questions.prompt: A classmate finds that (2, −1) is an eigenvector of some 2×2 matrix B with eigenvalue 4. Which other vector must also be an eigenvector of B for the eigenvalue 4?
choices: (2, 1), because it has the same size entries
(1, −2), because it uses the same numbers
questions.why: (−6, 3) is −3 times (2, −1). Any nonzero multiple of an eigenvector is also an eigenvector for the same eigenvalue. The zero vector is excluded by definition.

questions.prompt: A simulation repeatedly multiplies a starting vector by a matrix M. M has eigenvalue −3 with eigenvector (1, 2), and eigenvalue 2 with eigenvector (1, −1). After many steps from a typical starting vector, what happens?
choices: The vector lines up with (1, −1), because 2 is the largest eigenvalue
The vector stays roughly the same size, because the eigenvalues −3 and 2 cancel out
The vector lines up with (1, 2) and keeps growing, flipping direction each step
The vector settles down to zero, because one eigenvalue is negative
questions.why: Repeated multiplication lines vectors up with the eigenvector whose eigenvalue has the largest absolute value. That is −3 here. Because |−3| > 1, the process blows up, and the negative sign flips the direction each step.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what an eigenvector and an eigenvalue are and how you would find them for a 2×2 matrix. Name one limit or catch, for example why eigenvectors are not unique or why the zero vector is excluded.
lessons.modelAnswer: An eigenvector of a square matrix is a nonzero direction that the matrix does not rotate. It only scales it, so A·v = λ·v, and that scale factor λ is the eigenvalue. To find them, I move everything to one side to get (A − λI)·v = 0. A nonzero solution exists only when A − λI is singular, so I set its determinant to zero and solve the resulting characteristic polynomial for λ. Then, for each λ, I solve (A − λI)·v = 0 to get the direction. For [[2,1],[1,2]] that gives λ = 3 with (1,1) and λ = 1 with (1,−1). One catch is that an eigenvector is really a whole line of answers: any nonzero multiple works. The zero vector is excluded because it would satisfy the equation for every λ and tell us nothing.
rubricPoints: States that A·v = λ·v with v nonzero, and that λ is the scale factor.
Explains that eigenvalues come from solving det(A − λI) = 0, the characteristic polynomial.
Describes finding each eigenvector by solving (A − λI)·v = 0 for that λ.
Notes that eigenvectors are defined only up to a nonzero multiple.
Explains why the zero vector is excluded.

suggested.rationale: No OpsForge mission or planned engine covers linear algebra, so working through exam-style matrices by hand and then explaining the method back builds this skill best.

lessons.plain: Interpolation means filling in the gaps between values you already know. Suppose you measured the temperature at 9:00, 10:00 and 11:00, and someone asks what it was at 10:30. You draw a smooth curve that passes exactly through your measured points, then read the answer off that curve. It is like connecting the dots in a children's puzzle, except you choose a sensible curve instead of straight lines. Interpolation lets you treat a short table of numbers as if it were a full function you can evaluate anywhere inside the measured range. It does not reliably tell you what happens outside that range.
lessons.guessPrompt: You know a quantity equals 1 when x is 0, 3 when x is 1, and 7 when x is 2. Without any formula, what would you guess the value is at x = 1.5, and why?
lessons.teach:
Interpolation is the task of building a function that passes exactly through a set of known data points, called nodes, so you can estimate values between them. The most common choice is a polynomial, a sum of powers of x such as x² + x + 1. Its degree is the highest power. A key fact: through n+1 points with distinct x-values there is exactly one polynomial of degree at most n. That uniqueness is why the method works. The answer is fixed, and different formulas are just different ways of writing the same polynomial.

The Lagrange form writes the polynomial as a weighted sum of basis polynomials. Each basis polynomial equals 1 at its own node and 0 at every other node. The Newton form builds the polynomial one node at a time using divided differences. A divided difference is a slope of slopes. The first-order difference is (change in y)/(change in x) between neighbouring nodes. Each higher order divides the change in the previous differences by the x-span they cover. Newton's form is convenient because adding a new point only adds one new term.

Worked example with points (0,1), (1,3), (2,7). The zeroth-order values are 1, 3 and 7. The first-order differences are (3−1)/(1−0)=2 and (7−3)/(2−1)=4. The second-order difference is (4−2)/(2−0)=1. Newton's form gives P(x) = 1 + 2x + 1·x(x−1) = x² + x + 1. Check: P(2)=7. Estimate: P(1.5)=4.75.

A common mistake is fitting one high-degree polynomial through many equally spaced points. The curve can wiggle wildly near the ends, which is called the Runge phenomenon. A spline avoids this by using low-degree pieces, usually cubics, joined smoothly at the nodes. A second mistake is extrapolation, meaning evaluating the polynomial outside the range of the nodes, where errors grow quickly. In a running system, such as a sensor dashboard, either mistake produces confident but false readings.

questions.prompt: A greenhouse controller logs temperature (in degrees above a baseline) at three times: hour 1 reads 2, hour 3 reads 8, and hour 4 reads 14. You build the Newton-form interpolating polynomial. The zeroth-order values are 2, 8 and 14. The first-order divided differences are (8−2)/(3−1) = 3 and (14−8)/(4−3) = 6. MISSING STEP: the second-order divided difference. With it, the polynomial is P(x) = 2 + 3(x−1) + c·(x−1)(x−3), where c is that second-order difference. Check: P(4) = 2 + 9 + 3c should equal 14. What is the second-order divided difference c?
questions.why: A higher-order divided difference divides the change in the previous differences (6−3) by the full x-span they cover (from x=1 to x=4, so 3), giving 1, and P(4) = 2 + 9 + 3 = 14 confirms it.

questions.prompt: A water utility records pressure at five pump stations, each at a different distance along a pipeline (all x-values distinct). Two engineers each build an interpolating polynomial through all five points. One uses the Lagrange form and the other uses the Newton form, and their formulas look different on paper. Which statement is true?
choices: They have found two different polynomials of degree 5, and both pass through the points
They have written the same polynomial of degree at most 4 in two different ways
Only the Newton version is exact, because Lagrange basis polynomials are approximations
There are infinitely many degree-4 polynomials through five points, so the results will usually disagree between nodes
questions.why: Through n+1 points with distinct x-values there is exactly one polynomial of degree at most n, so five points fix a single polynomial of degree at most 4, and the two forms are just different ways of writing it.

questions.prompt: A civil engineering team has 15 strain readings taken at equally spaced positions along a bridge deck. They fit a single degree-14 polynomial through all of them. Between the middle readings the curve looks reasonable, but near the two ends of the deck it swings far above and below the measured values. What is happening, and what is the usual fix?
choices: The readings must contain measurement noise, because an interpolating polynomial can never overshoot between nodes
This is the Runge phenomenon, and the usual fix is a spline made of low-degree pieces, typically cubics, joined smoothly at the nodes
This is extrapolation error, and the fix is to add more equally spaced readings so the polynomial degree rises
The Newton form is unstable here, and switching to the Lagrange form will remove the swings
questions.why: A single high-degree polynomial through many equally spaced points tends to wiggle wildly near the ends (the Runge phenomenon), and a spline avoids this by using low-degree pieces joined smoothly.

questions.prompt: A shipping company interpolates fuel use at three cruising speeds: 2, 5 and 9 knots. Using the Lagrange form, it builds the basis polynomial that belongs to the node at 5 knots. What values does this basis polynomial take at 2, 5 and 9 knots?
choices: 0 at 2 knots, 1 at 5 knots, 0 at 9 knots
The measured fuel use at each of the three speeds
0 at 2 knots, 5 at 5 knots, 0 at 9 knots
1 at 2 knots, 1 at 5 knots, 1 at 9 knots
questions.why: Each Lagrange basis polynomial equals 1 at its own node and 0 at every other node, and the measured values enter only as the weights in the sum.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how polynomial interpolation turns a few data points into an estimate between them, and describe one situation where it gives bad answers and what you would use instead.
lessons.modelAnswer: Interpolation fits a function that passes exactly through the known points so we can estimate values in between. With n+1 points at distinct x-values there is exactly one polynomial of degree at most n through them. Lagrange and Newton forms are just two ways to write that same polynomial. Newton's form uses divided differences, slopes of slopes, and it is handy because adding a point adds only one term. For example, (0,1), (1,3) and (2,7) give x² + x + 1, so the estimate at 1.5 is 4.75. The limits: if you push one high-degree polynomial through many evenly spaced points, it oscillates badly near the ends. That is the Runge phenomenon, and a cubic spline, made of smooth low-degree pieces, is the better tool there. Also, interpolation is only trustworthy inside the data range. Extrapolating beyond it can be badly wrong.
rubricPoints: Defines interpolation as a function passing exactly through known points to estimate values between them.
States that the interpolating polynomial through n+1 distinct points is unique, with Lagrange and Newton being different forms of it.
Describes divided differences or basis polynomials correctly.
Names the Runge phenomenon or high-degree oscillation as a limit.
Offers splines as the remedy and warns against extrapolation.

suggested.rationale: Interpolation is mastered by working exam-style problems, such as building a divided-difference table and judging when a spline beats a single polynomial, and no current mission covers numerical math.

lessons.plain: Calculus gives exact formulas for slopes (derivatives) and areas (integrals), but real problems often hand you only a table of measured values, or a function too messy to work with by hand. Numerical differentiation estimates a slope from nearby sample points. Numerical integration estimates an area by chopping it into simple shapes and adding them up. Think of judging a car's speed from two dashcam frames a split second apart, or measuring an oddly shaped garden by covering it with thin strips and summing their areas. The answers are approximations, and the skill is knowing how close they are and how to make them closer.
lessons.guessPrompt: You know f(1.0) = 1.00 and f(1.1) = 1.21. Without any formula, what would you guess the slope of f near x = 1 is, and do you think your guess is a little too high, too low, or exact?
lessons.teach:
Numerical differentiation estimates a derivative from function values at nearby points. The distance between those points is the step size, written h. A finite difference is the estimate itself. The forward difference uses (f(x+h) − f(x)) / h. The central difference uses (f(x+h) − f(x−h)) / (2h) and is usually more accurate because errors on the two sides largely cancel. Truncation error is the error from replacing the true limit with a finite step. Forward difference truncation error shrinks in proportion to h. Central difference error shrinks in proportion to h squared.

Numerical integration, also called quadrature, estimates an integral by summing simple shapes. The trapezoidal rule joins neighbouring points with straight lines and adds the trapezoid areas. Simpson's rule fits parabolas through groups of three points. It needs an even number of intervals and is far more accurate for smooth functions.

Worked example with f(x) = x², where the true derivative at 1 is 2. Take h = 0.1. Forward: (1.21 − 1.00)/0.1 = 2.1, which is off by 0.1. Central: (1.21 − 0.81)/0.2 = 2.0, which is exact here. Now integrate x² from 0 to 2, where the true value is 8/3 ≈ 2.667, using h = 1 and points 0, 1, 2 with values 0, 1, 4. Trapezoid: h × (0/2 + 1 + 4/2) = 3, too big. Simpson: (h/3) × (0 + 4×1 + 4) = 8/3, exact, because Simpson's rule is exact for polynomials up to cubics.

A common mistake is assuming a smaller h always helps. Round-off error is the error from the computer storing numbers with limited digits. For derivatives, f(x+h) and f(x) become nearly equal as h shrinks. Subtracting them loses significant digits, and dividing by a tiny h magnifies that loss. Past a certain point the estimate gets worse. Noisy measured data makes this much worse. A system that estimates speed by differencing jittery sensor readings at very fine steps will report wildly swinging values. Integration averages noise out and is therefore far more forgiving than differentiation.

questions.prompt: A lab estimates the derivative of f(x) = x³ at x = 2. The true value is 12. They use step size h = 0.1, the distance between the sample points. Step 1: f(2.1) = 9.261, f(2) = 8, and f(1.9) = 6.859. Step 2: the forward difference is (9.261 − 8)/0.1 = 12.61, which is off by 0.61. Step 3 (missing): compute the central difference estimate, which uses the points on both sides of x = 2. Step 4: compare the error of Step 3 with the 0.61 error of the forward difference. What is the result of Step 3?
questions.why: The central difference is (f(2.1) − f(1.9))/(2h) = (9.261 − 6.859)/0.2 = 2.402/0.2 = 12.01, which is off by only 0.01 because errors on the two sides largely cancel.

questions.prompt: An engineer integrates g(x) = x³ from 0 to 2 using Simpson's rule, which fits a parabola through groups of three points. She uses h = 1, so the points are 0, 1 and 2, with values 0, 1 and 8. What value does Simpson's rule give?
questions.why: Simpson gives (h/3) × (0 + 4×1 + 8) = (1/3) × 12 = 4, which matches the true value exactly because Simpson's rule is exact for polynomials up to cubics.

questions.prompt: A developer estimates a derivative with a forward difference. Shrinking the step size h from 0.01 to 0.0001 improves the answer. Shrinking it further to 0.000000000001 makes the answer much worse. What is the best explanation?
choices: Truncation error grows as h shrinks, so very small steps always lose accuracy
The forward difference only works for step sizes larger than 0.001
Simpson's rule should have been used, because it needs an even number of intervals
Round-off error: f(x+h) and f(x) become nearly equal, so subtracting them loses significant digits, and dividing by the tiny h magnifies that loss
questions.why: Truncation error shrinks as h shrinks. Below some point, round-off from subtracting nearly equal stored numbers, then dividing by a tiny h, takes over and makes the estimate worse.

questions.prompt: Using the central difference, which takes points on both sides of x, a team measures a truncation error of about 0.08 with step size h = 0.2. Truncation error is the error from using a finite step instead of the true limit. Ignoring round-off error, roughly what truncation error should they expect with h = 0.1?
choices: About 0.02
About 0.16
About 0.08
About 0.04
questions.why: Central difference truncation error shrinks in proportion to h squared, so halving h cuts the error to about a quarter: 0.08/4 = 0.02.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would estimate a derivative and an integral from sampled data, and describe the tradeoff in choosing the step size h.
lessons.modelAnswer: To estimate a derivative, take function values at points a small step h apart and compute a finite difference. The central version, (f(x+h) − f(x−h))/(2h), is usually better than the forward one because its truncation error shrinks like h² rather than h. To estimate an integral, slice the interval into pieces and add simple shapes. The trapezoidal rule uses straight-line tops. Simpson's rule uses parabolas, needs an even number of slices, and is much more accurate on smooth functions. The tradeoff is the step size. A smaller h reduces truncation error. For derivatives, though, it also means subtracting nearly equal numbers and dividing by something tiny, so round-off error and any measurement noise get amplified. There is a sweet spot, not a 'smaller is always better' rule. Integration is more forgiving because summing tends to average noise out.
rubricPoints: States that finite differences estimate derivatives from nearby values separated by a step h.
Notes that central difference is generally more accurate than forward difference.
Describes trapezoidal and Simpson's rules as summing simple shapes, with Simpson more accurate for smooth functions.
Explains that shrinking h cuts truncation error but raises round-off error for derivatives.
Mentions that differentiation amplifies noise while integration tends to smooth it.

suggested.rationale: Writing small functions for forward and central differences and the trapezoidal and Simpson rules, then watching the error change as h shrinks, makes the truncation-versus-round-off tradeoff concrete.

lessons.plain: Many real problems describe how something changes rather than what it is: how fast a tank drains, how a population grows, how a rocket speeds up. These change rules are called differential equations, and most cannot be solved with a neat formula. A numerical solution builds the answer step by step instead. It starts from a known value, uses the rule to estimate where things are heading, takes a small step in that direction, and repeats. It is like crossing a dark field with a flashlight: look at the direction the ground slopes, walk a few paces, look again. Smaller paces keep you closer to the true path, but the trip takes more steps.
lessons.guessPrompt: If y starts at 1 and its rate of change always equals its current value, and you estimate y at time 1 by taking two steps of size 0.5, each using the slope from the start of the step, will your estimate be too high or too low compared with the true answer, and why?
lessons.teach:
A differential equation (DE) is an equation relating a quantity to its rate of change, written y' = f(t, y), where y' is the slope of y with respect to time t. An initial value problem gives a starting point, y(t0) = y0. A numerical method produces approximate values y1, y2, ... at times spaced by a step size h.

The simplest is Euler's method: y(n+1) = y(n) + h times f(t(n), y(n)). It works because, over a short step, a smooth curve looks almost like its tangent line, so following the current slope lands close to the true curve.

Worked example: y' = y, y(0) = 1, target t = 1 (exact answer e, about 2.718). With h = 0.5: step 1, slope is 1, so y1 = 1 + 0.5(1) = 1.5. Step 2, slope is 1.5, so y2 = 1.5 + 0.5(1.5) = 2.25. Error about 0.47. With h = 0.25 the four values are 1.25, 1.5625, 1.953, 2.441, error about 0.28. Halving h roughly halved the error, which is what first order means: global error, the total error accumulated at the end, shrinks in proportion to h. The local error, made in one step, is proportional to h squared. Higher-order methods such as fourth-order Runge-Kutta (RK4) sample the slope at several points inside each step and average them; their global error shrinks like h to the fourth power, so halving h cuts error about sixteenfold.

A common mistake is ignoring stability. For y' = -50y, the true solution decays quickly, but Euler with h = 0.1 multiplies y by (1 - 5) = -4 each step, so the answer oscillates and explodes. Equations with such fast-decaying parts are called stiff; they need a tiny h or an implicit method, which uses the slope at the end of the step. In a running simulation, an unstable step size silently produces garbage or overflow, so step size must be chosen for both accuracy and stability.

questions.prompt:
A city water utility models a reservoir's level y (in metres) with y' = 3 - y, starting empty: y(0) = 0. An analyst uses Euler's method, y(n+1) = y(n) + h times f(t(n), y(n)), with step size h = 0.2.

Step 1: the slope at y0 = 0 is 3 - 0 = 3, so y1 = 0 + 0.2(3) = 0.6.
Step 2: ???
Step 3: the slope at y2 is 3 - 1.08 = 1.92, so y3 = 1.08 + 0.2(1.92) = 1.464.

Which line correctly fills in Step 2?
choices: The slope is still 3 from the start, so y2 = 0.6 + 0.2(3) = 1.2.
questions.why: Euler re-evaluates the slope at the current value (3 - 0.6 = 2.4), multiplies it by h, and adds the result to the current value, giving 0.6 + 0.48 = 1.08.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm simulates a delivery drone's battery drain with fourth-order Runge-Kutta (RK4). With step size h = 0.1 the global error at the end of the run is about 0.008. If they rerun with h = 0.05, roughly what global error should they expect?
choices: About 0.004
About 0.008, because step size does not affect error
About 0.0005
About 0.002
questions.why: RK4's global error shrinks like h to the fourth power, so halving h divides the error by about 2^4 = 16, and 0.008 / 16 = 0.0005.

questions.prompt: A chemistry lab models a reactant that decays as y' = -30y, starting at y(0) = 2. A student applies Euler's method with h = 0.1. What happens to the computed values?
choices: Each step multiplies y by 0.7, so the values decay smoothly toward zero, matching the true solution.
Each step multiplies y by 1 - 0.3 = 0.7 at first, then the step size automatically shrinks to keep the run stable.
Each step multiplies y by -3, but because the true solution decays, the error cancels out after a few steps.
Each step multiplies y by 1 - 3 = -2, so the values flip sign and grow in size, even though the true solution decays.
questions.why: Euler gives y(n+1) = y(n) + 0.1(-30 y(n)) = (1 - 3) y(n) = -2 y(n), so the values oscillate and explode, an instability caused by the step size being too large for this fast-decaying equation.

questions.prompt: An engineer at a power company finds that a circuit model contains a component that decays extremely fast, and an explicit Euler run with a moderate step size blows up. Which statement correctly names the situation and a suitable fix?
choices: The equation is unstable by nature; no numerical method can handle it, so the true solution must also blow up.
The equation has large local error; the fix is to keep h the same and run more total steps past the target time.
The equation is first order; the fix is to switch to RK4, since a higher order always removes instability at any step size.
The equation is stiff; the fix is a much smaller step size or an implicit method, which uses the slope at the end of the step.
questions.why: Equations with fast-decaying parts are called stiff, and they need either a tiny h or an implicit method that evaluates the slope at the end of each step to stay stable.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how Euler's method approximates the solution of a differential equation, and describe the tradeoff involved in choosing the step size, including one way it can go wrong.
lessons.modelAnswer: We start from the known initial value and repeatedly follow the slope the equation gives us: new value equals old value plus step size times the slope at the current point. That works because over a short step the curve is close to its tangent line. The catch is that every step adds a little error, and with Euler the total error at the end shrinks only in proportion to the step size, so halving h roughly halves the error while doubling the work. Methods like RK4 sample several slopes per step and converge much faster, at more cost per step. Step size also affects stability: on a stiff equation like y' = -50y, a step of 0.1 makes each update multiply by -4, so the answer blows up even though the true solution decays. Then you need a smaller step or an implicit method.
rubricPoints: States the Euler update: new value equals old value plus step size times current slope.
Explains that it works because a curve is close to its tangent line over a short step.
Notes Euler is first order: global error shrinks roughly in proportion to step size.
Names the cost tradeoff: smaller steps or higher-order methods like RK4 mean more computation.
Identifies instability on stiff equations when the step size is too large.

suggested.rationale: Coding an Euler loop and watching the error halve with h, then blow up on a stiff equation, teaches the method and its limits better than reading alone.

lessons.plain: Root-finding means hunting for the input that makes a function equal zero, when you cannot solve the equation neatly with algebra. Instead of one formula, you make a guess, check how wrong it is, and improve it, over and over, until the answer is close enough. It is like the children's game of hot and cold: each hint narrows where the hidden object can be. Some methods are slow but can never get lost. Others are very fast but can wander off if your first guess is poor. Choosing between them means trading speed against safety.
lessons.guessPrompt: You know a function is negative at x = 1 and positive at x = 2, and its graph has no gaps. Where would you check next to find where it crosses zero, and why?
lessons.teach:
A root of a function f is an input x where f(x) = 0. Root-finding methods are iterative, meaning each step improves on the last guess, and they home in on a root when algebra cannot solve the equation directly.

Bisection starts with an interval [a, b] where f(a) and f(b) have opposite signs. If f is continuous (no jumps), it must cross zero inside, by the Intermediate Value Theorem. Check the midpoint m, keep whichever half still has a sign change, and repeat. Each step halves the interval, so it always converges, but slowly.

Newton's method uses the derivative f'(x), the slope of the curve. From a guess x, follow the tangent line to where it hits zero: x_new = x − f(x)/f'(x). Near a simple root it converges quadratically, roughly doubling the correct digits each step. The secant method replaces f'(x) with the slope through the last two guesses, avoiding derivatives at the cost of slightly slower convergence.

Worked example: find √2, the root of f(x) = x² − 2. Bisection on [1, 2]: f(1) = −1, f(2) = 2. Midpoint 1.5 gives 0.25, positive, so keep [1, 1.5]. Midpoint 1.25 gives −0.4375, negative, so keep [1.25, 1.5]. Progress is steady but slow. Newton from x = 1, with f'(x) = 2x: x = 1 − (−1)/2 = 1.5; then 1.5 − 0.25/3 ≈ 1.4167; then ≈ 1.414216, six correct digits after three steps.

Common mistake: trusting Newton blindly. If f'(x) is near zero the step shoots far away, and a poor starting guess can cycle or diverge. Bisection fails if the starting interval has no sign change.

In running code, always stop on a tolerance (|f(x)| or the step size small enough) and a maximum iteration count; otherwise a divergent case loops forever or returns garbage. Hybrid methods combine bisection's safety with Newton's speed.

questions.prompt:
A solar-panel company's sizing script needs the square root of 7, which is the root of f(x) = x² − 7. It uses Newton's method, x_new = x − f(x)/f'(x), with derivative f'(x) = 2x, starting from x = 3.

Step 1: f(3) = 9 − 7 = 2 and f'(3) = 6, so x = 3 − 2/6 ≈ 2.6667.
Step 2: f(2.6667) ≈ 7.1111 − 7 = 0.1111 and f'(2.6667) ≈ 5.3333, so x = ?

Which completion of step 2 is correct?
questions.why: Newton subtracts f(x) divided by the slope at the current guess, so the step is 2.6667 − 0.1111/5.3333 ≈ 2.6458, which is already close to √7 ≈ 2.6458.

questions.prompt: A logistics team uses bisection to find a root of f(x) = x³ − x − 3. They start on the interval [1, 2], where f(1) = −3 and f(2) = 3. At the midpoint 1.5, f(1.5) = 3.375 − 1.5 − 3 = −1.125. Which interval should the next step use?
choices: [1, 2], because the midpoint did not give zero
questions.why: f(1.5) is negative and f(2) is positive, so the sign change, and therefore the root, lies in [1.5, 2].

questions.prompt: An analyst runs Newton's method on f(x) = x² − 9, whose positive root is 3. The derivative is f'(x) = 2x, and the starting guess is x = 0.001, so f'(0.001) = 0.002. What does the first Newton step produce?
choices: About 4500, far from the root, because the nearly flat tangent line sends the step a long way
About 0.001, essentially no change, because a small derivative makes the step tiny
An immediate halt, because the starting interval has no sign change
About 3 right away, because Newton's method converges quadratically
questions.why: Dividing f(x) ≈ −9 by the tiny slope 0.002 gives a huge step of about 4500, which shows how a derivative near zero throws Newton's method far off.

questions.prompt: A developer is writing a production root-finding loop that may sometimes be handed a starting guess for which Newton's method diverges or cycles. Which stopping rule makes the loop safe?
choices: Stop only when the step size falls below a tolerance
Stop when |f(x)| or the step size is below a tolerance, or when a maximum iteration count is reached
Stop only when f(x) equals exactly zero
Always run exactly three iterations, since Newton usually gives six correct digits by then
questions.why: A tolerance ends the loop once the answer is good enough, and a maximum iteration count stops a divergent or cycling case from looping forever or returning garbage.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how bisection and Newton's method each find a root, and tell them when you would pick one over the other, naming the tradeoff.
lessons.modelAnswer: Both methods find where f(x) = 0 by improving a guess repeatedly. Bisection needs an interval where f changes sign; since a continuous function must cross zero there, I check the midpoint, keep the half that still changes sign, and repeat. It halves the error each step, so it is guaranteed to converge but slow. Newton's method takes my current guess, draws the tangent line using the derivative, and jumps to where that line hits zero. Near the root it roughly doubles the correct digits each step, so it is far faster, but it needs the derivative and a decent starting guess; if the slope is near zero or I start badly, it can diverge or cycle. I would use bisection when reliability matters or I lack a good guess, Newton when I have a derivative and a close guess, and in code I would always add a tolerance and an iteration cap.
rubricPoints: Defines a root as an input where f(x) equals zero.
Explains bisection keeps the half-interval with a sign change and always converges, but slowly.
Explains Newton follows the tangent line using the derivative and converges very fast near the root.
Names Newton's risks: zero or tiny derivative, bad starting guess, divergence.
Mentions stopping rules: a tolerance plus a maximum iteration count.

suggested.rationale: Coding bisection and Newton loops with tolerances and iteration caps, then watching them converge or diverge, builds the intuition faster than reading.

lessons.plain: Solving a linear system means finding values for several unknowns that make a set of straight-line equations all true at once, like finding the price of an apple and a banana from two shopping receipts. With two or three unknowns you can do it by hand. Real problems such as structural models, circuit simulations and graphics can involve thousands or millions of unknowns, so we use step-by-step recipes a computer can follow. Numerical methods are those recipes. Because a computer keeps only a limited number of digits, they must also stop small rounding slips from snowballing into a wrong answer.
lessons.guessPrompt: A computer keeps only about 16 significant digits. Suppose solving a system requires you to divide by a coefficient of 0.0000001 when you could have rearranged the equations and divided by 5 instead. Which choice would you trust more, and why?
lessons.teach:
A linear system is a set of equations like ax + by = c, where every unknown appears only to the first power. It can be written as Ax = b: A is the matrix (a grid) of coefficients, x is the list of unknowns, and b is the list of right-hand sides.

The main direct method is Gaussian elimination. You subtract multiples of one equation from the others to clear out unknowns until the system becomes triangular, meaning the last equation has one unknown, the one above it has two, and so on. Then back substitution solves from the bottom up. The number you divide by at each step is called the pivot.

Worked example: 2x + y = 5 and 4x + 3y = 11. The pivot is 2. Subtract 2 times row one from row two, which gives (4−4)x + (3−2)y = 11−10, so y = 1. Back substitute: 2x + 1 = 5, so x = 2. Check: 4(2) + 3(1) = 11.

Partial pivoting means swapping rows so the largest available number in the current column becomes the pivot. Dividing by a tiny pivot makes huge multipliers, and those magnify rounding error. LU decomposition stores the elimination as a lower-triangular matrix L times an upper-triangular matrix U. You then reuse the factorization cheaply for many different b vectors.

For very large sparse systems, where most entries are zero, iterative methods are often better. They start with a guess and refine it. Jacobi updates every unknown using the previous guess. Gauss-Seidel uses each new value as soon as it is computed. Both are guaranteed to converge when A is diagonally dominant, meaning each diagonal entry is larger in size than the sum of the other entries in its row.

A common mistake is computing the inverse of A and multiplying it by b. This costs more and is less accurate than elimination or LU. Skipping pivoting is just as risky. In a running simulation, it can quietly produce garbage numbers that look plausible.

questions.prompt: A small machine shop models two production constraints with the system 3x + 2y = 12 and 6x + 7y = 33. Using Gaussian elimination: Step 1, the pivot is 3, so the multiplier for row two is 6 ÷ 3 = 2. Step 2, subtract 2 times row one from row two: (6 − 6)x + (7 − 4)y = 33 − 24. Step 3: ???. Step 4, back substitute into row one: 3x + 2(3) = 12, so 3x = 6 and x = 2. Step 5, check: 6(2) + 7(3) = 33. What belongs in Step 3?
choices: 3y = 9, so y = 3
questions.why: Row two becomes 0x + 3y = 9 after subtracting twice row one from both sides, so y = 3, and that value is what the back substitution in Step 4 uses.

questions.prompt: A team wants to use the Jacobi or Gauss-Seidel method and needs a coefficient matrix that is guaranteed to converge. Which 2×2 matrix (rows listed in order) is diagonally dominant?
questions.why: In each row the diagonal entry is larger in size than the other entry (4 > 1 and 3 > 2). Every other option has a row where the diagonal entry is equal to or smaller than the off-diagonal entry.

questions.prompt: A structural analysis tool must solve Ax = b for the same coefficient matrix A but 500 different load vectors b. Which approach fits best?
choices: Factor A once into L and U, then reuse that factorization for each b
Compute the inverse of A once and multiply it by each b
Run full Gaussian elimination from scratch for every b
Always switch to Jacobi iteration, since it works for any matrix
questions.why: LU decomposition records the elimination once, so each new b can be solved cheaply. Using the inverse costs more and is less accurate. Repeating elimination wastes work, and Jacobi is only guaranteed to converge for diagonally dominant matrices.

questions.prompt: During elimination, the candidate entries in the current column (from the current row downward) are 0.002, 9, and 4. With partial pivoting, which value becomes the pivot, and why?
choices: 0.002, because it is already in the pivot position and swapping rows changes the answer
Any of them, because pivot choice only affects speed, not accuracy
4, because it is the middle value and balances the multipliers
9, because it is the largest, so dividing by it keeps the multipliers small and limits rounding error
questions.why: Partial pivoting swaps rows so the largest available entry becomes the pivot. Dividing by a tiny pivot such as 0.002 creates huge multipliers that magnify rounding error.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would solve Ax = b on a computer, when you would pick a direct method versus an iterative one, and what tradeoff or risk comes with each choice.
lessons.modelAnswer: For a moderate, dense system I'd use Gaussian elimination. You subtract multiples of rows to make the matrix triangular, then back-substitute from the last equation up. I'd always use partial pivoting, which means swapping rows so the largest entry in each column is the divisor. A tiny pivot creates huge multipliers that blow up rounding error. If I need to solve with the same A but many right-hand sides, I'd factor it once into LU and reuse that. I would not compute the inverse, because it's slower and less accurate. For a huge sparse system, elimination can fill in zeros and use too much memory and time, so I'd use an iterative method like Jacobi or Gauss-Seidel. The tradeoff is that iterative methods only give an approximate answer, and convergence is guaranteed only under conditions such as diagonal dominance. Without that, the iterations might wander off instead of settling.
rubricPoints: Describes elimination to triangular form followed by back substitution.
Explains partial pivoting and why small pivots amplify rounding error.
Mentions LU factorization as reusable for many right-hand sides.
Contrasts direct methods with iterative methods for large sparse systems.
Names a limit of iterative methods, such as convergence requiring diagonal dominance.
Warns against solving by explicitly computing the inverse.

suggested.rationale: No current mission or planned engine covers numerical linear algebra, so reasoning through exam-style systems helps most. The learner can practise choosing a method, deciding when to pivot and tracing an elimination.

lessons.plain: Error analysis means checking how far a calculated answer is from the true one, and working out why. Computers cannot store most numbers exactly, and many math methods stop early rather than running forever, so nearly every numerical answer is slightly off. Error analysis asks three questions: how big is the gap, where did it come from, and does it grow as the calculation goes on? Think of photocopying a photocopy. Each copy is only a little blurrier, but after many rounds the image can become unreadable. Error analysis is how you predict the blur and keep it small enough to trust.
lessons.guessPrompt: You measure a 2-meter board and are off by 1 centimeter. You then measure a 5-centimeter screw and are also off by 1 centimeter. Which measurement is worse, and why?
lessons.teach:
Error analysis is the study of how far a computed answer is from the true answer, where that gap comes from, and how it grows during a calculation. Absolute error is the size of the gap: |true value − approximation|. Relative error is the absolute error divided by |true value|. It measures the mistake against the size of the thing being measured.

Errors have two main sources. Round-off error happens because computers store real numbers in floating point, a format that keeps only a fixed number of significant digits (about 16 decimal digits in standard double precision). Most numbers therefore get rounded slightly. Truncation error happens when a method replaces an infinite or exact process with a finite one, such as stopping a series after a few terms.

Worked example: the true value of π is 3.14159265..., and we approximate it as 3.14. Step 1: the absolute error is 3.14159265 − 3.14 = 0.00159265. Step 2: the relative error is 0.00159265 / 3.14159265 ≈ 0.000507, about 0.05%. Step 3: a relative error near 5×10⁻⁴ means roughly three significant digits are correct. Now compare an error of 0.0016 on a true value of 0.003. That is about 53% relative error. The absolute error is the same, but the quality is very different.

Errors also propagate, meaning each operation carries earlier errors forward and adds its own round-off. A problem is ill-conditioned when small input changes cause large output changes. An algorithm is stable when it does not magnify errors beyond what the problem itself forces.

A common mistake is subtracting two nearly equal numbers, which is called catastrophic cancellation. Suppose 1.234567 and 1.234561 are each correct to seven digits. Their difference, 0.000006, has only one meaningful digit left. The usual fix is to rewrite the formula so it avoids the subtraction.

In a running system, unchecked error shows up as financial totals drifting, simulations diverging, or tests like 0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3 failing. For that reason, floating-point values should be compared within a tolerance.

questions.prompt: A shipping company's warehouse scale weighs a test pallet whose true mass is known to be 80.00 kg. The scale reads 80.40 kg. Step 1: the absolute error is |80.00 − 80.40| = 0.40 kg. Step 2: [missing]. Step 3: the same scale weighs a parcel whose true mass is 2.00 kg and reads 2.40 kg. The absolute error is again 0.40 kg, but the relative error is 0.40 / 2.00 = 0.20, or 20%. The pallet reading is therefore far more trustworthy than the parcel reading. Which choice correctly completes Step 2?
choices: The relative error is 0.40 kg, the same as the absolute error.
The relative error is 0.40 / 80.00 = 0.005, about 5%.
The relative error is 0.40 / 80.00 = 0.005, about 0.5%.
The relative error is 80.00 / 0.40 = 200.
questions.why: Relative error is the absolute error divided by the size of the true value, so 0.40 / 80.00 = 0.005, which is 0.5%.

questions.prompt: A weather-modelling program estimates a function by adding up only the first six terms of an infinite series and then stopping. Which kind of error is introduced by stopping after six terms?
choices: Ill-conditioning, because the program is using a series
Round-off error, because floating point keeps only about 16 significant digits
Truncation error, because a finite process replaces an infinite one
Catastrophic cancellation, because the terms are being added together
questions.why: Truncation error comes from cutting an infinite or exact process down to a finite one, such as stopping a series early.

questions.prompt: A lab instrument reports two readings, 9.876543 and 9.876540, each correct to seven digits. An engineer computes their difference, 0.000003, and uses it in further calculations. What is the main problem, and what is the usual fix?
choices: Round-off from the subtraction itself. Repeat the subtraction more times and average.
The readings are ill-conditioned. Store them with fewer digits.
Truncation error. Add more terms to the calculation.
Catastrophic cancellation leaves only one meaningful digit. Rewrite the formula to avoid the subtraction.
questions.why: Subtracting nearly equal numbers cancels the matching leading digits and leaves few meaningful ones, and the standard remedy is to rewrite the formula so the subtraction is avoided.

questions.prompt: In a payroll service, a test adds 0.10 and 0.20 in floating point and checks whether the result is exactly equal to 0.30. The test sometimes fails, even though the arithmetic looks correct. What is the best change?
choices: Switch the test to compare absolute errors instead of relative errors.
Treat the failure as a truncation error and add more terms.
Add the numbers in the reverse order so the round-off error disappears.
Check whether the result is within a small tolerance of 0.30 instead of testing exact equality.
questions.why: Floating point rounds most decimal values slightly, so the values should be compared within a tolerance rather than tested for exact equality.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate the difference between absolute and relative error, and between round-off and truncation error. Then name one situation where a tiny round-off error can become a large error in the final answer.
lessons.modelAnswer: Absolute error is the raw gap between the true value and our approximation. Relative error divides that gap by the true value, so it tells us how big the mistake is compared with the quantity itself. Relative error is usually the better measure of quality: being off by 0.001 is fine on a value of 1000 but terrible on a value of 0.002. Round-off error comes from the computer storing numbers with a limited number of digits. Truncation error comes from the method itself, like stopping a series early. The tradeoff is that taking more steps or terms cuts truncation error but adds more operations, and each operation contributes round-off. A tiny round-off error becomes large when we subtract two nearly equal numbers. The matching leading digits cancel, only the noisy trailing digits remain, and the relative error jumps. Ill-conditioned problems amplify small input errors in a similar way.
rubricPoints: Defines absolute error as the size of the gap between true and approximate values.
Defines relative error as absolute error divided by the true value and says why it better reflects quality.
Distinguishes round-off error (limited stored digits) from truncation error (finite approximation of an exact process).
Identifies catastrophic cancellation or ill-conditioning as a way small errors grow large.
Names a tradeoff or limit, such as more steps reducing truncation error while adding round-off.

suggested.rationale: Error analysis is best learned by reasoning through exam-style calculations, such as computing relative error and spotting cancellation, and no listed mission or engine practices numerical error directly.

lessons.plain: A group is a collection of things together with one way of combining any two of them, where the combining behaves predictably. Four rules must hold: combining two members always gives another member, grouping does not matter when you combine three, there is a do-nothing member, and every member has an undo partner. Think of turning a dial with four clicks: any two turns give another turn, not turning is the do-nothing move, and every turn can be reversed by turning back. Many different-looking systems, such as clock arithmetic, rotations of a shape and shuffles of cards, all follow these same four rules.
lessons.guessPrompt: Under ordinary addition, every whole number has an undo partner: 5 is undone by -5. Under ordinary multiplication, does every nonzero whole number have a whole-number undo partner that brings you back to 1? Can you name one that fails?
lessons.teach:
A group is a set G together with a binary operation, written here as *. A binary operation is a rule that takes any two members of G and returns one result. The pair (G, *) is a group when four axioms, or required rules, hold.
