Step 3, design the to-be: patients confirm their insurance online before the visit, so the billing check happens ahead of time. Step 4, monitor the KPI again: check-in cycle time falls to about 25 minutes. Which choice correctly fills in Step 2?
choices: Throw out the whole check-in process and redesign it from scratch before collecting any timing data
Ask the receptionist which step feels slowest and remove the nurse's vital-signs step to save time
Buy workflow software that routes each check-in through the same four steps automatically, so every task is handed off faster
Measure how long each step takes, which shows that most of the 90 minutes is spent waiting for the billing office to confirm insurance
questions.why: After modeling the as-is process, you measure each step to find where the delay really is, and that measurement is what justifies moving the insurance check before the visit.

questions.prompt: An online bookstore's process team draws a diagram of how customer returns are handled today, showing every step, who does it, and what passes between steps. In BPM terms, what is this diagram called?
choices: The to-be model
A key performance indicator
The process owner's report
The as-is model
questions.why: The as-is model is the diagram of the process as it currently runs. The to-be model is the improved version you plan to move to.

questions.prompt: A shipping company's employee-onboarding process is slow and confusing. Leadership decides to scrap it completely and design a brand-new onboarding process from a blank page, accepting more risk in exchange for a possible large gain. Which improvement style is this?
choices: Executing the to-be process with workflow software
Business process reengineering (BPR)
Monitoring, because the company is reacting to a KPI
Continuous improvement, because the company is still improving the process
questions.why: BPR means throwing out the old process and redesigning it from scratch. It is riskier but can bring large gains. Continuous improvement uses small, steady changes instead.

questions.prompt: A university's purchase-approval process sends every request, even a $5 stapler, through four separate sign-offs. Without changing those steps, the IT team installs workflow software that routes the request to all four approvers automatically. What is the most likely result?
choices: The wasteful sign-offs still happen, only faster, and the waste is locked into the software, so it becomes harder to change later
The software removes the unnecessary sign-offs on its own, so the process is fixed
Cycle time stops being a useful KPI, because automated processes cannot be measured
The process no longer needs a process owner, because software is now accountable for its results
questions.why: Automating a broken process before fixing it makes the software perform the same wasteful steps faster, which locks in the waste and makes it harder to change later.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain business process management to a teammate in your own words, walk through its lifecycle, and name one limit or tradeoff, such as when automating a process can backfire or why reengineering is risky.
lessons.modelAnswer: BPM means treating how we get work done as something we deliberately design, measure and improve. A business process is a repeatable chain of steps with a trigger and a result, like turning a refund request into a payment. The lifecycle is a loop: model the as-is process, design a better to-be version, execute it, monitor it with KPIs like cycle time or error rate, then optimize and repeat. A process owner is accountable for results across every department involved. The big tradeoff is between continuous improvement, which is small and safe, and reengineering, which redesigns from scratch and can deliver big gains but disrupts people and can fail. Another limit is that automation only helps a sound process; automating a broken one just makes waste happen faster and harder to remove.
rubricPoints: Defines a business process as a repeatable set of steps from a trigger to a valuable result.
Describes the BPM lifecycle of modeling, executing, monitoring and optimizing as a repeating loop.
Distinguishes the as-is model from the to-be model.
Mentions measuring with KPIs such as cycle time and names the process owner's accountability.
Names a tradeoff such as continuous improvement versus reengineering, or the danger of automating a broken process.

suggested.rationale: BPM here is a conceptual vocabulary and lifecycle, so explaining it back with a worked example best shows the learner truly understands it.

lessons.plain: Technical writing for information systems documentation means writing clear, accurate text that helps a specific reader understand or use a computer system. It covers user guides for people who use the system, procedures for staff who run it, and technical descriptions for people who build or fix it. The goal is not to sound impressive. The goal is that the reader can act correctly without asking you. Think of a recipe card: it names the dish, lists what you need, then gives numbered steps in order. A cook who has never met the author can still make the meal. Good system documentation works the same way.
lessons.guessPrompt: A note left for the night shift says: "If the report fails, fix the server and rerun it." What questions would a new employee have after reading that note?
lessons.teach:
Technical writing is writing whose job is to transfer usable knowledge to a reader, not to entertain or persuade. In information systems, the documents usually fall into three types. A user guide explains how ordinary users do tasks. A procedure, sometimes called a runbook, is a step-by-step set of instructions that operations staff follow to run or repair a system. A technical specification describes how a system is built, for example its parts, data and rules.

Every good document starts with two decisions. The audience is the specific person who will read it and what they already know. The purpose is what that reader must be able to do afterward. These two choices decide your vocabulary, your level of detail and the order of the content. Clarity then comes from habits. Use plain language, which means common words and short sentences. Use active voice, which means the actor comes first, as in "Click Save" rather than "Save should be clicked." Put actions in numbered steps, one action per step. Define each term the first time you use it. Keep a revision history, which is a dated record of what changed, so readers can trust that the document is current.

Here is a worked example. Start with this note: "If the report fails, fix the server and rerun it." First, name the audience: a new night operator. Second, state the purpose: restart the nightly sales report. Third, replace the vague verbs with numbered actions. Step 1 tells the operator to open the job monitor. Step 2 tells them to check whether the status says Failed. Step 3 tells them to restart the report service. Step 4 tells them to rerun the job and confirm that the status says Complete. Finally, add a line saying whom to call if the job fails twice.

The most common mistake is writing for yourself and skipping steps that feel obvious to you. In a running system, that gap leads to guessed actions, longer outages and repeated calls to the one person who knows the answer.

questions.prompt: A small dental clinic has this note taped to the reception desk: "Backups should be checked and any problems handled." A manager rewrites it using good technical writing. Step 1: Name the audience: a part-time receptionist with no IT training. Step 2: [missing]. Step 3: Replace the vague wording with numbered actions in active voice. For example: "1. Open the backup app on the office PC. 2. Read the date beside Last Backup. 3. If the date is not today, call the IT contractor." Step 4: Add a dated revision history line at the bottom. Which choice correctly fills Step 2?
choices: Rewrite the note in passive voice so it sounds more formal and official to the receptionist.
Combine all of the checks into one long step so the receptionist can do them in a single pass.
State the purpose: after reading, the receptionist must be able to confirm that last night's backup worked and report it if it did not.
Describe how the backup software is built, including its components, data stores and rules.
questions.why: Every good document starts with two decisions, audience and purpose, and the purpose states what the reader must be able to do afterward, which then shapes the vocabulary, detail and order.

questions.prompt: A regional warehouse company writes a document for its developers that lists the parts of its inventory system, the database tables it stores and the rules that reject an order with a negative quantity. Which document type is this?
choices: A revision history, because it is a dated record of what changed in the system
A technical specification, because it describes how the system is built: its parts, data and rules
A user guide, because it explains how ordinary staff complete everyday tasks
A runbook, because it gives operations staff step-by-step instructions to repair the system
questions.why: A technical specification describes how a system is built, including its parts, data and rules, and that matches this document.

questions.prompt: A city utility is writing a user guide for call-centre staff who look up customer accounts. Which step best follows the clarity habits of technical writing?
choices: Step 3: Utilise the alphanumeric identifier input field to initiate retrieval.
Step 3: Enter the customer ID, press Search, print the bill, and email it to the customer.
Step 3: The customer ID should be entered and the Search button should be pressed.
Step 3: Type the customer ID into the Customer ID box.
questions.why: It uses plain language and active voice, with the action first, and it contains exactly one action per numbered step.

questions.prompt: At a nonprofit, the only network administrator writes a runbook for resetting the office VPN, which is a secure connection into the office network. He leaves out "log in to the firewall console" because it feels obvious to him. A new volunteer must use the runbook during an outage. What is the most likely result?
choices: The volunteer guesses at the missing action, the outage lasts longer, and the administrator gets repeated calls.
The runbook becomes a technical specification, because it now leaves out user actions.
The volunteer finishes faster, because a shorter document is always clearer.
Nothing changes, because experienced readers always fill in missing steps correctly.
questions.why: Writing for yourself and skipping steps that feel obvious is the most common mistake, and in a running system it leads to guessed actions, longer outages and repeated calls to the one person who knows the answer.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what makes system documentation good, using a procedure as your example, and name one tradeoff you face when deciding how much detail to include.
lessons.modelAnswer: Good documentation starts with knowing who will read it and what they need to do afterward. For a procedure, such as restarting a failed nightly report, the reader is often a new operator under pressure. So I write numbered steps with one action each, use active voice like "Open the job monitor," and define any term they may not know. I end with a check that confirms success and say whom to contact if it still fails. I also keep a revision history so people know the steps are current. The tradeoff is detail versus length. If I skip steps that feel obvious to me, a beginner guesses and may make things worse. If I explain everything, experts skim and miss the critical step, and a long document is harder to keep up to date. I handle this by aiming at the least experienced likely reader and keeping the steps short.
rubricPoints: Identifies audience and purpose as the first decisions in writing documentation.
Names a document type such as a user guide, procedure or specification and what it is for.
Describes clarity techniques such as numbered steps, active voice, plain language and defined terms.
Mentions verification or escalation steps, or keeping a revision history so the document stays current.
States a real tradeoff, such as completeness versus length or the effort of keeping documents up to date.

suggested.rationale: Technical writing is learned by producing clear explanations for a specific reader, so explaining a procedure back in your own words is the core skill to practise.

lessons.plain: Structured programming is a way of writing programs so they read top to bottom like a clear recipe instead of a tangle of jumps. Every program is built from just three building blocks: doing steps in order, choosing between paths, and repeating steps. Each block has one way in and one way out, so you can understand any piece without tracing the whole program. Think of assembling flat-pack furniture: numbered steps, an occasional 'if you have model B, do this', and 'repeat for all four legs'. C++ is the language this course uses to practise that discipline.
lessons.guessPrompt: If a program could only do three things (run steps in order, choose between two paths, or repeat some steps), do you think you could still write a program that averages a list of test scores? Which of the three would you need?
lessons.teach:
Structured programming is a discipline in which every program is composed from three control structures. Sequence means statements run one after another in the order written. Selection means the program picks one path based on a condition (in C++, an if or switch statement). Iteration means a block repeats while a condition holds (in C++, a while, do-while or for loop). Each structure has a single entry and a single exit, so blocks can be nested inside each other like boxes inside boxes. A C++ program starts in a function called main, which is the entry point where execution begins. A variable is a named storage spot with a type, such as int for whole numbers or double for decimals.

Why it works: a well-known result in computer science shows these three structures are enough to express any computation, so unrestricted jumps (the goto statement) are never required. Because each block enters and exits in one place, you can reason about it alone, test it alone, and replace it without breaking its neighbours. This pairs naturally with top-down design: you break the problem into steps, then refine each step.

Worked example: average three scores, 80, 90 and 70. Sequence: set total to 0 and count to 0. Iteration: for each score, add it to total and add 1 to count. After the first pass total is 80, then 170, then 240, and count is 3. Selection: if count is greater than 0, compute average as 240 divided by 3, which is 80; otherwise report that there are no scores. Sequence again: print the result.

A common mistake is forgetting to initialize a variable, for example declaring total without setting it to 0. In C++ an uninitialized local variable holds whatever leftover value sits in memory, so the average comes out wrong in an unpredictable way. Another is jumping around with goto or deeply tangled nesting. In a running system, unstructured code produces bugs that are hard to locate because control can arrive at a line from many places.

questions.prompt: A weather station logs four afternoon temperatures: 28, 33, 31 and 25 degrees. A program must count how many readings are above 30. Here it is, traced step by step. Step 1 (sequence): declare an int variable hotCount and set it to 0. Step 2 (iteration): repeat the next step once for each of the four readings. Step 3: MISSING. Step 4 (sequence): after the loop ends, print hotCount, which shows 2. Which choice correctly fills Step 3 so the program prints 2?
choices: Iteration: while the current reading is greater than 30, keep adding 1 to hotCount.
Sequence: add 1 to hotCount for every reading, whatever its value.
Selection: if hotCount is greater than 0, add the current reading to hotCount.
Selection: if the current reading is greater than 30, add 1 to hotCount; otherwise do nothing.
questions.why: Only a selection that tests each reading against 30 adds 1 for 33 and 31 and skips 28 and 25, giving 2.

questions.prompt: An online bookshop's program applies a 10 percent discount to an order only when the order total is over $50; otherwise it charges the full price. Which control structure handles this choice?
choices: Sequence, because the statements run in the order written
A goto statement that jumps to the discount code
Selection, such as an if statement
Iteration, such as a for loop
questions.why: Picking one of two paths based on a condition (total over $50) is selection, written in C++ with an if or switch.

questions.prompt: A parking garage program declares a local variable int carsParked; without giving it a value, then adds 1 to it each time a car enters. After 12 cars enter, what will the program most likely report?
choices: An error-free 13, because the counter starts at 1
An unpredictable number, because the variable began with whatever leftover value was in memory
Exactly 0, because the variable was never set
Exactly 12, because C++ starts every int at 0
questions.why: An uninitialized local variable in C++ holds leftover memory contents, so adding 12 to it gives a wrong, unpredictable total.

questions.prompt: A team rewriting a payroll program replaces scattered goto jumps with blocks that each have a single entry and a single exit. What is the main benefit of this change?
choices: The program needs fewer variables because blocks share storage
The program can now express calculations that were impossible with goto
Each block can be reasoned about, tested and replaced on its own without breaking its neighbours
Execution no longer has to start in the main function
questions.why: Single-entry, single-exit blocks can be understood and tested in isolation, whereas goto lets control arrive at a line from many places, making bugs hard to find.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain structured programming to a teammate who has only written quick scripts: what the three structures are, why single entry and single exit matter, and one limit or tradeoff of sticking strictly to the rules.
lessons.modelAnswer: Structured programming means building every program from three pieces: sequence, where statements run in order; selection, where an if or switch picks one path; and iteration, where a loop repeats while a condition is true. Each piece has one way in and one way out, so I can nest them and still read any block on its own without wondering where else control might jump in from. That makes code easier to test and debug, and it fits top-down design, where I break a task into steps and refine each. It has been shown these three are enough for any computation, so goto is unnecessary. The tradeoff is that strict single-exit style can sometimes force extra flag variables or deeper nesting, for example to stop a search early, which can make a short routine slightly wordier than a direct jump would be.
rubricPoints: Names sequence, selection and iteration as the three structures.
Explains that each block has a single entry and single exit.
States that these three structures can express any computation, so goto is unnecessary.
Connects the discipline to easier reading, testing and debugging.
Names a real tradeoff, such as extra flags or deeper nesting to honour single exit.

suggested.rationale: There is no C++ mission yet, but this mission makes the learner combine sequence, selection and iteration to solve a real task, which is exactly the structured habit that transfers directly to C++.

lessons.plain: Object-oriented programming is a way of organizing a program around objects. An object is a self-contained bundle holding some data and the actions allowed on that data. A class is the blueprint that describes what every object of a certain kind holds and can do. Think of a cookie cutter and cookies: the class is the cutter, and each object is one cookie. The cookies share a shape, but each can have different sprinkles. The key benefit is protection. Outside parts of the program change an object's data only by asking it through its approved actions, so the object can refuse requests that would break it.
lessons.guessPrompt: Suppose a program tracks bank accounts and any line of code can directly set an account's balance to any number. What could go wrong, and how might you stop a balance from ever being set to a nonsense value?
lessons.teach:
Object-oriented programming (OOP) organizes a program around objects, each bundling data with the operations allowed on that data. A class is the blueprint. It declares member variables, which are the data each object holds, and member functions, also called methods, which are the actions an object can perform. An object, or instance, is one concrete thing built from a class.

Encapsulation means keeping the data hidden behind the methods. In C++ you mark each member private, so only the class's own functions can touch it, or public, so any code can use it. A constructor is a special member function with the same name as the class. It runs automatically when an object is created, so every object starts in a valid state.

This works because outside code can change the data only through methods. The class can then enforce its rules in one place instead of trusting every caller.

Worked example: a class BankAccount has a private double balance. It has a constructor BankAccount(double start) that sets balance to start. It also has a public deposit(double amt) that adds amt only if amt is greater than 0, and a public getBalance() that returns balance. Here is the trace. BankAccount a(100); runs the constructor, so a's balance is 100. a.deposit(50); passes the check, so the balance becomes 150. a.deposit(-20); fails the check, so the balance stays 150. BankAccount b(10); creates a separate object with its own balance of 10, and a is unaffected. If you write a.balance = -500; in main, the program will not compile, because balance is private.

One common mistake is making every member public to save effort. Another is skipping the constructor, which in C++ leaves a member like balance holding whatever leftover value was in memory. In a running program, either mistake lets invalid data spread quietly. When a wrong value finally shows up, any line in the program could have caused it, so debugging becomes a hunt through the whole codebase instead of one class.

questions.prompt: A class Thermostat has a private int target. Its constructor Thermostat(int start) sets target to start. A public setTarget(int t) changes target to t only if t is between 50 and 90, inclusive. A public getTarget() returns target. Trace: Thermostat t(68); runs the constructor, so target is 68. t.setTarget(72); passes the check, so target becomes 72. t.setTarget(120); [missing step]. Thermostat u(55); creates a separate object whose target is 55, and t is unaffected. Which choice correctly fills the missing step?
choices: The value 120 passes the check because setTarget is public, so target becomes 120
The check fails, so target resets to the constructor's starting value of 68
The check fails, so target stays at 72
The program will not compile, because 120 is outside the allowed range
questions.why: The setTarget method changes target only when the new value passes its rule, so a failed check leaves the current value of 72 unchanged.

questions.prompt: A library program defines one class called Book. In main, it creates three Book variables: novel, atlas and cookbook. Each one holds its own title and page count. How many classes and how many objects (instances) does this code have?
choices: One class and three objects
Three classes and three objects
One class and one object shared by all three names
Three classes and one object
questions.why: A class is the blueprint, so Book is a single class, and each variable built from it is a separate object with its own data.

questions.prompt: A class Scoreboard has a private int score and a public addPoints(int p) method. In main, a programmer writes s.score = 999; for a Scoreboard object s. What happens?
choices: score becomes 999, because main owns the object s
The line runs, but the change is quietly ignored
The program will not compile, because score is private
score becomes 999, but only after addPoints is called first
questions.why: A private member can be touched only by the class's own functions, so outside code such as main cannot assign to it directly.

questions.prompt: A class Counter has a private int count, but the programmer writes no constructor that sets count. In C++, what value does count hold right after a Counter object is created?
choices: Always 0, because C++ clears new member variables
Nothing, because the object cannot be created without a constructor
Whatever leftover value happened to be in that memory
The value of count in the most recently created Counter
questions.why: Without a constructor setting it, the member keeps whatever leftover value was already in memory, so the object can start in an invalid state.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate, in your own words, what a class, an object, and encapsulation are, and why making data private helps. Name one cost or tradeoff of this approach.
lessons.modelAnswer: A class is a blueprint that lists the data each object holds and the functions it can run. An object is one actual instance made from that blueprint, with its own copy of the data. So two BankAccount objects each have their own balance. Encapsulation means marking the data private and exposing only public methods, like deposit or getBalance. Because outsiders must go through those methods, the class can check every change, such as rejecting a negative deposit, in one place. A constructor makes sure each object starts valid instead of holding leftover memory garbage. The payoff is that bugs about that data can only come from inside the class, which makes them much easier to find. The tradeoff is extra upfront design and some boilerplate, like writing getter functions. For a tiny throwaway program, that structure can feel like more work than it saves.
rubricPoints: Defines a class as a blueprint of member data plus member functions.
Defines an object as a separate instance with its own copy of the data.
Explains encapsulation as private data reached only through public methods.
Says why this helps: rules are enforced in one place and bugs are easier to locate.
Mentions the constructor's role in starting objects in a valid state.
Names a real tradeoff, such as extra design effort or boilerplate.

suggested.rationale: No current mission or planned engine practises C++ classes, and explaining why encapsulation protects an object's data is the core understanding this objective needs.

lessons.plain: Input and output, often shortened to I/O, is how a program talks with the outside world. Output is anything the program sends out, such as text printed on the screen. Input is anything the program takes in, such as numbers a user types on the keyboard. In C++ both travel through streams, which you can picture as conveyor belts carrying characters one after another. Your program puts characters onto the output belt, and it picks characters off the input belt in the exact order they arrived. Learning I/O means learning how to load and unload those belts correctly.
lessons.guessPrompt: A program asks for your age and then for your full name. You type 21, press Enter, and the program immediately finishes with a blank name before you can type anything. What do you think happened to that Enter key press?
lessons.teach:
A stream is an ordered flow of characters between a program and a device. In C++ you get the standard streams by writing #include <iostream>. cout is the standard output stream, usually the screen, and cin is the standard input stream, usually the keyboard. The insertion operator << pushes a value onto an output stream, as in cout << "Age: " << age. The extraction operator >> pulls a value off an input stream and converts it to the variable's type, as in cin >> age. endl writes a newline and flushes, meaning it forces any waiting output to appear now.

This works because typed characters wait in a buffer, which is a holding area, until your program extracts them. The >> operator skips leading whitespace (spaces, tabs, newlines), reads as many characters as fit the type, and stops at the next whitespace. It leaves that stopping character behind in the buffer. For a whole line that includes spaces, use getline(cin, name), which reads everything up to the next newline and then throws that newline away.

Worked example. The user types 21, presses Enter, then types Ana Lee. The buffer first holds "21\n". The statement cin >> age reads 21 and stops at \n, leaving \n in the buffer. Then getline(cin, name) runs, sees \n first, and returns an empty string right away. The name is blank and the user never got a chance to type it.

The common mistake is mixing >> and getline without clearing that leftover newline. The fix is to call cin.ignore() or use cin >> ws before getline, which discards the leftover whitespace. A related mistake is reading a name with cin >> name, which keeps only "Ana". If the user types letters where a number is expected, cin enters a fail state. In that state every later read quietly does nothing until you call cin.clear() and discard the bad input, so a running program can loop forever or work with garbage values.

questions.prompt: A library checkout kiosk asks for a number of books and then the patron's full name. Step 1: cout << "Books: "; runs. Step 2: cin >> books; runs. The patron types 3 and presses Enter, so the buffer holds "3\n". books becomes 3, and "\n" is left behind in the buffer. Step 3: [missing]. Step 4: getline(cin, patron); runs. The patron types Maria Gomez and presses Enter, and patron correctly holds "Maria Gomez". Which statement belongs in Step 3 so that Step 4 works as described?
choices: cin >> ws;
cin >> patron;
cin.clear();
cout << endl;
questions.why: cin >> ws discards the leftover newline (and any other whitespace) from the input buffer, so getline waits for and reads the full name instead of returning an empty string at once.

questions.prompt: An inventory program has an int variable count. The input buffer currently holds "  57 12\n" (two spaces, then 57, a space, 12 and a newline). The program runs cin >> count; once. What does count hold, and what character is now first in the buffer?
choices: count is 57, and the space just before 12 is next in the buffer
count is 5712, because >> keeps reading digits across the space
count gets no value, because >> refuses input that begins with spaces
count is 57, and the buffer is now completely empty
questions.why: The >> operator skips leading whitespace, reads 57, and stops at the next whitespace, leaving that space in the buffer.

questions.prompt: A travel booking program declares a string variable city and runs cin >> city; to read where the user wants to go. The user types San Diego and presses Enter. What does city hold right after that statement?
choices: An empty string
"San Diego"
"San"
"Diego"
questions.why: The >> operator stops at the first whitespace, so it keeps only "San". Reading a full line that contains spaces needs getline.

questions.prompt: A thermostat program runs in a loop. On each pass it reads an int temperature with cin >> temp;. On one pass the user types warm instead of a number, and the program never calls cin.clear(). What is the most likely result?
choices: cin turns warm into a temperature reading and carries on with the loop as if nothing happened
The program always halts at once and prints a clear error message explaining the bad input
cin quietly skips the word warm and then waits normally for the next number the user types
cin goes into a fail state, later reads do nothing, and the loop may repeat forever
questions.why: Letters where a number is expected put cin in a fail state. Every later read then does nothing until cin.clear() is called and the bad input is discarded, so the loop can run forever or work with garbage values.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how cin >> and getline differ in what they read and what they leave behind, and describe the bug that shows up when you mix them, including how to fix it.
lessons.modelAnswer: cout and cin are streams. Characters flow through them in order, and anything typed waits in a buffer until we extract it. cin >> skips leading whitespace, reads one token converted to the variable's type, and stops at the next space or newline. It leaves that character sitting in the buffer. getline reads a whole line, spaces included, up to the newline, and then discards the newline. The tradeoff is that >> is convenient for numbers and single words but can't read a name like "Ana Lee", while getline reads full lines but gives no type conversion. Mixing them causes a classic bug. After cin >> age, the Enter key's newline is still waiting, so the next getline returns an empty string at once. You fix it with cin.ignore() or cin >> ws before the getline. Also, if non-numeric text hits a numeric >>, cin goes into a fail state and must be cleared before it will read again.
rubricPoints: Defines cin and cout as input and output streams that use the >> and << operators.
States that >> stops at whitespace and leaves the delimiter in the buffer.
States that getline reads a full line including spaces and consumes the newline.
Explains the leftover-newline bug when >> is followed by getline, and the ignore or ws fix.
Names a limit, such as >> not reading multi-word input or cin entering a fail state on bad input.

suggested.rationale: No listed mission or engine runs C++ console I/O, so the most useful practice is walking through what each read leaves in the buffer and explaining it back.

lessons.plain: Control flow is how a program decides what to do next instead of just running every line once from top to bottom. A conditional is a fork in the road: if something is true, take one path, otherwise take another. A loop is a repeat button: keep doing the same steps while something stays true, or a set number of times. Think of a recipe that says "if the dough is sticky, add flour" and "stir until smooth." Together, these two tools let a short program handle many different situations and large amounts of work without you writing every step by hand.
lessons.guessPrompt: Suppose a program starts a counter at 1, adds the counter to a running total, then adds 1 to the counter, and repeats these steps as long as the counter is 3 or less. What total do you think it ends with, and how many times did it repeat?
lessons.teach:
Control flow means the order in which a program's statements run. By default C++ runs statements top to bottom; conditionals and loops change that order.

A condition is an expression that evaluates to true or false, such as x > 5 or count == 0. A conditional statement runs code only when a condition holds. In C++ the if statement checks a condition; an optional else branch runs when it is false, and else if lets you test several conditions in order, taking the first one that is true.

A loop repeats a block of code, called the loop body. Each pass through the body is an iteration. A while loop checks its condition before every iteration and stops once the condition is false. A for loop packs three parts into one line: a starting step (int i = 1), a condition (i <= 3), and an update run after each iteration (i++, meaning add 1 to i). A do-while loop checks its condition after the body, so the body always runs at least once.

Worked example: int total = 0; for (int i = 1; i <= 3; i++) total += i;
Start: i is 1, 1 <= 3 is true, total becomes 1. Update: i is 2, 2 <= 3 is true, total becomes 3. Update: i is 3, still true, total becomes 6. Update: i is 4, 4 <= 3 is false, the loop ends. Result: total is 6 after three iterations.

A common mistake is writing = (assignment) where you meant == (comparison). if (x = 0) stores 0 in x and treats the result as false, so the branch silently never runs. A related mistake is a loop whose condition never becomes false, for example forgetting the i++ update. That is an infinite loop: the program never finishes, keeps a processor core busy, and must be killed. Off-by-one errors, like writing i < 3 when you meant i <= 3, quietly skip or add an iteration and produce wrong answers rather than crashes.

questions.prompt:
A warehouse tracks how many days a pallet of 20 boxes lasts when 6 boxes ship each day:
int stock = 20; int days = 0; while (stock > 0) { stock = stock - 6; days++; }
Trace so far. Check 1: 20 > 0 is true, so stock becomes 14 and days becomes 1. Check 2: 14 > 0 is true, so stock becomes 8 and days becomes 2. Check 3: 8 > 0 is true, so stock becomes 2 and days becomes 3. Check 4: [missing step]. Check 5: -4 > 0 is false, so the loop ends with days equal to 4.
Which choice correctly fills in Check 4?
choices: 2 > 0 is false, so the loop ends with days equal to 3
2 > 0 is true, so stock becomes -4 and days becomes 4
2 > 0 is true, so stock becomes -4 but days stays 3
2 > 0 is true, so stock becomes 0 and days becomes 4
questions.why: A while loop checks its condition before every iteration, and 2 > 0 is true, so the whole body runs again: stock becomes 2 - 6 = -4 and days increases to 4.

questions.prompt: A kiosk program must show a welcome screen once before it checks whether the user wants to continue. The screen must appear even if the 'continue' condition is false from the start. Which kind of C++ loop guarantees that its body runs at least once?
choices: A for loop, because its starting step always runs
A do-while loop, because it checks its condition after the body
A while loop, because it checks its condition before each iteration
An if statement with an else branch
questions.why: A do-while loop runs the body first and checks the condition afterward, so the body always runs at least once. A while loop or a for loop can skip the body entirely if the condition is false at the start.

choices: warm mild
warm
hot
cold
questions.why: The else if chain tests its conditions in order and takes only the first one that is true. Here 85 > 90 is false and 85 > 70 is true, so the program prints "warm" and skips the remaining branches.

questions.prompt: A theater program is meant to print seat numbers 1 through 10. It uses for (int seat = 1; seat < 10; seat++) cout << seat;. What happens when it runs?
choices: It crashes with an error when seat reaches 10
It never finishes because the condition never becomes false
It prints 1 through 10 correctly
It prints 1 through 9 and finishes with no error, so the mistake goes unnoticed unless someone checks the output
questions.why: This is an off-by-one error. When seat reaches 10, the condition 10 < 10 is false, so seat 10 is skipped. Off-by-one errors quietly produce wrong results rather than crashing, and the loop still ends normally.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate the difference between an if statement and a while loop in C++, using a small example, and name one risk or tradeoff that comes with loops.
lessons.modelAnswer: Both an if and a while test a condition, an expression that is true or false. The difference is how often they act on it. An if checks once: if the condition is true the body runs one time, otherwise it is skipped or the else branch runs. A while checks before every iteration and keeps running the body until the condition turns false. For example, if (balance < 0) prints a warning once, while while (balance < 0) would keep repeating its body as long as the balance stays negative. That points to the main risk: something inside the loop has to change the condition, or you get an infinite loop that hangs the program and burns CPU. Loops also invite off-by-one errors, such as using < instead of <=, which give slightly wrong results without any crash.
rubricPoints: States that a condition evaluates to true or false.
Explains that if runs its body at most once while a loop repeats its body while the condition holds.
Gives a concrete example of each.
Names infinite loops as a risk because the condition never becomes false.
Mentions off-by-one or = versus == as a subtle error source.

suggested.rationale: Although that mission uses Python rather than C++, it makes the learner write real loops and conditions over data, which is the same control-flow reasoning this objective builds.

lessons.plain: A function is a named, reusable chunk of a program that does one job. You give it some inputs, it does its work, and it can hand one result back. Think of a kitchen blender: you put in ingredients, press the button, and get a smoothie, without thinking about the motor each time. In C++ you write the recipe once, called defining the function, and then use it wherever you need it, called calling the function. Functions keep programs short, let you fix a bug in one place instead of ten, and let you test each small piece on its own.
lessons.guessPrompt: Suppose a function receives a number, adds 1 to its own copy of that number, and returns nothing. If the main program passes in a variable holding 5, what do you think that variable holds after the call, and why?
lessons.teach:
A function is a named, reusable block of code that does one job. In C++ its definition has four parts. The return type is the kind of value it hands back, such as int or double; void means it hands back nothing. Then come its name, a parameter list in parentheses, and a body in braces. Parameters are local variables that receive the inputs. A return statement ends the function and sends a value back to the caller, the code that used it. Calling a function means writing its name followed by arguments, the actual values passed in. The compiler reads top to bottom and must know about a function before it is called. If the definition sits below main, you place a prototype above main. A prototype is a declaration: just the first line of the function, ending in a semicolon.

Why it works: each call gets its own fresh parameters and local variables. A function therefore behaves the same everywhere it is used. You can test it once and trust it.

Worked example: define int square(int n) { return n * n; } and in main write int y = square(4) + 1;. Step 1: main reaches square(4) and pauses. Step 2: the argument 4 is copied into the parameter n. Step 3: the body computes 16. Step 4: return sends 16 back, and n disappears. Step 5: main resumes, computes 16 + 1, and stores 17 in y.

By default C++ uses pass by value, which means the parameter is a copy of the argument. Writing an ampersand, as in void addOne(int& x), makes x a reference instead. A reference is another name for the caller's own variable, so changes inside the function reach the caller.

Common mistake: writing void addOne(int x) { x = x + 1; } and expecting the caller's variable to grow. Only the copy changes. A second mistake is forgetting return in a non-void function. That may compile with only a warning, but the result is unpredictable. In a running program both bugs are silent. Nothing crashes; you simply get wrong numbers, such as an account balance that never updates.

questions.prompt: A game tracks player points with this function, defined above main: void addBonus(int& points, int bonus) { points = points + bonus; }. In main: int score = 40; addBonus(score, 15); cout << score;. Trace: Step 1: main reaches addBonus(score, 15) and pauses. Step 2: points becomes another name for score because of the ampersand, and the value 15 is copied into bonus. Step 3: ??? Step 4: the function ends, and its parameter bonus disappears. Step 5: main resumes and prints 55. Which choice correctly fills Step 3?
choices: The body computes 55, and a return statement sends 55 back to main, which stores it in score.
The body adds 15 to a copy of score, so score itself stays 40 until main updates it.
The body adds 15 to bonus, making bonus 30, and score is left unchanged.
The body adds 15 to points, and because points is a reference, score itself becomes 55.
questions.why: The ampersand makes points a reference, another name for the caller's variable score, so adding 15 to points changes score directly, with no return value needed in a void function.

questions.prompt: A student writes main first and places this function below it: double average(double a, double b) { return (a + b) / 2; }. main calls average(8.0, 6.0). The compiler reads top to bottom. Which line, placed above main, lets the call compile?
choices: void average(double a, double b);
double average(double a, double b);
average(a, b);
double average;
questions.why: A prototype is the function's first line, with the same return type, name and parameters, ending in a semicolon. It tells the compiler about the function before main calls it.

questions.prompt: A warehouse program has void doubleStock(int n) { n = n * 2; }. In main: int stock = 12; doubleStock(stock); cout << stock;. What is printed?
choices: 0, because n disappears when the function ends
Nothing, because a void function cannot be called with an argument
12, because n is only a copy of stock
24, because the function doubled the value it received
questions.why: There is no ampersand, so C++ uses pass by value. n is a copy of stock, and only the copy is doubled.

questions.prompt: A shop program has int computeTax(int price) { int tax = price / 10; }. Note that there is no return statement. main uses int t = computeTax(200);. What is the most accurate description of what happens?
choices: It may compile with only a warning, but the value stored in t is unpredictable.
The compiler automatically returns tax, so t is always 20.
The program crashes at the call, which makes the bug easy to spot.
The function returns 0 by default because its return type is int.
questions.why: Forgetting return in a non-void function may compile with just a warning. The result is unpredictable, and the bug is silent rather than causing a crash.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how a C++ function call moves data in and out, using a small example of your own. Include the difference between pass by value and pass by reference, and name one tradeoff of choosing reference parameters.
lessons.modelAnswer: A function is a named block that does one job. Its header gives a return type, a name, and parameters; the body does the work. When I call average(a, b), the values of a and b are copied into the parameters. The body runs, and return hands one value back to the spot where I made the call. That is pass by value: the function works on copies, so my original variables are safe. If I declare a parameter with an ampersand, like int& total, it is a reference. That means it is an alias for my actual variable, so the function can change it. The tradeoff is that references let a function update the caller's data, but they also let it change things by accident. That makes bugs harder to trace. I would use value parameters unless the function truly needs to modify its input.
rubricPoints: Defines a function as a named, reusable block with a return type, name, parameters and body.
Distinguishes parameters, which receive input, from arguments, the values passed in a call.
Traces a call: arguments are copied in, the body runs, and return sends a value back to the caller.
Explains that pass by value works on a copy, while a reference parameter can change the caller's variable.
Names a tradeoff, such as references allowing accidental changes to caller data.

suggested.rationale: OpsForge has no C++ mission or engine, and the core skill is tracing what a call does to its data, which explaining it back tests well.

lessons.plain: A pointer is a variable that holds the location of another piece of data instead of the data itself. Every value your program stores lives somewhere in the computer's memory, and each spot in memory has a numbered location called an address. A pointer remembers one of those addresses. Think of a house and a slip of paper with its street address written on it. The slip is not the house, but by following it you can reach the house, look inside, or change what is there. Several slips can point to the same house, and a slip can be rewritten to point somewhere else.
lessons.guessPrompt: If two people each hold a slip of paper with the same house address, and one of them goes to the house and paints the door red, what colour does the other person find when they follow their slip?
lessons.teach:
A pointer is a variable whose value is a memory address. Memory is the computer's working storage, divided into numbered cells, and an address is the number that identifies where a value sits. In C++ you declare a pointer with a star after the type, so int* p means p can hold the address of an int. The address-of operator, written &, gives you the address of an existing variable. The dereference operator, also written * but used in front of a pointer in an expression, follows the address and gives you the value stored there. Memory referencing is the general act of reaching data through its address rather than by its own name.

This works because the pointer and the data are separate. Copying a pointer copies only the address, so many pointers can share one value, and functions can change a caller's data by receiving its address.

Worked example. Line one: int score = 10; puts 10 in some cell, say address 5000. Line two: int* p = &score; stores 5000 in p. Line three: *p = 25; follows address 5000 and writes 25 there. Now printing score shows 25, even though we never wrote score by name. Printing p shows the address, not 25.

A pointer that refers to nothing should hold nullptr, a special value meaning no address. Dereferencing nullptr is an error.

Common mistake: keeping a pointer to memory that no longer belongs to you, called a dangling pointer. This happens when a pointer refers to a local variable after its function returns, or to memory released with delete. The address still exists in the pointer, but the data there may have been reused. The consequence in a running program is unpredictable behaviour: wrong values, a crash, or a security hole, often appearing far from the real bug. Always set a pointer to nullptr after releasing what it points to, and never return the address of a local variable.

questions.prompt: A cinema booking program tracks free seats. Line one: int seats = 18; stores 18 in a memory cell, say address 3100. Line two: int* s = &seats; stores the address 3100 in the pointer s. Line three is missing. Line four: printing seats shows 30, even though seats was never written by name after line one. Which statement belongs on line three?
choices: &seats = 30;
int other = 30; s = &other;
questions.why: The dereference operator in *s follows address 3100 and writes 30 into the cell that seats occupies, so seats now reads 30.

questions.prompt: A game stores a player's lives: int lives = 3; is placed at address 8040, and then int* ptr = &lives; runs. What do printing ptr and printing *ptr show?
choices: ptr shows 3 and *ptr shows 8040
Both show 8040
Both show 3
ptr shows 8040 and *ptr shows 3
questions.why: A pointer's own value is an address (8040), and dereferencing it with * follows that address to the stored value (3).

questions.prompt: A warehouse program runs int boxes = 7; then int* x = &boxes; then int* y = x; then *y = 12;. What value does printing boxes show afterward?
choices: 7, because only y was changed
An error, because two pointers cannot share one variable
The address of boxes
questions.why: Copying x into y copies only the address, so both pointers refer to boxes, and writing through *y changes boxes to 12.

questions.prompt: A function in a payroll program declares a local variable int bonus = 500; and returns &bonus to its caller. The caller later dereferences the returned pointer. What is the problem?
choices: The pointer is dangling, because bonus no longer belongs to the program after the function returns, so reading it gives unpredictable behaviour.
The program cannot compile, because a function can never return a pointer.
None. The address is still stored in the pointer, so the value 500 is guaranteed to be there.
The pointer automatically becomes nullptr when the function returns, so the program reliably stops with a clear error.
questions.why: A local variable stops belonging to you when its function returns, so the returned address is a dangling pointer whose memory may have been reused, which can cause wrong values, crashes or security holes.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate in your own words what a pointer is, what & and * do, and name one risk or tradeoff of reaching data through pointers.
lessons.modelAnswer: A pointer is just a variable that stores a memory address, the numbered location where some other value lives. Using & on a variable gives me its address, so I can store that in a pointer. Putting * in front of the pointer follows that address so I can read or change the actual value. For example, if p holds the address of score, writing *p = 25 changes score to 25. That is useful because copying an address is cheap and lets several parts of the program, including functions, share and modify the same data. The tradeoff is safety: the pointer does not know whether the memory it names is still valid. If the data was freed or went out of scope, I have a dangling pointer, and using it can crash the program or silently corrupt data. Dereferencing nullptr is also an error, so I should check pointers and reset them after freeing memory.
rubricPoints: States that a pointer holds a memory address, not the value itself.
Explains that & gets a variable's address.
Explains that * on a pointer follows the address to read or change the value.
Mentions a benefit such as sharing data or letting functions modify the caller's data.
Names a risk such as dangling pointers or dereferencing nullptr and its effect on a running program.

suggested.rationale: No listed mission or planned engine exercises C++ memory, and being able to explain clearly how an address, the & operator and dereferencing relate is the core skill this objective tests.

lessons.plain: An array and a list are two ways a program can keep a collection of items in order. An array is like a row of numbered lockers built side by side: you can walk straight to locker 37 because you know exactly where it sits, but the row has a fixed length and squeezing a new locker into the middle means shifting everything over. A linked list is more like a scavenger hunt. Each card holds one item plus a note saying where the next card is. Adding a card anywhere is easy, but finding the 37th card means following the trail from the start.
lessons.guessPrompt: You keep 1,000 names in a row of numbered boxes packed side by side, and you need to add a new name at the very front. Roughly how many names have to move? Would that change if each name instead sat on a card that simply said where the next card was?
lessons.teach:
An array is a fixed number of same-type elements stored in one contiguous block of memory. Contiguous means the elements sit next to each other with no gaps. Each element has an index, a position number that starts at 0 in C++. Because every element is the same size, the computer finds element i by taking the start address and adding i times the element size. That is why reading any element by index takes the same short time no matter how big the array is. Programmers call that constant time, written O(1).

A linked list is a chain of nodes. A node is a small record holding one value and a link to the next node. The first node is the head, and the last node's link is empty, which marks the end. The nodes can live anywhere in memory, because each link says where to go next.

Worked example: insert 5 at the front of [8, 3, 9]. In an array, first make sure there is room. Then move 9 from index 2 to index 3, move 3 to index 2, and move 8 to index 1. Finally write 5 at index 0. With n elements that is n moves, so the cost grows with the size, written O(n). In a linked list, you create a node holding 5, point its link at the current head (8), and make the new node the head. That is two steps whatever the length, so it is O(1). The tradeoff runs the other way for lookups. Reading the third item is instant in the array. In the list you must follow links from the head, which is O(n).

C++'s std::vector is a resizable array. When it fills up, it allocates a bigger block and copies every element across.

A common mistake is the off-by-one error. In an array of size 4, the valid indices are 0 through 3, so writing to index 4 is out of bounds. C++ does not check this for you. The write lands on whatever memory comes next, and a running program can then return garbage values, crash, or behave unpredictably long after the bad line ran.

questions.prompt: A weather station program stores 6 daily temperature readings in a C++ array of ints. Each int takes 4 bytes, and the array's block of memory starts at address 2000. The program needs the reading at index 3. Step 1: Every element is the same size, 4 bytes, so the position can be calculated directly. Step 2: [missing]. Step 3: The computer reads the value stored at that address. This takes the same short time whether the array holds 6 readings or 6 million, so it is O(1). Which choice correctly fills in Step 2?
choices: Add the element size times one more than the index, because counting starts at 1: 2000 + 4 × 4 = 2016.
Start at address 2000 and follow each element's link to the next one until the third link is reached.
Add the index to the start address: 2000 + 3 = 2003.
Add the index times the element size to the start address: 2000 + 3 × 4 = 2012.
questions.why: An array is contiguous with same-size elements and indices starting at 0, so element i is at the start address plus i times the element size: 2000 + 3 × 4 = 2012.

questions.prompt: In a linked list, what is a node?
choices: A small record that holds one value and a link to the next node.
The index number of an element, starting at 0.
A larger block of memory that a std::vector allocates when it fills up.
One slot in a contiguous block of memory, found by its index.
questions.why: A linked list is a chain of nodes, and each node holds one value plus a link that says where the next node is.

questions.prompt: A help-desk app keeps 500 support tickets in order. New urgent tickets are added to the front many times a day, and the app almost never looks up a ticket by its position number. Which statement about the choice of structure is correct?
choices: Both structures cost the same for front insertion, because the computer can calculate any address instantly.
A linked list suits this, because adding at the front just creates a node, links it to the old head, and makes it the new head, which is O(1).
A linked list is worse here, because adding a node at the front means following links through all 500 tickets first.
An array is better here, because inserting at the front of an array takes the same time no matter how many tickets there are.
questions.why: Front insertion into an array means shifting every existing element (O(n)), while a linked list does it in a fixed few steps (O(1)), and the slow position lookup of a list barely matters here.

questions.prompt: A C++ program declares an array of 6 scores and then runs a loop that writes to indices 0 through 6. What is the most accurate description of the result?
choices: The array automatically grows to 7 elements, the same way a std::vector resizes when it fills up.
The write to index 6 is out of bounds. C++ does not check it, so the value lands on whatever memory comes next, and the program may later show garbage values, crash, or behave unpredictably.
The program refuses to compile, because C++ checks every array index before the program runs.
Nothing goes wrong, because index 6 is the last valid position in an array of size 6.
questions.why: An array of size 6 has valid indices 0 through 5, so index 6 is an off-by-one write past the end that C++ does not catch, and it can corrupt nearby memory.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how an array differs from a linked list, and tell them when you would pick each one, naming the cost you pay for that choice.
lessons.modelAnswer: An array stores its elements side by side in one block, numbered from index 0. Because of that layout, the program can jump straight to any element with simple arithmetic, so reading by index is O(1). The price is that the size is fixed. Inserting or deleting near the front means shifting every later element, which is O(n). A linked list stores each value in a node that links to the next one. Inserting at the head, or next to a node you already hold, just means rewiring a link, so it is O(1). But reaching the k-th item means walking from the head, which is O(n), and every node carries the extra memory of its link. I'd choose an array or vector when I mostly read by position. I'd choose a list when I constantly insert and remove at the ends or in the middle. With arrays I also stay careful with bounds, because C++ won't stop me from writing past the last element.
rubricPoints: An array is a contiguous, fixed-size block with zero-based indices.
Array access by index is O(1), but inserting in the middle or front is O(n) because elements shift.
A linked list is a chain of nodes, each holding a value and a link to the next.
List insertion at a known spot is O(1), but reaching the k-th item is O(n).
The choice depends on whether the workload is mostly reads by position or mostly inserts and deletes.
It mentions a risk such as out-of-bounds indexing or the extra memory each link costs.

suggested.rationale: That mission has the learner choose a data structure by weighing the cost of each operation, which is the same reasoning behind choosing between an array and a linked list.

lessons.plain: Recursive programming means writing a function that solves a problem by calling itself on a smaller version of the same problem, until the problem is so small the answer is obvious. Think of a stack of nested boxes. To count them, you open the outer box, note "one," and hand the remaining boxes to someone who follows the exact same rule. That keeps going until someone opens a box that is empty and simply says "zero." Each person then adds their one and passes the total back out. The "empty box" stopping point matters most, because without it the process never ends.
lessons.guessPrompt: If a function computes the sum 1 + 2 + ... + n by returning n plus the sum up to n - 1, what must it do when n reaches 0, and what do you think happens if you forget that rule?
lessons.teach:
A recursive function is a function that calls itself. Every correct recursive function has two parts. The base case is an input small enough to answer directly, with no further call. The recursive case breaks the input into a smaller piece and calls the same function on it. Each call must move closer to the base case.

This works because of the call stack. The call stack is the region of memory where the program keeps track of functions that have started but not yet finished. Each call gets its own stack frame, which is a private record of that call's parameters, local variables, and the place to return to. Because every frame is separate, many paused copies of the same function can exist at once without mixing up their values.

Here is a worked example. Factorial of n, written n!, is n times (n - 1) times ... down to 1. In C++ you might write: int fact(int n) { if (n <= 1) return 1; return n * fact(n - 1); }. Now trace fact(3). fact(3) is not a base case, so it needs 3 * fact(2) and pauses. fact(2) needs 2 * fact(1) and pauses. fact(1) hits the base case and returns 1. Then the paused calls finish in reverse order. fact(2) computes 2 * 1 = 2 and returns it. fact(3) computes 3 * 2 = 6 and returns it. At the deepest point, three frames sat on the stack.

A common mistake is a missing or unreachable base case. For example, if the test were n == 1, then calling fact(0) or fact(-2) would skip right past 1 and never stop. In a running program, frames keep piling up until the call stack runs out of memory. This is called a stack overflow, and it usually crashes the program outright.

Recursion is clearest for problems that are self-similar, such as walking a tree, binary search, and merge sort. A loop can always replace it, and a loop uses less memory because it does not stack up frames.

questions.prompt: A recursive function adds the whole numbers from n down to 1: int sumTo(int n) { if (n <= 0) return 0; return n + sumTo(n - 1); }. Here is a trace of sumTo(3). Step 1: sumTo(3) is not a base case, so it needs 3 + sumTo(2) and pauses. Step 2: sumTo(2) needs 2 + sumTo(1) and pauses. Step 3: sumTo(1) needs 1 + sumTo(0) and pauses. Step 4: sumTo(0) hits the base case and returns 0. Step 5: sumTo(1) computes 1 + 0 = 1 and returns it. Step 6: ???. Step 7: sumTo(3) computes 3 + 3 = 6 and returns it. What is Step 6?
choices: sumTo(2) computes 2 + 0 = 2 and returns it
sumTo(0) returns 1, since base cases return 1
sumTo(2) calls sumTo(1) again to fetch its value
sumTo(2) computes 2 + 1 = 3 and returns it
questions.why: Paused calls finish in reverse order, so sumTo(2) resumes next and adds its own n (2) to the 1 just returned by sumTo(1), giving 3.

questions.prompt: A recursive function is called with a different value at each level, and many paused copies of it exist at the same time. What keeps each copy's parameter values from getting mixed up?
choices: All copies share one set of variables, and each copy overwrites them in turn
The compiler turns the recursive calls into a loop before the program runs
The base case saves every earlier value before it returns
Each call gets its own stack frame holding its own parameters, local variables and return point
questions.why: Every call gets a separate stack frame, which is a private record of that call's values. That is why paused copies stay independent.

questions.prompt: Consider int countDown(int n) { if (n == 0) return 0; return countDown(n - 1); }. When countDown(4) runs, how many stack frames for countDown are on the call stack at the deepest point?
questions.why: The calls countDown(4), (3), (2), (1) and (0) all start before any of them finishes, so five frames are stacked at once.

questions.prompt: A function is written as int hops(int n) { if (n == 0) return 0; return 1 + hops(n - 2); }. What happens when a program calls hops(5)?
choices: It returns 0 right away, because 5 is not equal to 0
It runs as a loop and uses no stack memory
It never reaches the base case, so frames pile up until a stack overflow crashes the program
It returns 3, because the input drops 5, 3, 1 and then stops
questions.why: The input goes 5, 3, 1, -1, -3 and so on, and it skips past 0. The base case is never reached, so frames keep piling up until the call stack runs out of memory.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how a recursive function works and why it doesn't run forever, and name one limit or tradeoff of using recursion instead of a loop.
lessons.modelAnswer: A recursive function solves a problem by calling itself on a smaller version of that problem. It needs two pieces. The base case is a small input it answers directly. The recursive case shrinks the input and calls itself again. It stops because every call moves closer to the base case. Once the base case returns, the paused calls finish one by one in reverse order. They can stay separate because each call gets its own stack frame on the call stack, holding its own parameters and locals. For fact(3), you get fact(3), then fact(2), then fact(1) returning 1, and the results come back as 2 and then 6. The tradeoff is memory. Each pending call takes up stack space, so very deep recursion can cause a stack overflow and crash the program, while a loop would use constant space. A missing or unreachable base case causes the same crash.
rubricPoints: Defines recursion as a function calling itself on a smaller subproblem.
Names the base case and the recursive case and what each does.
Explains that each call must progress toward the base case so the process ends.
Mentions that each call gets its own stack frame on the call stack.
Names a limit, such as stack overflow from deep recursion or a missing base case, or the extra memory cost compared with a loop.

suggested.rationale: The core skill is tracing calls and explaining base case, recursive case, and stack behaviour, and no listed mission or planned engine exercises C++ recursion directly.

lessons.plain: Sorting means putting items in order, such as numbers from smallest to largest or names from A to Z. An internal sorting algorithm does this while all the data fits in the computer's working memory (RAM) at once, usually in an array. Think of sorting a hand of playing cards: you might pick up each new card and slide it into the right spot, or you might scan for the smallest card and move it to the front. Each method is a different algorithm, which is a step-by-step recipe. Some recipes are simple but slow down badly as the pile grows. Others are trickier but stay fast.
lessons.guessPrompt: If someone handed you 10 shuffled playing cards and asked you to sort them in your hand, what steps would you follow? Would your method take about 10 times longer or about 100 times longer with 100 cards?
lessons.teach:
An internal sorting algorithm puts a collection in order while all of it sits in main memory (RAM), usually an array. The opposite is external sorting, which is used when the data is too large for memory and must be sorted in chunks on disk. Most beginner sorts are comparison sorts. A comparison sort decides the order only by comparing two elements at a time and then swapping or shifting them.

Three simple sorts each take time proportional to n squared, written O(n²). Here n is the number of items, and O(n²) means the work grows with the square of n. Selection sort finds the smallest remaining item and swaps it into the next position. Bubble sort repeatedly swaps neighbours that are out of order, so large values drift toward the end. Insertion sort takes each item and slides it left into place among the items already sorted.

Two faster sorts use divide and conquer, which means splitting the problem into smaller pieces, solving those, and combining the results. They reach O(n log n). Merge sort splits the array into halves, sorts each half, and merges the halves back together. It needs extra memory. Quicksort picks a pivot, which is one chosen element. It moves smaller items to the pivot's left and larger items to its right, then sorts each side. Quicksort works in place, meaning it needs no second array, but it slows to O(n²) when pivots are chosen badly.

Worked example: insertion sort on [5, 2, 4, 1]. Take 2. The 5 is bigger, so shift it right, giving [2, 5, 4, 1]. Take 4. Shift the 5 right, then stop because 2 is smaller, giving [2, 4, 5, 1]. Take 1. Shift 5, 4 and 2 right and place 1 at the front, giving [1, 2, 4, 5]. On already-sorted data, each item stops at once, so insertion sort is fast on nearly sorted input.

A sort is stable if equal items keep their original relative order. Insertion sort and merge sort are stable. Selection sort and quicksort usually are not.

A common mistake is wrong loop bounds. For example, a loop that compares a[j] with a[j+1] while j runs all the way to n-1 reads past the end of the array. In C++ this is undefined behaviour, so the program may crash or silently produce wrong results. In a running system, using an O(n²) sort on a million records can turn a job that should take under a second into one that takes hours.

questions.prompt: A warehouse app uses bubble sort to put four bin weights in ascending order: [7, 3, 8, 2] (kilograms). Bubble sort repeatedly swaps neighbours that are out of order. Here is the first pass. Step 1: compare 7 and 3. 7 is bigger, so swap them, giving [3, 7, 8, 2]. Step 2: compare 7 and 8. They are already in order, so there is no swap. Step 3: compare 8 and 2. 8 is bigger, so swap them, giving ______. The largest value, 8, has now drifted to the end. Later passes finish the sort and give [2, 3, 7, 8]. What array belongs in the blank after Step 3?
questions.why: Swapping only the neighbours 8 and 2 in [3, 7, 8, 2] gives [3, 7, 2, 8], and one bubble pass does not fully sort the array.

questions.prompt: A gym's member list is already in sign-up order. Staff now want it sorted by membership tier. Members who share the same tier must stay in their original sign-up order. Based on stability, which sort should they use?
choices: Selection sort, because it makes the fewest swaps
Quicksort, because it is O(n log n) on average
Merge sort, because it is stable
Any comparison sort, since all comparison sorts keep equal items in order
questions.why: A stable sort keeps equal items in their original relative order. Merge sort is stable, while selection sort and quicksort usually are not.

questions.prompt: A library keeps its catalogue array of 50,000 titles in alphabetical order. Each day, a handful of new titles are added at the end, and then the array is sorted again. Which simple sort suits this nearly sorted data especially well?
choices: Selection sort, because it always scans for the smallest remaining item
External sorting, because 50,000 items is too many for one array
Insertion sort, because most items stop at once when they are already in place
Bubble sort, because large values drift toward the end
questions.why: On nearly sorted input, insertion sort shifts almost nothing for most items, so it runs fast.

questions.prompt: A weather program stores 10 temperature readings in a C++ array named a, with valid indexes 0 through 9. A loop compares a[j] with a[j+1] while j runs from 0 up to and including 9. What is the problem?
choices: The loop runs too few times to be O(n²)
When j is 9, a[j+1] reads a[10], past the end of the array, which is undefined behaviour
Nothing is wrong, because j stays within 0 to 9
The last reading is never compared, so the sort is merely incomplete
questions.why: Reading a[10] goes past the array's end. In C++ that is undefined behaviour, so the program may crash or silently give wrong results. The loop should stop at j = 8.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate the difference between a simple sort like insertion sort and a faster one like merge sort or quicksort, including when the simple one is still a reasonable choice and what each faster one costs you.
lessons.modelAnswer: All of these are internal sorts, meaning the whole array fits in memory. Insertion sort walks through the array and slides each item left until it sits in the right place among the items already sorted. It is easy to write, stable, and needs no extra memory. On random data it is O(n²), so doubling the data roughly quadruples the work. Merge sort and quicksort split the problem into smaller pieces and reach O(n log n), which matters once you have thousands or millions of items. Each faster sort has a cost. Merge sort needs extra memory for merging. Quicksort works in place, but bad pivot choices can drop it to O(n²), and it usually is not stable. Insertion sort is still a good pick for small arrays or nearly sorted data, because there each item barely moves and the sort runs close to linear time.
rubricPoints: Internal sorting means all the data is in memory, usually an array.
Insertion, selection and bubble sort are O(n²), while merge sort and quicksort average O(n log n).
Insertion sort is fast on small or nearly sorted input.
Merge sort trades extra memory for a guaranteed O(n log n) and stability.
Quicksort is in place but can degrade to O(n²) with poor pivots and is usually unstable.

suggested.rationale: This mission has the learner compare sorting algorithms by how their work grows, which matches the core judgement this objective builds.

lessons.plain: An internal searching algorithm is a step-by-step method for finding one item inside a collection that is held entirely in the computer's working memory, such as an array in a running program. Think of looking up a name in a phone book. You could read every entry from the top until you hit the name, which always works but is slow. Or, because the book is in alphabetical order, you could open it in the middle, see whether the name comes before or after, and throw away half the book each time. Those two habits are the two classic searches: linear search and binary search.
lessons.guessPrompt: You have 1,000 numbers sorted from smallest to largest, and you may only ask whether the middle number of the remaining range is too big, too small or a match. Roughly how many questions do you think you need, in the worst case, to find a number or decide it is not there?
lessons.teach:
An internal search finds a target value in data stored in main memory (RAM, the fast working memory a running program uses), as opposed to an external search over data on disk. In C++ the data is usually an array, a block of same-type values reached by an index starting at 0.

Linear search checks element 0, then 1, then 2, and so on, until it finds the target or runs out of elements. It works on any order of data. Its cost grows in step with the size n, written O(n) in Big-O notation, which describes how work grows as input grows. Doubling the array roughly doubles the worst-case work.

Binary search works only on sorted data. It keeps two indexes, low and high, marking the range that could still hold the target. It checks the middle index, mid. If the middle value is too small, the target must be to the right, so low becomes mid + 1. If it is too big, high becomes mid - 1. Each step halves the range, so the cost is O(log n): about 10 checks for 1,000 items and about 20 for a million.

Worked example: find 25 in [3, 8, 12, 17, 25, 31, 40]. Start low = 0, high = 6. mid = 3, value 17, which is less than 25, so low = 4. mid = (4 + 6) / 2 = 5, value 31, which is greater than 25, so high = 4. mid = 4, value 25, a match at index 4. That took three checks, where linear search needed five. If low ever passes high, the target is absent.

The common mistake is running binary search on unsorted data. It does not crash. It quietly reports "not found" for values that are really present, so a running program returns wrong answers with no error. A second mistake is an off-by-one bound, such as setting low = mid instead of mid + 1, which can loop forever. Sorting first costs time, so binary search pays off when you search the same data many times.

questions.prompt:
A clinic stores its sorted appointment codes in an array: [5, 14, 22, 29, 36, 47, 58] (indexes 0 to 6). A binary search looks for code 22.

Step 1: low = 0, high = 6, so mid = 3. The value at index 3 is 29.
Step 2: ???
Step 3: mid = (0 + 2) / 2 = 1. The value is 14, which is less than 22, so low = 2.
Step 4: mid = (2 + 2) / 2 = 2. The value is 22, a match at index 2.

Which choice correctly fills in Step 2?
choices: 29 is greater than 22, so low = 4
29 is greater than 22, so high = 2
29 is greater than 22, so high = 3
29 is greater than 22, so low = 2
questions.why: The middle value 29 is too big, so the target can only be to the left, and high moves to mid - 1 = 2, which matches the (0 + 2) used in Step 3.
