questions.prompt: A delivery app holds 300 driver ID numbers in an array in RAM, in no particular order. It needs to check once whether ID 7741 is in the list, and the list will not be searched again. Which approach fits best?
choices: Binary search directly, starting with low = 0 and high = 300
Sort the array first, then binary search, since sorting is free
Linear search, since it works on any order and no sort is needed
Binary search directly, since it is O(log n) and always faster
questions.why: Binary search needs sorted data, and sorting costs time that only pays off over many searches, so a single search of unsorted data calls for linear search.

questions.prompt: A warehouse system uses linear search over its inventory array. The inventory grows from 30,000 items to 60,000 items. Roughly what happens to the worst-case number of checks for one search?
choices: It stays about the same, since the array is still in RAM
It roughly halves, since there are more chances to find a match
It goes up by only about one check
It roughly doubles, to about 60,000 checks
questions.why: Linear search is O(n), so its worst-case work grows in step with the size, and doubling the array roughly doubles the checks.

questions.prompt: A developer runs binary search on an array of order numbers that was never sorted: [90, 12, 55, 31, 78]. They search for 12, which really is in the array. What is the most likely outcome?
choices: It finds 12 but takes O(n) time instead of O(log n)
It may quietly report not found, with no error or crash
The program crashes with an error about unsorted data
It always finds 12, because binary search checks every element
questions.why: Binary search assumes sorted order to decide which half to discard, so on unsorted data it can discard the half holding the target and silently return a wrong not-found result.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate the difference between linear search and binary search, when you would choose each, and what the tradeoff or limit of binary search is.
lessons.modelAnswer: Both are internal searches, which means they look for a value in data already held in memory, like an array. Linear search walks the elements one by one from the start until it finds the target or reaches the end. It works on any data, sorted or not, but its worst case grows directly with size, O(n). Binary search needs sorted data. It checks the middle of the remaining range and throws away the half that cannot contain the target, so it needs only about log2 of n checks. That is around 20 for a million items. The limit is the sorting requirement. On unsorted data binary search silently gives wrong "not found" answers, and sorting costs time up front. So I would use linear search for small or one-off searches on unsorted data, and sort once and use binary search when I will search the same data many times. I would also watch the low and high bounds to avoid off-by-one bugs.
rubricPoints: Defines internal search as searching data held in main memory, such as an array.
Describes linear search as checking each element in order, with O(n) worst-case cost, on any data.
Describes binary search as repeatedly halving a sorted range, with O(log n) cost.
States that binary search requires sorted data and gives wrong results otherwise.
Names the tradeoff that sorting costs time up front, so binary search pays off for repeated searches.
Mentions careful handling of the low and high bounds to avoid off-by-one errors or infinite loops.

suggested.rationale: This mission has the learner compare logarithmic and linear search growth and pick the right algorithm, which is the core skill in this objective.

lessons.plain: A linked list stores items as a chain: each item sits in its own small box called a node, and each node holds the item plus an arrow pointing to the next box. Think of a scavenger hunt where every clue tells you where the next clue is. A stack and a queue are rules for adding and removing items. A stack is like a pile of plates: you add and remove only at the top, so the last plate in is the first out. A queue is like a checkout line: people join at the back and leave from the front, so the first in is the first out.
lessons.guessPrompt: You put the letters A, then B, then C into a pile of plates (a stack) and also into a checkout line (a queue). Which letter comes out first from each one?
lessons.teach:
A linked list is a sequence built from nodes. A node is a small record holding one value and a pointer, which is a stored memory address that refers to another node. The list keeps a pointer called head to the first node; the last node's pointer is null, meaning it points nowhere. Many lists also keep a tail pointer to the last node. Because nodes are linked by pointers rather than packed side by side like an array, you can insert or remove at a known spot just by rewiring pointers, which takes constant time, written O(1), meaning the cost does not grow with list size. The price is that reaching the 500th item means walking 499 links, which is O(n), linear in the number of items.

A stack is a collection with last-in, first-out (LIFO) order. Push adds an item on top; pop removes the top item. A queue is first-in, first-out (FIFO). Enqueue adds at the back; dequeue removes from the front. Both are abstract data types: they are defined by their operations, and either a linked list or an array can implement them.

Worked example, a queue built on a linked list with head and tail. Start empty: head and tail are null. Enqueue A: make node A; head and tail both point to A. Enqueue B: set A's next pointer to B, then move tail to B. Enqueue C: B's next becomes C, tail moves to C. Dequeue: save the value at head (A), move head to A's next (B), and free node A. The list is now B then C, and every step was O(1).

A common mistake is forgetting the edge cases. When you dequeue the last remaining node, head becomes null but tail still points at the freed node, so the next enqueue writes into memory you no longer own. In a running program that causes crashes or corrupted data, and forgetting to free removed nodes in C++ leaks memory until the process runs out.

questions.prompt: A photo editor keeps its undo history as a stack built on a linked list. The top of the stack is the node that head points to. The stack currently holds edit 18 on top with edit 7 beneath it, so head points to node 18 and node 18's next pointer points to node 7. The user makes edit 25, which must be pushed. Step 1: create a new node holding 25. Step 2: ______. Step 3: move head so it points to node 25. The stack now reads 25, then 18, then 7, and the push took O(1) time. Which action completes Step 2?
choices: Walk to node 7 at the bottom and attach node 25 after it
Set node 25's next pointer to point at node 18, the current head
Set head to null so the old nodes can be freed first
Set node 18's next pointer to point at node 25
questions.why: The new top node must link to the old top before head moves, so the rest of the stack stays reachable and the push stays O(1).

questions.prompt: A pharmacy fills prescriptions strictly in the order customers dropped them off: the earliest drop-off is filled first. Which abstract data type matches this behavior, and which operation removes the next prescription to fill?
choices: A queue (first-in, first-out); dequeue removes from the front
A queue (first-in, first-out); enqueue removes from the back
A stack (last-in, first-out); pop removes from the top
A stack (last-in, first-out); push removes from the bottom
questions.why: Serving the earliest arrival first is FIFO order, which is a queue, and dequeue is the operation that removes from the front.

questions.prompt: A music app stores a playlist of 3,000 songs as a linked list with only a head pointer. To read the 1,200th song, starting at head, how many links must be followed, and how does this cost grow with list size?
choices: 1,199 links; the cost is O(n), linear in the number of items
0 links; reaching any position is O(1)
1,200 links; the cost stays constant no matter how long the list is
3,000 links; the whole list is always walked, so the cost is O(1)
questions.why: Nodes are reached only by following pointers from head, so the 1,200th node is 1,199 links away, and that walk grows linearly with position, O(n).

questions.prompt: A help-desk ticket system uses a queue built on a linked list with head and tail pointers. Exactly one ticket, node T9, is in the queue. The dequeue code saves T9's value, moves head to T9's next (null), and frees T9, but never changes tail. What is the likely result when the next ticket is enqueued?
choices: Nothing goes wrong, because head is null so the queue is correctly treated as empty
The enqueue writes through tail into freed memory, risking crashes or corrupted data
The program runs slower, since enqueue now takes O(n) time instead of O(1)
The new ticket is placed at the front automatically because head is null
questions.why: Tail still points at the freed node T9, so enqueue updates memory the program no longer owns; dequeuing the last node must also set tail to null.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how a stack and a queue differ, how a linked list can implement each one, and name one tradeoff of using a linked list instead of an array.
lessons.modelAnswer: A stack is last-in, first-out: push puts an item on top and pop takes the top item back off, like a pile of plates. A queue is first-in, first-out: enqueue adds to the back and dequeue removes from the front, like a line at a store. A linked list is a chain of nodes, each holding a value and a pointer to the next node. For a stack, I push and pop at the head, so both are O(1). For a queue, I keep a head and a tail pointer, enqueue at the tail and dequeue at the head, also O(1). The tradeoff versus an array is that a linked list grows without resizing and inserts cheaply by rewiring pointers, but it costs extra memory per node and cannot jump straight to the nth item; finding it means walking the chain in O(n). I also have to handle the empty case and free removed nodes.
rubricPoints: Defines a stack as LIFO with push and pop.
Defines a queue as FIFO with enqueue and dequeue.
Describes a linked list as nodes holding a value and a pointer to the next node.
Explains how head (and tail for a queue) make the operations O(1).
Names a tradeoff such as no direct indexing (O(n) access) or extra pointer memory.
Mentions an edge case such as the empty list or freeing removed nodes.

suggested.rationale: No listed mission or planned engine has the learner build these structures, and explaining LIFO versus FIFO and the pointer wiring back in their own words is the core skill to check.

lessons.plain: A graph is a way to describe things and the connections between them: cities joined by roads, people joined by friendships, web pages joined by links. The things are called nodes and the connections are called edges. A tree is a special kind of graph shaped like a family tree or a folder system. It has one starting point at the top, every item hangs under exactly one parent, and you can never loop back to where you started. Programs use trees and graphs to model real relationships and then walk through them in a planned order to answer questions like what is reachable or what the shortest route is.
lessons.guessPrompt: You have a map of airline routes between cities. You want the trip from city A to city F that uses the fewest flights. Would you first check every city one flight from A, then every city two flights away, and so on? Or would you follow one route as far as it goes before trying another? Which approach do you think guarantees the fewest flights, and why?
lessons.teach:
A graph is a set of vertices (also called nodes, the things being modeled) joined by edges (connections between pairs of vertices). An edge is directed if it is one-way, like following someone online, and undirected if it is two-way, like a road. A graph is weighted when each edge carries a number such as a distance. A path is a sequence of edges leading from one vertex to another. A cycle is a path that returns to its start.

A tree is a graph that is connected, meaning every vertex can be reached, and has no cycles. One vertex is chosen as the root. Every other vertex has exactly one parent (the vertex above it) and may have children (the vertices below it). A vertex with no children is a leaf. The height of a tree is the number of edges on its longest root-to-leaf path. A binary tree allows each vertex at most two children, called left and right.

Programs usually store a graph in one of two ways. An adjacency list gives each vertex a list of its neighbors, which saves space when there are few edges. An adjacency matrix is an n-by-n table where entry [i][j] marks an edge. It answers 'is there an edge here?' instantly but always uses n² space.

Traversal means visiting every reachable vertex exactly once. Breadth-first search (BFS) uses a queue and explores layer by layer, so in an unweighted graph it finds the path with the fewest edges. Depth-first search (DFS) uses a stack or recursion and follows one branch as deep as it can before backing up. Trees also have named visiting orders. Preorder visits the node and then its children. Inorder, used in binary trees, visits the left subtree, then the node, then the right subtree. Postorder visits the children and then the node.

Here is BFS traced from A, with undirected edges A-B, A-C, B-D, C-D and D-E. Start with the queue holding A, and mark A as visited. Remove A and add B and C, marking both. Remove B and add D, marking it. Remove C. D is already marked, so skip it. Remove D and add E. Remove E. The visit order is A, B, C, D, E, and E turns out to be three edges from A.

A common mistake is forgetting the visited mark. Tree code can skip it because trees have no cycles. In a graph with a cycle such as A-B-D-C-A, though, an unmarked traversal goes around forever. In a running system that shows up as a hung request or a stack overflow.

questions.prompt: A delivery company models its depots as an undirected graph with edges P-Q, P-R, Q-S, R-S, R-T and S-U. A breadth-first search (BFS, which uses a queue and explores layer by layer) starts at P. Step 1: the queue holds P, and P is marked visited. Step 2: remove P, add Q and R to the queue, and mark both. Step 3: remove Q. Its neighbors are P (already marked) and S, so add S and mark it. Step 4: ??? Step 5: remove S. Q and R are marked, so add U and mark it. Step 6: remove T. Step 7: remove U. The visit order is P, Q, R, S, T, U, and U is three edges from P. Which choice correctly describes Step 4?
choices: Remove R. Add S and T to the queue, because both are neighbors of R.
Remove R. Add T, then remove T right away to go as deep as possible before returning to S.
Remove S, because it was the vertex added most recently. Then add U and mark it.
Remove R. P and S are already marked, so skip them. Add T and mark it.
questions.why: A queue removes vertices in the order they were added, so R comes out next, and the visited marks mean only the unmarked neighbor T is added.

questions.prompt: A file system is modeled as a tree with root M. M has children N and O. N has one child, Q, and Q has one child, R. O has no children. Using the definition of height as the number of edges on the longest root-to-leaf path, what is the height of this tree?
questions.why: The longest root-to-leaf path is M-N-Q-R, which has 3 edges. Answering 4 is a common mistake that comes from counting the vertices on that path instead of the edges.

questions.prompt: A messaging app stores its users as a graph. It has 50,000 users, and each user is connected to only about 100 others. Which way of storing this graph makes the most sense, and why?
choices: An adjacency list (a list of each vertex's neighbors), because there are few edges compared with all possible pairs, so it saves a great deal of space
An adjacency matrix (an n-by-n table of edges), because it always uses less memory than a list
An adjacency matrix, because the 50,000-by-50,000 table needs only about 50,000 entries
An adjacency list, because it answers 'is there an edge between these two users?' instantly while a matrix cannot
questions.why: With few edges per vertex, a list stores only the connections that actually exist, while a matrix always needs n² entries (here 2.5 billion), however few edges there are.

questions.prompt: A city transit app runs depth-first search (DFS, which follows one branch as deep as possible before backing up) over its station graph to find every reachable station. The code worked on a branching tree of bus routes. On the new rail map, which has a loop line, requests hang and eventually crash with a stack overflow. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The rail map should have been stored as an adjacency matrix instead of an adjacency list
The traversal does not mark stations as visited, so it keeps going around the loop
The rail map is weighted, and DFS cannot read edge weights
DFS cannot work on undirected graphs, so the code must switch to BFS
questions.why: Tree code can skip visited marks because trees have no cycles, but a graph with a cycle sends an unmarked traversal around forever, which shows up as a hung request or a stack overflow.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate the difference between a tree and a general graph, and when you would use breadth-first versus depth-first search. Name one tradeoff, such as adjacency list versus matrix, or the cost of handling cycles.
lessons.modelAnswer: A graph is just vertices connected by edges. The edges can be one-way or two-way, and they can carry weights. A tree is a restricted graph: it is connected, has no cycles, and has a root, so every other node has exactly one parent. Because a tree can't loop, tree traversals like preorder, inorder and postorder don't need to track visited nodes. A general graph does need that tracking, or a cycle will trap the traversal forever. To traverse, BFS uses a queue and goes layer by layer, so it gives the fewest-edge path in an unweighted graph. DFS uses a stack or recursion and dives deep first, which is handy for exploring every branch. For storage there's a tradeoff. An adjacency list is compact when edges are few. An adjacency matrix checks any edge instantly but costs n² space even if the graph is sparse.
rubricPoints: Defines a graph as vertices joined by edges, possibly directed or weighted.
Defines a tree as a connected graph with no cycles and a root, where each non-root node has one parent.
Explains that BFS uses a queue, goes layer by layer, and finds fewest-edge paths in unweighted graphs.
Explains that DFS uses a stack or recursion and goes deep before backing up.
Notes that graph traversal needs a visited mark to avoid looping on cycles.
Names a tradeoff such as adjacency list versus adjacency matrix space and lookup speed.

suggested.rationale: No current mission or planned engine traces tree or graph traversals, so reasoning through exam-style tracing problems like the BFS example builds the skill best.

lessons.plain: Every program needs places in the computer's memory to keep its data. Static memory allocation means the amount of space is decided before the program runs, when the code is compiled, and it is reserved and released automatically. Dynamic memory allocation means the program asks for space while it is running, in whatever amount it turns out to need, and must give that space back when finished. Think of a restaurant. Static is a table for four booked a week ahead: fixed size, cleared for you when you leave. Dynamic is asking the host for chairs as guests arrive, and then remembering to return them.
lessons.guessPrompt: A program asks the user how many test scores they want to enter and only then stores them. Could the programmer have reserved exactly the right amount of memory when writing the code? Why or why not?
lessons.teach:
Static memory allocation means the size of a piece of memory is fixed when the program is compiled, which is when source code is translated into a runnable program. In C++ this covers global variables, which live for the whole run, and local variables such as int scores[100], which are created on the stack when a function starts and freed automatically when it returns. The stack is a region of memory that grows and shrinks in strict order as functions are called and finish.

Dynamic memory allocation means requesting memory at run time from the heap, a large pool of memory the program draws on in any order. In C++ the operator new reserves heap space and returns a pointer, a variable holding a memory address. The operator delete, or delete[] for arrays, gives that space back. Nothing frees heap memory for you; that is the price of flexibility.

Why have both? Static allocation is fast and automatic but rigid: the size must be known in advance, and the memory disappears when its function ends. Dynamic allocation fits sizes discovered while running and can outlive the function that made it.

Worked example. The user types 7. The program runs int* scores = new int[7]; and the heap hands back room for exactly seven integers, with scores holding its address. The program fills scores[0] through scores[6] and averages them. When finished it runs delete[] scores; and the seven slots return to the heap. A fixed int scores[100] would waste 93 slots here and fail outright for 150 scores.

Common mistake: forgetting delete, or losing the only pointer to a block. That block can never be returned, which is called a memory leak. A related error is using a pointer after deleting its memory, called a dangling pointer, which can cause crashes or corrupted data.

In a running system, a small leak in code that runs on every request makes a long-lived server's memory grow steadily until the operating system kills it or it slows to a crawl.

questions.prompt: A weather station logger only learns how many readings it will process when the operator types a number at run time. Today the operator types 48. The steps are: (1) read the count into int n, so n is 48. (2) [missing step]. (3) Store values in readings[0] through readings[47]. (4) Scan the array to find the highest temperature. (5) Run delete[] readings; so the 48 slots go back to the heap. Which line correctly fills step 2?
choices: double* readings; to declare a pointer without reserving any memory
double readings[10]; to reserve a small fixed array on the stack
delete[] readings; to clear out any old data before storing values
double* readings = new double[n]; to reserve n slots on the heap
questions.why: Because the size is only known at run time, the program must request exactly n slots from the heap with new and keep their address in a pointer, which step 5 later releases with delete[].

questions.prompt: Inside a function, a programmer writes char label[40]; to hold a product name. Which statement best describes this memory?
choices: It is static allocation: its size is fixed at compile time, it lives on the stack, and it is freed automatically when the function returns.
It is static allocation that stays alive for the whole run of the program, like a global variable.
It is dynamic allocation because its contents can change while the program runs.
It is dynamic allocation: it comes from the heap and must be released later with delete[].
questions.why: A local array with a fixed size is static allocation placed on the stack, and it disappears automatically when its function finishes.

questions.prompt: A function in a ticketing app builds a list of seats whose length depends on the event chosen, and the list must still exist after the function returns so other parts of the program can use it. What is the right approach?
choices: Declare a local array and pass the caller its address after the function returns.
Use new to allocate a fixed array of exactly 500 seats, then delete it before returning.
Use new to allocate the seats on the heap, return the pointer, and delete[] it once no part of the program needs it.
Declare a local array such as int seats[500]; inside the function, since it frees itself.
questions.why: Heap memory from new can match a size found at run time and outlives the function that created it, but someone must eventually free it with delete[].

questions.prompt: A long-running chat server allocates a 2 KB buffer with new for every incoming message but never calls delete on it. After a million messages, what is the most likely result?
choices: Nothing, because heap memory is freed automatically when each request's function returns.
A dangling pointer error, because each buffer was used after being deleted.
A memory leak: roughly 2 GB of unreturnable heap memory builds up until the server slows badly or the operating system kills it.
The memory is reclaimed because the buffers were allocated on the stack.
questions.why: Heap memory is never freed for you, so allocating without delete on every request leaks memory that grows steadily in a long-lived server.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate the difference between static and dynamic memory allocation in C++, when you would choose each, and what tradeoff or risk comes with dynamic allocation.
lessons.modelAnswer: Static allocation is memory whose size is settled at compile time, like a global variable or a local array such as int a[100]. Locals sit on the stack and are freed automatically when the function returns, so it is fast and you cannot forget to clean up. Its limit is rigidity: you must know the size in advance, and the data vanishes when the function ends. Dynamic allocation uses new to grab heap memory at run time in exactly the size you need, and that memory survives until you call delete. I would use it when the size depends on input or when data must outlive the function that created it. The tradeoff is responsibility: if I forget delete or lose the pointer, I leak memory, and on a long-running server leaks pile up until it crashes. Using memory after deleting it is another serious bug.
rubricPoints: Static allocation has its size fixed at compile time and is managed automatically.
Dynamic allocation requests heap memory at run time with new and releases it with delete.
Static is fast and safe but rigid in size and lifetime.
Dynamic suits sizes known only at run time or data that must outlive a function.
Forgetting delete causes memory leaks that grow in long-running programs.
Using memory after it is freed creates dangling pointer bugs.

suggested.rationale: No current mission or planned engine exercises C++ memory management, so explaining when to choose each kind of allocation and naming its risks is the most useful practice here.

lessons.plain: Hashing and tree-based searching are two ways to find a stored item quickly without checking every item one by one. Hashing turns a key, like a username, into a number that says which slot in an array to look in, much like a coat check giving you ticket 37 so the attendant goes straight to hook 37. A search tree keeps items in sorted order so each comparison throws away about half of what is left, like guessing a number when told higher or lower. Hashing is usually fastest for exact lookups. Trees are a little slower but keep everything in order.
lessons.guessPrompt: You have 1,000,000 names stored in sorted order and you may only ask whether the name you want comes before or after the one you are looking at. Roughly how many questions do you need, at most, to find one name?
lessons.teach:
A hash table is an array of slots, called buckets, plus a hash function: a rule that turns a key into a bucket number. The usual pattern computes a large number from the key, then takes it modulo the table size, meaning the remainder after division. Lookup, insert and delete jump straight to one bucket, so on average they take constant time, written O(1). When two keys land in the same bucket, that is a collision. Chaining handles it by keeping a small linked list in each bucket. Open addressing instead probes the next slots until it finds a free one. The load factor is the number of items divided by the number of buckets. As it rises, chains grow longer, so tables resize, usually by doubling and re-inserting every item.

A binary search tree (BST) is a tree where each node has at most two children, and every key in a node's left subtree is smaller than the node's key while every key in its right subtree is larger. A search compares the target with the root and goes left or right, discarding a whole subtree each step. The cost is the tree's height. A balanced tree, such as an AVL or red-black tree, rebalances itself after inserts to keep that height near log2 n, so operations take O(log n). A BST also gives keys in sorted order and supports range queries. A hash table cannot do either.

Worked example: a table has 7 buckets and the hash is key mod 7. Insert 15: 15 mod 7 = 1, so it goes in bucket 1. Insert 22: 22 mod 7 = 1, a collision, so with chaining bucket 1 now holds 15 then 22. To look up 22, compute bucket 1, then walk the chain: check 15, no match, check 22, found.

A common mistake is inserting already-sorted keys into a plain, unbalanced BST. Each new key becomes a right child, the tree turns into a long chain, and searches fall to O(n). A weak hash function that sends many keys to one bucket fails the same way. In a running system, this shows up as lookups that suddenly slow to a crawl as the data grows.

questions.prompt: A bike-rental shop stores rental IDs in a hash table with 11 buckets, using the hash function key mod 11 (the remainder after dividing by 11) and chaining (a small linked list in each bucket) for collisions. Step 1: insert 30. 30 mod 11 = 8, so 30 goes in bucket 8. Step 2: insert 52. 52 mod 11 = 8, a collision, so bucket 8 now holds 30 then 52. Step 3: insert 19. 19 mod 11 = 8, another collision, so bucket 8 now holds 30, 52, 19. Step 4: look up 19. Compute 19 mod 11 = 8 and go to bucket 8. Step 5: [missing]. Step 6: the third item checked matches, so 19 is found. Which choice correctly fills Step 5?
choices: Walk the chain in bucket 8, comparing each stored key with 19: 30 no, 52 no, 19 yes
Return 30 right away, because it is stored in the bucket that 19 hashes to
Move to bucket 9 and check it, then bucket 10, until an empty slot appears
Resize the table to 22 buckets and recompute 19 mod 22 to find it
questions.why: With chaining, every colliding key sits in one bucket's list, so after jumping to bucket 8 you compare 19 against each stored key in order until you reach a match.

questions.prompt: A ticketing service keeps 300 event records in a hash table with 120 buckets. The load factor is the number of items divided by the number of buckets. What is the load factor?
questions.why: Load factor = items / buckets = 300 / 120 = 2.5, meaning on average two or three items share each bucket.

questions.prompt: A warehouse app must often answer: "list every part number between 4000 and 4500, in sorted order." It also needs fast single lookups. Which structure fits best?
choices: A hash table, because it gives O(1) lookups and keeps keys sorted in its buckets
A plain linked list, because walking it in order handles any range
A balanced binary search tree, such as a red-black tree, because it keeps keys in sorted order
A hash table with open addressing, because probing visits keys in increasing order
questions.why: A balanced BST keeps O(log n) lookups and also supports sorted output and range queries, which a hash table cannot do.

questions.prompt: A sensor logger inserts readings into a plain, unbalanced binary search tree keyed by timestamp, and timestamps always arrive in increasing order. After 50,000 readings, searches have become very slow. What is the cause?
choices: Timestamps are too large to compare, so each search must scan both subtrees
Too many collisions in the tree's buckets have built up long chains
Each new key became a right child, so the tree is a chain with height near n and searches are O(n)
The tree rebalanced itself after every insert, which made each search take O(n)
questions.why: Sorted inserts into an unbalanced BST always go right, producing a long chain whose height grows with n, so the search cost (the height) becomes O(n).

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how a hash table and a balanced binary search tree each find a key, and say when you would choose the tree even though the hash table is usually faster.
lessons.modelAnswer: A hash table runs the key through a hash function to get a bucket index and jumps straight there. On average that is O(1). Collisions, where two keys share a bucket, are handled by chaining or probing. The table resizes when the load factor gets high so chains stay short. A binary search tree keeps smaller keys to the left and larger keys to the right, so each comparison discards a subtree. If it stays balanced, a search takes O(log n) steps. The tradeoff is ordering. A hash table scatters keys, so it cannot list them in sorted order or answer a question like 'all keys between 100 and 200' without scanning everything. A tree does both naturally. I would also watch the failure modes: a bad hash function or a high load factor degrades a hash table toward O(n), and an unbalanced tree fed sorted input degrades the same way.
rubricPoints: A hash function maps a key to a bucket, giving average O(1) lookups.
Collisions are handled by chaining or open addressing, and resizing keeps the load factor low.
A binary search tree uses the left-smaller, right-larger rule, so the cost depends on its height.
A balanced tree keeps its height near log n, giving O(log n) operations.
A tree supports sorted traversal and range queries, which a hash table cannot do.
Both structures degrade toward O(n) with a bad hash or an unbalanced tree.

suggested.rationale: That mission has the learner choose between hash tables and lists on real cost grounds, which directly exercises the lookup-speed reasoning in this lesson.

lessons.plain: Sorting means putting a collection of items into order, like arranging a hand of cards from low to high. Searching means finding where a particular item is, or confirming it is not there. Table access means jumping straight to an entry because you can calculate where it sits, like going directly to seat 14 in row C instead of checking every seat. These three ideas matter because the method you pick decides how much work grows as your data grows. A clever method stays quick with a million items. A careless one slows to a crawl.
lessons.guessPrompt: You have a printed phone book of 1,000 names in alphabetical order and want to find one name. Roughly how many names would you need to look at if you open near the middle and keep halving, compared with reading from the first page?
lessons.teach:
Sorting means rearranging items into order by a key, such as numbers from smallest to largest. Searching means finding where a key is stored, or proving it is absent. Table access means reaching an entry directly by computing its position instead of looking for it.

Linear search checks items one by one. On n items it may take n comparisons, written O(n), which means the work grows in proportion to n. Binary search works only on sorted data. It compares the target to the middle item, then throws away the half that cannot contain it. Each step halves the remaining range, so about log2 n steps are enough, written O(log n). That halving is why sorting first pays off when you search many times.

Worked example: find 23 in the sorted list 4, 8, 15, 16, 23, 42, 50, at positions 0 to 6. The middle is position 3, value 16. Since 23 is bigger, keep positions 4 to 6. The middle of that range is position 5, value 42. Since 23 is smaller, keep position 4. Position 4 holds 23, so it is found in three comparisons. Linear search would need five.

Simple sorts need O(n²) comparisons in the worst case. Insertion sort takes each item and slides it left until it sits in order. Selection sort repeatedly picks the smallest remaining item. Merge sort splits the list, sorts each half, and merges them back together. Quicksort splits the items around a chosen pivot value. Both average O(n log n), which is far faster for large n.

Table access uses arithmetic. Row-major order means a two-dimensional table is stored row by row. In that layout, the entry at row r, column c of a table with C columns sits at position r×C + c. For C = 10, row 2, column 3 is position 23, reached in one step. That is O(1), meaning constant time regardless of table size.

A common mistake is running binary search on unsorted data. It silently returns wrong answers rather than errors. In a running system, an O(n²) sort or repeated linear searches on growing data turn a fast request into one that times out.

questions.prompt:
A warehouse system stores bin numbers in a sorted list: 3, 9, 14, 27, 33, 48, 61, 70, 85, at positions 0 to 8. It uses binary search to find 70. When a range has no exact middle, it picks the lower of the two middle positions.

Step 1: The range is positions 0 to 8. The middle is position 4, value 33. Since 70 is bigger, keep positions 5 to 8.
Step 2: ???
Step 3: The range is now positions 7 to 8. The middle is position 7, value 70. Found.

Which choice correctly fills in Step 2?
choices: Check position 5 next, value 48. Since 70 is bigger, move on to position 6.
The middle of 5 to 8 is position 6, value 61. Since 70 is bigger, go back and keep positions 0 to 3.
The middle of 5 to 8 is position 6, value 61. Since 70 is bigger, keep positions 7 to 8.
The middle of 5 to 8 is position 6, value 61. Since 70 is bigger, keep positions 5 to 6.
questions.why: Binary search compares the target with the middle item, which is 61 at position 6, and because 70 is larger it discards the lower half and keeps positions 7 to 8, matching the range in Step 3.

questions.prompt: A school stores its seating chart as a two-dimensional table in row-major order, with 12 columns per row. Rows and columns are numbered from 0. At what position is the entry at row 4, column 7 stored?
questions.why: In row-major order the position is r×C + c, which here is 4×12 + 7 = 55.

questions.prompt: A developer runs binary search to find a customer ID in a list that was never sorted. According to the idea behind binary search, what is the most likely result?
choices: The search still works but takes O(n) steps instead of O(log n).
The search may return a wrong answer, such as saying the ID is absent, without any warning.
The program stops with an error saying the list is unsorted.
The search sorts the list automatically and then finds the ID.
questions.why: Binary search throws away halves on the assumption that the data is sorted, so on unsorted data it can discard the half that actually holds the key and silently give a wrong answer.

questions.prompt: A library catalog holds about 1,000,000 records sorted by ID. In the worst case, about how many comparisons does binary search need to find one ID or prove it is missing?
choices: About 20
About 500,000
About 1,000
questions.why: Each binary search step halves the range, so about log2 of 1,000,000 steps are needed, which is roughly 20.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate when you would sort data and use binary search instead of just using linear search, and name the tradeoff or limit involved. Also say when direct table access beats both.
lessons.modelAnswer: Linear search checks every item, so its cost grows in step with the data, O(n). Binary search halves the range each step, so it needs only about log2 n comparisons. For a million items that is around 20 comparisons instead of up to a million. The catch is that binary search only works on sorted data, and sorting costs about O(n log n) with merge sort or quicksort, or O(n²) with simple sorts. If I search once, sorting first is not worth it, so I would just scan. If I search many times, or the data stays sorted as it changes, sorting once pays for itself. Running binary search on unsorted data gives wrong answers without any error. When I can compute an item's position directly, such as row r, column c being r×C + c in a row-major table, I skip searching entirely and get O(1) access.
rubricPoints: Linear search is O(n) and works on any order.
Binary search is O(log n) because it halves the range, but it requires sorted data.
Sorting has its own cost, so it only pays off when the data is searched repeatedly.
Simple sorts are O(n²) while merge sort and quicksort average O(n log n).
Direct table access computes a position, such as r×C + c, for O(1) lookup.

suggested.rationale: This mission has the learner compare search and sorting algorithms by how their work grows, which is exactly this objective.

lessons.plain: Recursion is a way of solving a problem by having a procedure call itself on a smaller version of the same problem, until the problem becomes so small the answer is obvious. Think of a set of nesting dolls: to count them, you open the outer doll, note one, and then count the dolls inside, which is the same task, just smaller. Eventually you reach the tiny solid doll that does not open, and you stop. Every recursive solution needs that stopping point plus a step that shrinks the problem toward it. When both are present, the small answers combine back into the full answer.
lessons.guessPrompt: If you wanted to add up the numbers 1 through 5, but you were only allowed to say "5 plus the sum of 1 through 4," what would you need to know before you could ever finish, and when would you finally stop asking?
lessons.teach:
Recursion is a technique where a function solves a problem by calling itself on a smaller instance of the same problem. A function is a named block of code that takes inputs and returns a result. Every correct recursive function has two parts. The base case is an input small enough to answer directly, with no further calls. The recursive case breaks the input into a smaller piece, calls the function on that piece, and combines the result.

Why it works: if each call moves strictly closer to the base case, the chain of calls must end. This is the same reasoning as mathematical induction from discrete math. You prove the smallest case directly, then show that a correct answer for size n-1 gives a correct answer for size n.

Worked example: sum(n) returns 0 when n is 0 (base case), otherwise n + sum(n-1). Trace sum(3). sum(3) needs sum(2). sum(2) needs sum(1). sum(1) needs sum(0). sum(0) returns 0. Now unwind: sum(1) returns 1+0=1, sum(2) returns 2+1=3, sum(3) returns 3+3=6.

Each pending call waits on the call stack. The call stack is the region of memory where the program keeps one frame per active function call. A frame holds that call's parameters and local variables. sum(3) briefly holds four frames at once.

Common mistake: a missing or unreachable base case. For example, calling sum(-1) with the code above never reaches 0. The calls never stop, and each new frame consumes stack memory until the program crashes with a stack overflow. Even a correct recursion that goes very deep, such as a million levels, can overflow, because the stack is limited in size.

Recursion shines on problems that are naturally self-similar, like trees, divide-and-conquer sorting, and backtracking searches. For a simple running total, an ordinary loop does the same work without the extra stack frames.

questions.prompt: A shipping company's software counts the ways to line up n different crates on a loading dock. It uses a recursive function: ways(1) returns 1 (base case), and otherwise ways(n) returns n * ways(n-1). Trace ways(4). ways(4) needs ways(3). ways(3) needs ways(2). ways(2) needs ways(1). ways(1) returns 1. Now unwind: ways(2) returns 2*1 = 2. [MISSING STEP]. ways(4) returns 4*6 = 24. Which line fills the missing step?
choices: ways(3) returns 3+2 = 5
ways(3) returns 3*1 = 3
ways(3) returns 3*6 = 18
ways(3) returns 3*2 = 6
questions.why: While unwinding, ways(3) combines its own n (3) with the result just returned by ways(2) (which is 2) using the recursive rule n * ways(n-1), so it returns 3*2 = 6.

questions.prompt: A library app uses a recursive function to count the books on a stack. If the stack is empty it returns 0 right away. Otherwise it removes the top book, calls itself on the remaining stack, and adds 1 to that result. Which part is what lets the chain of calls stop?
choices: Removing the top book before calling itself
Storing each call's local variables in a frame
Adding 1 to the result of the smaller call
Returning 0 right away for an empty stack, with no further calls
questions.why: The base case is the input small enough to answer directly with no further calls. The empty stack returning 0 is that base case, and it is what ends the chain of calls.

questions.prompt: A game timer uses this recursive function: tick(n) stops and returns when n equals 0, and otherwise calls tick(n-2). A player's setting causes tick(7) to be called. What happens?
choices: The values go 7, 5, 3, 1, -1, and so on, never hitting 0, so frames pile up until a stack overflow crashes the program
It reaches 0 after four calls and returns normally
It returns immediately because 7 is an odd number
It runs forever but uses no extra memory, so the program hangs without crashing
questions.why: Starting from an odd number and subtracting 2 skips over 0, so the base case is unreachable. Each new call adds a frame to the limited call stack until it overflows.

questions.prompt: A lab's data tool computes power(b, e) recursively: power(b, 0) returns 1 (base case), and otherwise power(b, e) returns b * power(b, e-1). When power(5, 4) is called, what is the largest number of frames for this function on the call stack at one moment?
questions.why: The calls power(5,4), power(5,3), power(5,2), power(5,1) and power(5,0) are all active at once before any of them returns, so five frames are on the stack together.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how recursion solves a problem, what two parts every recursive function needs, and describe one limit or tradeoff of using recursion instead of a loop.
lessons.modelAnswer: Recursion means a function solves a problem by calling itself on a smaller version of the same problem. You need a base case, an input small enough to answer directly, and a recursive case that shrinks the input, calls itself, and combines the result. For example, sum(n) is n plus sum(n-1), and sum(0) is 0. Because every call moves closer to the base case, the calls eventually stop and the answers unwind back up. It is basically induction turned into code. The tradeoff is memory: each active call keeps a frame on the call stack, so sum(n) holds about n frames at once. If the base case is missing or never reached, or the input is just very large, the stack fills up and the program crashes with a stack overflow. A loop uses constant stack space, so for simple linear tasks a loop is often safer. Recursion is the better fit for self-similar structures like trees.
rubricPoints: Defines recursion as a function calling itself on a smaller instance of the same problem.
Names the base case as the directly answerable stopping condition.
Names the recursive case as shrinking the input toward the base case and combining results.
Explains that each call uses a call-stack frame.
Identifies stack overflow from a missing base case or excessive depth as a limit.
Notes when a loop may be preferable, or when recursion fits naturally, as with trees.

suggested.rationale: No listed mission or planned engine has the learner write recursive functions, and explaining the base case, recursive case and stack tradeoff is the core understanding to build.

lessons.plain: An abstract data type, or ADT, is a description of a kind of data purely by what you can do with it, not by how it is stored. A C++ class is the tool that turns that promise into working code: it bundles the stored data with the operations allowed on it and hides the storage from everyone else. Think of a vending machine. You only see the buttons and the slot, so you trust that pressing a button gives a snack. The owner can rearrange the shelves inside without changing how anyone uses the machine.
lessons.guessPrompt: Suppose a Fraction type stores a numerator and a denominator, and any part of a program can change the denominator directly. What could go wrong, and how might you stop it?
lessons.teach:
An abstract data type (ADT) is a type defined by its operations and the rules they follow, called its interface, rather than by its storage, called its implementation. In C++ you build an ADT with a class, which is a user-defined type that groups data members (stored values) with member functions (operations). Members marked public are the interface that outside code may call. Members marked private can be touched only by the class's own functions. This hiding is called encapsulation.

Encapsulation matters because it lets the class guard an invariant, which is a rule that must stay true for every object at all times. A constructor, a special function that runs when an object is created, sets up the invariant first. Each public function then keeps it true.

Worked example: a Fraction ADT whose invariant is "the denominator is never zero, and it is always positive." The private data are int num and int den. The public operations are a constructor Fraction(int n, int d), add(Fraction other), and value(). Trace Fraction f(1, -2). The constructor sees that d is not zero, so creation is allowed. Then, because d is negative, it flips both signs and stores num = -1, den = 2. Next, f.add(Fraction(1, 2)) computes (-1*2 + 1*2) / (2*2) = 0/4, and the result keeps a positive denominator. Calling Fraction g(3, 0) is rejected in the constructor, for example by throwing an exception, which is C++'s way of signaling an error. No invalid Fraction can ever exist.

A common mistake is making the data members public "for convenience." Any caller can then write f.den = 0, and the invariant is gone. In a running system, that bad value can cause a crash or a wrong result far from where the mistake happened, which makes it hard to trace. Public data also locks you in: if you later change how the data is stored, every caller breaks. With private data, you can change the implementation freely as long as the interface behaves the same.

questions.prompt:
A bike-rental shop writes a C++ class called Dock to track how many bikes are parked at one station. Its invariant is "the number of bikes is never negative and never more than the dock's capacity." The private data are int bikes and int capacity. The public operations are a constructor Dock(int cap), parkBike(), and takeBike().

Step 1: Dock d(12) runs the constructor. It stores capacity = 12 and bikes = 0, so the invariant is true from the start.
Step 2: Riders call d.parkBike() three times. Each call checks that bikes is below 12 before adding one, so bikes becomes 3 and the invariant still holds.
Step 3: Riders call d.takeBike() three times, and bikes drops to 0.
Step 4 (missing): A rider calls d.takeBike() again while bikes is 0. What should takeBike do so the invariant stays true?
choices: Make bikes a public member so the calling code can check and repair the value itself
Reset capacity to 0 so that the negative count no longer looks out of range
Subtract one anyway so bikes becomes -1, and let the next parkBike() call bring it back to 0
Refuse the request, for example by throwing an exception, and leave bikes at 0
questions.why: Each public function must keep the invariant true, so takeBike has to reject a request that would make bikes negative instead of storing an invalid value.

questions.prompt: A teammate says, "Our Queue is an abstract data type." Which description best matches what makes something an abstract data type?
choices: It is any class that has at least one private data member
It is a type that cannot be used to create objects
It is defined by its operations and the rules they follow, not by how its data is stored
It is defined by the exact memory layout of its data members
questions.why: An ADT is defined by its interface (its operations and their rules), while the storage is a separate implementation detail.

questions.prompt: A weather app has a SensorLog class with private data and public functions record(double reading) and average(). The developers later switch the private storage from one container type to another, and record() and average() still behave exactly the same. What happens to the outside code that uses SensorLog?
choices: Only outside code that calls average() needs to change
Outside code keeps working unchanged because it only uses the public interface
Outside code must now access the new container directly to read values
All outside code must be rewritten because the storage changed
questions.why: Because the data is private, callers depend only on the interface, so the implementation can change freely as long as the interface behaves the same.

questions.prompt: A drawing program has a Rectangle class meant to keep the rule "width and height are always positive," but width and height are declared public. One module sets r.width = -5. Hours later, a different module that computes layouts crashes. What is the root problem?
choices: The layout module should have used a constructor instead of a member function
Public data members let outside code break the invariant, so the bad value caused a failure far from where it was set
The class should have had more public functions so callers could set width directly
Invariants only need to be true when the object is first created, so the crash is unrelated
questions.why: Making data public lets any caller violate the invariant, and the bad value can cause a crash or wrong result far from the mistake, which makes it hard to trace.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate why we implement an ADT as a C++ class with private data and public operations instead of a plain struct with public fields. Name one tradeoff or limit of this approach.
lessons.modelAnswer: An ADT says what a type can do, through its operations and their rules, and keeps quiet about how the data is stored. A C++ class lets us enforce that split. The data members are private, so only the class's own functions can change them. The public member functions are the only way in. Because of that, the constructor can establish an invariant, such as a Fraction's denominator never being zero, and every operation can keep it true. Callers can never create a broken object. We can also swap the internal storage later without touching any caller, as long as the interface behaves the same. The tradeoff is extra up-front work. You have to design and write the operations, and you may add small checking costs. Hiding the data also means callers can only do what the interface allows, so a badly designed interface makes the type awkward to use.
rubricPoints: Defines an ADT as a type described by its operations and rules, separate from its storage.
Explains that private data with public member functions is encapsulation.
Mentions invariants set up by the constructor and kept true by each operation.
Notes that the implementation can change without breaking callers.
Names a real tradeoff, such as extra design effort, checking cost, or a limiting interface.

suggested.rationale: No current mission or planned engine has the learner write C++ classes, and the core skill here is clearly explaining the split between interface and implementation and why invariants need private data.

lessons.plain: Information system security is about keeping computer systems and the data in them trustworthy. Most of the field rests on three goals: only the right people can see the data (confidentiality), the data is correct and has not been tampered with (integrity), and the system works when people need it (availability). Think of a bank vault. Confidentiality is that strangers cannot look inside. Integrity is that nobody can quietly swap the gold for painted lead. Availability is that the owner can still open it during business hours. A few more principles guide how you protect those three goals, such as giving people only the access they need.
lessons.guessPrompt: Someone breaks into a school's grade database and changes several grades, but they do not copy or publish anyone's records. Has security been broken, and if so, which goal was harmed?
lessons.teach:
Information system security means protecting data and the systems that handle it. The core model is the CIA triad. Confidentiality means information is seen only by those authorized to see it. Integrity means information stays accurate and is changed only by authorized people in authorized ways. Availability means the system and its data are usable when legitimately needed. A breach of any one of these is a security failure, even if the other two are fine.

Three supporting terms explain why protection is needed. A vulnerability is a weakness, such as an unpatched program or a weak password. A threat is anything that could exploit a weakness, such as an attacker, a careless employee, or a flood. Risk is the likelihood that a threat exploits a vulnerability, combined with how much damage would result. Security work is mostly about reducing risk to an acceptable level, because no system is perfectly safe.

Two design principles guide that work. Least privilege means each person or program gets only the access its job requires, so a mistake or compromise does limited damage. Defense in depth means stacking several independent protections, so one failing layer does not expose everything.

Worked example: a company keeps a payroll file. Step one, an intern can read it though they do not need it; that breaks least privilege and puts confidentiality at risk. Step two, a script bug overwrites salaries with zeros; integrity is harmed even though nobody outside saw anything. Step three, the server crashes on payday; availability is harmed. Three different events hit three different goals.

A common mistake is treating security as only keeping secrets. Teams that focus only on confidentiality often skip backups and change tracking. In a running system, that means a ransomware attack or a corrupted database can stop the business entirely, even when no data was leaked. Good security weighs all three goals together.

questions.prompt: A town library runs an online catalog where staff log in to manage book loans. A security analyst works through it. Step 1 (vulnerability): the staff login page allows unlimited password guesses, which is a weakness. Step 2 (threat): an outside attacker could run an automated tool that tries thousands of passwords, and that attacker could exploit the weakness. Step 3 (risk): ??? Step 4 (response): the library adds a lockout after 5 failed guesses and also requires a code sent to each staff member's phone. It accepts that some small risk remains, because no system is perfectly safe. Which statement correctly completes Step 3?
choices: Guessing tools are cheap and common, so the chance of an attack is high, and a captured staff account could alter loan records, so the damage would be real. Together these make the risk high.
The risk will be zero once the lockout is added, so the second protection in Step 4 is unnecessary.
The risk is the unlimited-guess login page itself, because that is the part of the system that could be attacked.
The risk is the outside attacker, because the attacker is the one who would cause the harm.
questions.why: Risk combines how likely it is that a threat exploits a vulnerability with how much damage would result, and only this choice weighs both of those.

questions.prompt: A fitness gym's class-booking website is flooded with junk traffic for two hours, and members cannot reserve classes. No member data is viewed, copied, or changed. Which security goal was harmed?
choices: Confidentiality
Availability
None of them, because no data was leaked or altered
Integrity
questions.why: Availability means the system is usable when it is legitimately needed, and the members could not use the site, so availability failed even though the other two goals held.

questions.prompt: A bakery chain installs a reporting program whose only job is to read daily sales totals and produce a chart. Which access setting follows the principle of least privilege?
choices: Full administrator access, so the program never runs into permission errors
Read and write access to all company files, in case the reports expand later
The same access as the finance manager who requested the report
Read-only access to the sales totals and nothing else
questions.why: Least privilege gives a program only the access its job requires, so read-only access to the sales totals limits the damage if the program has a bug or is compromised.

questions.prompt: A small dental clinic strongly encrypts every patient file so that outsiders cannot read them. However, it keeps no backups and does not track changes. A disk failure then corrupts the appointment database, and the clinic cannot operate for a week. Nothing was leaked. Which statement best describes this?
choices: It was only a hardware problem, and hardware problems fall outside information security
It shows that encryption was the wrong choice and should be removed
It was a security failure, because integrity and availability were harmed, and the clinic focused only on keeping secrets
It was not a security failure, because confidentiality was fully protected
questions.why: A breach of any one goal of the CIA triad counts as a security failure, and treating security as only confidentiality led the clinic to skip backups and change tracking.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what the CIA triad is and how least privilege and defense in depth support it, and name one tradeoff or limit of applying these principles.
lessons.modelAnswer: Security has three goals, called the CIA triad. Confidentiality means only authorized people see data. Integrity means data stays accurate and is changed only in approved ways. Availability means the system works when it is needed. Losing any one is a security failure; a corrupted database or a crashed server counts just as much as a leak. We reduce risk, meaning the chance a threat exploits a vulnerability times the damage, rather than eliminating it. Least privilege gives each user or program only the access it needs, so one compromise does limited harm. Defense in depth layers independent protections so one failure does not expose everything. The tradeoff is that the goals can pull against each other: tighter access and more layers protect confidentiality but add friction and can hurt availability if legitimate users get blocked. No setup makes risk zero, so we aim for acceptable risk.
rubricPoints: Defines confidentiality, integrity and availability correctly.
States that harming any one goal is a security failure.
Explains risk as a threat exploiting a vulnerability, weighted by impact.
Describes least privilege as granting only the access a job needs.
Describes defense in depth as layering independent protections.
Names a real tradeoff, such as stricter controls reducing usability or availability, or risk never reaching zero.

suggested.rationale: These are foundational concepts, and the core skill is being able to classify situations by which goal and principle they involve and explain that clearly.

lessons.plain: A security policy is an organization's written statement of what must be protected, who is responsible, and what behavior is required or forbidden. It sets the rules; other documents explain how to follow them. Developing a policy means deciding those rules with the people affected and getting leadership to approve them. Applying it means turning the rules into daily practice, checking that people follow them, and updating them when things change. Think of house rules for a shared apartment: everyone agrees that the door stays locked and guests sign in, someone checks, and the rules change when a new roommate moves in.
lessons.guessPrompt: If a company's policy says 'all laptops must be encrypted' but never says who checks or what happens if one is not, what do you think will happen over a year?
lessons.teach:
A security policy is a high-level, management-approved document stating an organization's security goals, scope (which people, systems and data it covers), responsibilities, and consequences for violations. It is deliberately short and stable. Beneath it sit supporting documents. A standard is a mandatory, specific requirement, such as 'passwords must be at least 14 characters.' A procedure is step-by-step instructions for doing a task, such as how to reset a password. A guideline is recommended but optional advice.

This layering works because the policy changes rarely and needs top-level approval, while standards and procedures can be updated as technology changes without rewriting the whole policy.

Development follows a lifecycle: assess risks to learn what needs protection, draft with input from stakeholders (the people affected, such as IT, legal, HR and staff), get approval from leadership, publish and train people, enforce and monitor, then review on a schedule (often yearly) or after an incident.

Worked example: a small clinic worries about lost laptops exposing patient records. Step one, the risk assessment finds unencrypted laptops leave the building daily. Step two, a draft remote-device policy states that all portable devices holding patient data must protect that data, with IT responsible for enforcement. Step three, the clinic director signs it. Step four, a standard requires full-disk encryption, a procedure shows staff how to enable it, and training is held. Step five, IT runs a monthly check and finds two unencrypted laptops, which are fixed. Step six, a year later the policy is reviewed when the clinic adds tablets.

A common mistake is copying a policy template without fitting it to real risks, or writing rules nobody can follow or check. In a running organization, such a policy becomes shelf-ware: people ignore it, exceptions pile up undocumented, and when a breach happens the organization cannot show it took reasonable care, which can bring legal and regulatory penalties.

questions.prompt: A regional bakery chain with 12 stores is worried that cashiers share logins on its payment terminals. Step 1: a risk assessment finds that 9 of the 12 stores use one shared cashier login, so nobody can tell who made a refund. Step 2: a draft access policy, written with input from IT, HR and store staff, says every person using payment systems must have their own account and makes store managers responsible for this. Step 3: missing. Step 4: a standard requires a unique login per cashier and a lockout after 5 failed attempts, a procedure shows managers how to create accounts, and staff are trained. Step 5: a monthly audit finds 2 stores still sharing a login, and both are fixed. Step 6: the policy is reviewed when the chain adds online ordering. What belongs in Step 3?
choices: The chain's owner or senior leadership formally approves and signs the policy.
IT runs an audit of all 12 stores before anyone has been told about the new rules.
The 5-attempt lockout setting is moved into the policy itself so the policy is more specific.
The IT manager publishes the draft right away, because IT wrote most of it and understands the systems best.
questions.why: A security policy is a management-approved document, so after drafting it needs sign-off from top leadership before it is published, backed by standards and procedures, and enforced.

questions.prompt: An online retailer's security documents include this line: 'All office Wi-Fi networks must use WPA3 encryption.' WPA3 is a specific wireless encryption setting. Which type of document does this line belong in?
choices: A standard, because it is a mandatory and specific technical requirement.
A policy, because it uses the word 'must' and applies to the whole office.
A procedure, because it tells IT staff exactly how to configure the router.
A guideline, because Wi-Fi settings are advice that staff can choose to follow.
questions.why: A standard is a mandatory, specific requirement. It does not give step-by-step instructions, which would make it a procedure, and it is not optional, which would make it a guideline.

questions.prompt: A logistics company's leadership-approved policy says all remote access must be protected by strong authentication. A separate standard says remote logins need a password plus a code sent by text message. The company now wants to require codes from an authenticator app instead of text messages. What is the best approach?
choices: Leave the documents as they are and add an optional guideline that suggests using the authenticator app.
Rewrite the whole policy and send it back to leadership, because any security change requires a new policy.
Update the standard and leave the high-level policy unchanged, so it does not need new top-level approval.
Turn the policy into a step-by-step procedure so that future changes are easier to make.
questions.why: This is the reason for layering the documents: specific technical requirements sit in standards that can change with technology, while the short, stable policy stays the same.

questions.prompt: A 20-person software startup copies a security policy template from a large bank without changing it. The template refers to mainframe systems the startup does not have, and to rules nobody checks. Staff ignore the policy, and exceptions are never written down. Later, customer data is breached. What is the most likely outcome?
choices: Nothing changes, because security policies only matter to companies that hold a certification.
Responsibility passes to the bank, because the startup used the bank's policy template.
The startup is protected, because it had a written security policy in place when the breach happened.
The policy has become shelf-ware, and the startup may struggle to show it took reasonable care, which risks legal or regulatory penalties.
questions.why: A template that is not fitted to real risks, and contains rules nobody can follow or check, gets ignored. After a breach, the organization then cannot show reasonable care and may face penalties.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate the difference between a security policy and the standards and procedures under it, walk through how a policy gets developed and applied, and name one tradeoff or limit in making policies strict.
lessons.modelAnswer: A security policy is leadership's approved statement of what we protect, who is responsible, and what happens if rules are broken. It stays high level. Standards turn it into mandatory specifics, like encryption settings, and procedures give the step-by-step how-to. Guidelines are just recommendations. We build a policy by assessing risk, drafting with the affected groups like IT, legal and HR, getting management sign-off, then publishing and training people. Applying it means enforcing and monitoring compliance, handling exceptions on record, and reviewing it yearly or after incidents. The tradeoff is that a stricter policy reduces risk but costs usability and effort; if rules are too hard to follow, people find workarounds and the policy stops being followed at all. A policy is also only as good as its enforcement, since unchecked rules give false confidence.
rubricPoints: Defines a security policy as a high-level, management-approved statement of goals, scope, responsibilities and consequences.
Distinguishes policy from standards (mandatory specifics), procedures (steps) and guidelines (optional advice).
Describes the lifecycle: risk assessment, stakeholder drafting, approval, publication and training, enforcement and monitoring, review.
Notes that application requires enforcement, monitoring and documented exceptions.
Names a tradeoff such as strictness versus usability or the risk of unenforced shelf-ware policies.

suggested.rationale: Policy work is mainly judgment, so reasoning through an exam-style scenario about drafting and enforcing a policy for a specific organization builds the skill best.

lessons.plain: A security mechanism is the actual tool or technique that enforces a protection, as opposed to the rule that says what should be protected. If a rule says only accountants may open payroll files, the mechanisms are the login prompt that checks who you are, the permission list that says who may open each file, the scrambling of the file's contents so stolen copies are useless, and the record of who opened what. Think of a building: the rule is that only staff may enter after hours, while the mechanisms are the badge reader, the locked doors, the safe, and the security camera.
lessons.guessPrompt: Suppose a company's rule is that only the finance team may read the payroll spreadsheet. List three different things a computer system could do to make that rule actually hold, even if someone tries to break it.
lessons.teach:
A security mechanism is a concrete technical means of enforcing a protection. A security policy is the statement of what must be protected and from whom; the mechanism is how the system carries it out. Four families of mechanism cover most cases.

Authentication is proving identity, for example with a password plus a one-time code from a phone (using two different kinds of proof is called multi-factor authentication). Authorization is deciding what an identified user may do, often using an access control list (ACL), which is a list attached to a resource naming who may read, write, or run it. Encryption is transforming data with a secret value called a key so that only key holders can read it; it protects data stored on disk and data moving across a network. Auditing is keeping an audit log, a tamper-resistant record of who did what and when, so misuse can be detected and investigated.

These work because each closes a different gap: authentication stops strangers, authorization limits insiders, encryption protects data when the other controls are bypassed (a stolen laptop, a tapped network), and auditing catches what slipped through.

Worked example: Alice requests payroll.csv. Step one, the system authenticates her with password and code; both match, so she is identified as alice. Step two, it checks the file's ACL: the finance group may read, and alice is in finance, so access is allowed. Step three, the file is decrypted with a key the server holds, because it is stored encrypted on disk. Step four, an audit log entry records that alice read payroll.csv at 10:42. If Bob from sales tried, step one would succeed but step two would deny him, and the denial would be logged.

A common mistake is treating authentication as if it were authorization: assuming that once someone has logged in, they may see everything. In a running system this means any valid account, including a phished intern's, can read every file, and one stolen password becomes a full data breach. Strong protection comes from layering the mechanisms so that each one enforces part of the policy.

questions.prompt:
A dental clinic stores patient X-rays on a server. Logins need a password plus a phone code, each folder has an access control list (ACL, a list on a resource naming who may read, write, or run it), the disks are encrypted with a key held by the server, and an audit log records every file read. One night a thief steals a backup drive and plugs it into his own computer. Trace what protects the X-rays.

Step 1: The thief never logs in to the clinic's system, so authentication is never involved.
Step 2: He reads the drive directly on his own machine, so the clinic's ACLs are never checked.
Step 3: ???
Step 4: Because the theft happened outside the clinic's system, the audit log holds no record of it, so the clinic has to notice the loss another way, such as a missing-equipment check.

Which statement correctly fills Step 3?
choices: The X-rays are stored encrypted and he lacks the key held by the clinic's server, so the files are unreadable.
Multi-factor authentication asks him for a phone code before the files open, so the X-rays stay protected.
The ACL is copied onto the drive with the files, so his computer must still refuse to open the X-rays.
The audit log on the drive records his attempt to read the files and blocks the read before it completes.
questions.why: Encryption protects data even when the other controls are bypassed, because without the key the stolen data cannot be read.

questions.prompt: A city water utility writes: "Only billing staff may view customer bank details." The IT team then sets up an access control list on the billing database that grants read access to the billing group only. Which statement correctly describes these two things?
choices: The access control list is the security policy, and the written rule is the mechanism that carries it out.
Both are security policies, because neither one encrypts the bank details on disk.
Both are security mechanisms, because each one limits who can see the bank details.
The written rule is the security policy, and the access control list is the mechanism that enforces it.
questions.why: A policy states what must be protected and from whom, and a mechanism is the concrete technical means that enforces it, here the ACL.

questions.prompt: At a logistics company, a warehouse clerk signs in with a valid password and phone code, then finds that he can open every executive salary file on the shared drive. Which mechanism is missing or misconfigured?
choices: Authentication, because his password and phone code should have been rejected.
Auditing, because a tamper-resistant log should have stopped him from opening the files.
Authorization, because nothing restricts what an identified user is allowed to access.
Encryption, because the salary files should be unreadable to anyone who has logged in.
questions.why: Proving identity (authentication) worked correctly; the problem is that no authorization control, such as an ACL, limits what that identified user may do.

questions.prompt: A university finds that 300 student grade records were changed overnight. Every account involved logged in correctly and had permission to edit grades. Which mechanism gives investigators the best way to find out who made the changes and when?
choices: Encryption, because only key holders could have changed the grade records.
Multi-factor authentication, because it records the phone code used for each edit.
An audit log, because it keeps a tamper-resistant record of who did what and when.
An access control list, because it lists every edit made to each grade record.
questions.why: Auditing exists to catch what slipped through the other controls by recording actions so misuse can be detected and investigated.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate the difference between authentication, authorization, encryption, and auditing as mechanisms, using one example request, and name a limit of relying on any single one of them.
lessons.modelAnswer: A policy says what should be protected; mechanisms are how the system enforces it. Take a user opening the payroll file. Authentication checks who they are, say with a password and a phone code. Authorization then checks the file's access control list to decide whether that identity may read it. Encryption keeps the file's contents scrambled with a key, so a stolen disk or intercepted network copy is unreadable. Auditing writes a log entry of who accessed it and when, so misuse can be spotted later.
