The general solution is X(t) = c1 e^(3t)(1, 1) + c2 e^(-t)(1, -1), which means x = c1 e^(3t) + c2 e^(-t) and y = c1 e^(3t) - c2 e^(-t). Because the eigenvalue 3 is positive, the deviations grow without bound unless c1 = 0, so in general they do not die out.

scenarios.title: Late and Damaged Parcels at Brightline Parcel Co.
scenarios.scenario:
You have just joined Brightline Parcel Co., a fictional regional delivery company, as a junior analyst. Your manager wants a short probability write-up on last quarter's deliveries. A few terms first. An event is a set of possible outcomes, such as "this package arrived late." The union of two events, written A ∪ B, means "A happens, or B happens, or both." The intersection, written A ∩ B, means "both A and B happen." The complement of A, written A^c, means "A does not happen."

Pick one package at random. Let A be the event that it arrived damaged and B the event that it arrived late. The records show P(A) = 0.10, P(B) = 0.20, and P(A ∩ B) = 0.05.

A random variable is a number whose value depends on chance. Let X be the number of customer complaints in one day. X is discrete, meaning it takes separate countable values. The records show P(X = 0) = 0.5, P(X = 1) = 0.3, and P(X = 2) = 0.2. Each complaint costs the company $40 in refunds. The expected value of X, written E[X], is the long-run average: multiply each possible value by its probability, then add the results.

Let T be the delivery time in minutes on one local route. T is continuous, meaning it can take any value in a range. It follows a uniform distribution from 20 to 50 minutes. Uniform means every equal-length stretch of time inside that range is equally likely. The density, which is the height of the probability curve, is constant at 1/(50 − 20) = 1/30. For a continuous variable, the probability of landing in an interval equals the area under the density over that interval.

1. Using set notation, find the probability that a package is damaged or late, P(A ∪ B). Then find the probability that a package is neither damaged nor late.
2. A coworker's draft report instead lists P(A) = 0.10, P(B) = 0.20, and P(A ∩ B) = 0.15. Explain, using the properties of probability, why these numbers cannot all be correct.
3. Find E[X], the expected number of complaints per day, and the expected daily refund cost. Also confirm that the distribution of X is valid.
4. For the delivery time T, find P(T > 40) and E[T]. Then explain what P(T = 40), the probability of exactly 40 minutes, equals, and why.
subParts: Union and complement with set notation
Expected value of a discrete distribution
modelAnswer: Use the addition rule: P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A ∩ B) = 0.10 + 0.20 − 0.05 = 0.25. The intersection is subtracted because packages that are both damaged and late were counted once inside P(A) and again inside P(B). "Neither damaged nor late" is the complement of A ∪ B, so P((A ∪ B)^c) = 1 − 0.25 = 0.75. A common mistake is to simply add 0.10 + 0.20 = 0.30, which double-counts the overlap.

The event A ∩ B (damaged and late) is contained inside A (damaged), because every package that is both damaged and late is also damaged. A key property of probability is that if one event sits inside another, its probability cannot be larger. So P(A ∩ B) must be at most P(A) = 0.10, but the draft gives 0.15. That breaks the rule. You can also see the problem with the addition rule: it would give P(A ∪ B) = 0.10 + 0.20 − 0.15 = 0.15, which is smaller than P(B) = 0.20. That is impossible, because B is contained inside A ∪ B. The draft numbers must contain an error.

Validity check: every probability is between 0 and 1, and 0.5 + 0.3 + 0.2 = 1.0, so the distribution is valid. Expected value: E[X] = 0(0.5) + 1(0.3) + 2(0.2) = 0 + 0.3 + 0.4 = 0.7 complaints per day. Each complaint costs $40, so the expected daily cost is 40 × 0.7 = $28. This is a long-run average: no single day has exactly 0.7 complaints, but budgeting about $28 per day matches the company's average over many days.

P(T > 40) is the area under the density from 40 to 50, which is the width times the height: (50 − 40) × (1/30) = 10/30 = 1/3, or about 0.333. For a uniform distribution, the expected value is the midpoint of the range, so E[T] = (20 + 50)/2 = 35 minutes. P(T = 40) is 0. A single point has zero width, so the area above it is zero. For a continuous variable, only intervals have positive probability. A related consequence is that P(T ≥ 40) and P(T > 40) are both 1/3.

scenarios.title: Sustainable Harvest Planning at Clearbrook Fish Farms
scenarios.scenario:
Clearbrook Fish Farms is a fictional company that raises trout in a large managed lake. Management wants to take a fixed number of fish out every year without wiping out the stock, and they have asked you, a new junior analyst, to model it.

A mathematical model is a set of equations that stands in for a real situation so you can reason about it. Here you will use a differential equation, which describes how a quantity changes over time by giving its rate of change. Let P(t) be the number of fish at time t, measured in years, so dP/dt is the change in fish per year.

The biologists report three facts. First, when fish are scarce the population grows at about 50 percent per year. This is the intrinsic growth rate, r = 0.5 per year. Second, the lake can support at most about 10,000 fish because food and space run out. This ceiling is the carrying capacity, K = 10,000. Third, management plans to remove H = 800 fish per year at a steady rate. This is called constant harvesting.

A standard way to combine the first two facts is the logistic growth term, rP(1 - P/K). It acts like ordinary growth rP when P is small. The factor (1 - P/K) slows growth as P nears K and makes it zero at P = K. Harvesting is a steady loss, so it is subtracted.

To study behavior without solving the equation, you use two analytical tools. An equilibrium is a population value where dP/dt = 0, so the population stays put if it starts there. You find equilibria by setting the right-hand side, call it f(P), equal to zero and solving. An equilibrium is stable if nearby populations move back toward it. It is unstable if nearby populations move away from it. For a one-variable model, check the sign of the derivative f'(P) at the equilibrium. Negative means stable, and positive means unstable.

When you need numbers over time, you can use a simulation. One simple method is Euler's method. It steps forward with the rule P_next = P_now + h times f(P_now), where h is the step size. The idea is to assume the current rate holds for one short step. A common beginner mistake is to forget that every assumption built into a model, such as a constant growth rate or exactly 800 fish removed every year, may fail in the real lake. Results are only as trustworthy as those assumptions.

Your tasks:
1. Write the differential equation for P(t) using the values given.
2. Find both equilibrium populations and classify each as stable or unstable, showing the derivative test.
3. Starting from P(0) = 3,000 fish, use Euler's method with step size h = 1 year to estimate the population after 1 year and after 2 years.
4. Name two assumptions in this model that may not hold at the real lake, and explain what could go wrong for the farm if each one fails.
modelAnswer: The model is dP/dt = 0.5P(1 - P/10000) - 800. The first term is logistic growth, with intrinsic growth rate r = 0.5 per year and carrying capacity K = 10,000 fish. The constant 800 is the steady harvest in fish per year, and it is subtracted because it removes fish. Full credit needs the correct structure: growth term minus harvest, with the given values.

Set f(P) = 0.5P - 0.00005P^2 - 800 = 0. Multiply by -20,000 to get P^2 - 10000P + 16,000,000 = 0. The quadratic formula gives P = (10000 ± sqrt(100,000,000 - 64,000,000)) / 2 = (10000 ± 6000) / 2. So the equilibria are P = 2,000 and P = 8,000. The derivative is f'(P) = 0.5 - P/10000. At P = 2,000, f'(2000) = 0.3, which is positive, so 2,000 is unstable. At P = 8,000, f'(8000) = -0.3, which is negative, so 8,000 is stable. In practical terms, populations above 2,000 drift toward 8,000. Populations below 2,000 shrink toward collapse under this harvest.

Step 1: f(3000) = 0.5 × 3000 × (1 - 0.3) - 800 = 1050 - 800 = 250. So P(1) ≈ 3000 + 1 × 250 = 3,250 fish. Step 2: f(3250) = 0.5 × 3250 × (1 - 0.325) - 800 = 1625 × 0.675 - 800 = 1096.875 - 800 = 296.875. So P(2) ≈ 3250 + 296.875 ≈ 3,547 fish. The population is rising, which is consistent with starting above the unstable equilibrium of 2,000 and heading toward 8,000. Accept small rounding differences.

Any two well-reasoned assumptions earn credit. One assumption is a fixed growth rate r = 0.5. A disease, cold year or pollution could lower the real rate. With a lower rate, the unstable threshold rises and the stable level falls, and the same 800-fish harvest could push the stock into collapse. A second assumption is a fixed carrying capacity K = 10,000. If food supply drops, K shrinks, and the safe margin above the collapse threshold shrinks with it. A third assumption is that exactly 800 fish are removed smoothly every year. Real harvests are uneven and estimates of fish counts are uncertain. Overharvesting in a bad year could drop P below 2,000, after which the population keeps declining even if harvest returns to normal. A fourth assumption is that the model ignores randomness, age structure and fish entering or leaving the lake. The model's precise numbers therefore give false confidence. The consequence for the farm is that a plan that looks safe on paper could lead to loss of the stock, so the farm should monitor the actual population and keep a safety margin.

scenarios.title: Forecasting Flour Orders at Brightwell Bakery Supply
scenarios.scenario:
You have just joined Brightwell Bakery Supply, a fictional wholesaler that sells 25 kg bags of flour to local bakeries, as a junior data analyst. Your manager, Dana, wants to understand what drives weekly sales and to plan next week's stock.

A colleague has already fit some models on 52 weeks of data. A regression model is an equation that predicts one quantity, called the response variable, from one or more other quantities, called predictors. Here the response is weekly flour sales in bags. Each fitted equation has an intercept, which is the predicted response when every predictor is zero, and one slope (also called a coefficient) per predictor, which is the predicted change in the response for a one-unit increase in that predictor.

Model A is a simple linear regression, meaning a straight-line model with one predictor. It uses ad spend in hundreds of dollars: Sales = 120 + 4.5 × AdSpend. Its R-squared is 0.62. R-squared is the share of the variation in sales that the model explains, from 0 to 1.

Model B is a multiple linear regression, meaning a linear model with two or more predictors. It adds the average weekly temperature in degrees Celsius: Sales = 95 + 3.8 × AdSpend + 1.2 × Temperature. Its R-squared is 0.71 and its adjusted R-squared is 0.69. Adjusted R-squared is a version of R-squared that is reduced a little for each extra predictor, so a new predictor only raises it if it genuinely helps.

Your colleague also plotted the residuals of Model B. A residual is the actual sales value minus the model's predicted value for that week. In a plot of residuals against predicted sales, the points sit tightly around zero for low predictions and spread out more and more as predictions grow, like a funnel opening to the right.

Finally, actual sales for the last four weeks were 150, 162, 158 and 170 bags (weeks 1 to 4). The previous exponential smoothing forecast for week 4 was 160 bags.

1. Using Model A, explain in plain words what the slope of 4.5 means, and predict sales for a week with $1,000 of ad spend.
2. Using Model B, predict sales for a week with $1,000 of ad spend and an average temperature of 15 °C. Explain why the ad-spend slope changed from 4.5 to 3.8, and say whether adding temperature was worthwhile based on the figures given.
3. Name the regression assumption the funnel-shaped residual plot suggests is broken, and explain what that means for the model's use in the business.
4. Forecast week 5 sales two ways: a 3-week moving average, and simple exponential smoothing with smoothing constant alpha = 0.3.
subParts: Interpret the simple regression and predict
Two time series forecasts for week 5
modelAnswer: The slope of 4.5 means that each extra $100 of ad spend (one unit of AdSpend) goes with about 4.5 more bags sold per week on average, according to this straight-line model. It describes an association in past data and does not by itself prove that ads cause the sales. $1,000 is 10 units of AdSpend, so the predicted sales are 120 + 4.5 × 10 = 120 + 45 = 165 bags.

Prediction: 95 + 3.8 × 10 + 1.2 × 15 = 95 + 38 + 18 = 151 bags. In a multiple regression, each slope is the effect of that predictor while the other predictors are held fixed. In Model A, the ad-spend slope also picked up part of the temperature effect, for example if ads tended to run in warmer weeks. Once temperature is in the model, that share moves to the temperature slope, so the ad-spend slope falls to 3.8. Adding temperature looks worthwhile. R-squared rose from 0.62 to 0.71, and adjusted R-squared is still high at 0.69. Adjusted R-squared penalises extra predictors, so this means temperature added real explanatory power and was not just noise. Model A's adjusted R-squared is not given, but it can be no higher than its 0.62 R-squared, so 0.69 is a clear improvement.

The funnel shape suggests the constant-variance assumption is broken. This assumption, called homoscedasticity, says the spread of the residuals should be about the same at every level of the predicted value. When the spread instead grows with the prediction, it is called heteroscedasticity. Here, predictions for big weeks are much less reliable than predictions for small weeks. Standard errors, confidence intervals and p-values computed in the usual way can then be misleading, and a single plus-or-minus margin quoted for every week would be too wide for quiet weeks and too narrow for busy ones. In business terms, Brightwell could understock in busy weeks. A common fix is to transform the response, for example by modelling the logarithm of sales, or to use methods that allow the variance to change. The model should then be rechecked with a new residual plot.

3-week moving average: the forecast is the mean of the three most recent weeks, (162 + 158 + 170) / 3 = 490 / 3 ≈ 163.3 bags. Simple exponential smoothing: the new forecast equals the old forecast plus alpha times the old forecast's error, F5 = F4 + alpha × (A4 − F4) = 160 + 0.3 × (170 − 160) = 160 + 3 = 163 bags. Equivalently, 0.3 × 170 + 0.7 × 160 = 51 + 112 = 163. Both methods suggest about 163 bags for week 5.

scenarios.title: Brightwater Cold Storage: How Long Can the Freezer Door Stay Open?
scenarios.scenario:
You have just joined Brightwater Cold Storage, a fictional company that runs refrigerated warehouses for grocery suppliers. Your manager asks you to run a small end-to-end project, the kind of independent project a computational math capstone asks for. A capstone project means you pick a real problem, build a mathematical model, solve it with a computer method, check it against real data, and then explain the results in writing and out loud. This exercise is practice only and does not count as course credit or work experience.

The problem: when a loading door is open, a chilled room warms up. Company policy says the room must stay at or below 8 degrees Celsius. Managers want to know how many minutes a door can stay open, starting from a room at 2 degrees, on a 20 degree day.

The model. A differential equation is an equation that describes how fast a quantity changes, rather than giving the quantity directly. Newton's law of cooling is a simple differential equation. It says an object's temperature changes at a rate proportional to the gap between its temperature and the surrounding temperature. Written out, dT/dt = k(T_out - T). Here T is room temperature in degrees Celsius, t is time in minutes, T_out is the outside temperature (20), and k is a rate constant. A rate constant is a number that sets how quickly the gap closes. From past sensor logs, k is about 0.1 per minute. This equation has an exact solution, a formula you can check by hand: T(t) = 20 - 18e^(-0.1t).

The computer method. Euler's method is the simplest way to solve a differential equation step by step on a computer. You start from a known value and repeatedly apply new value = old value + h times (rate at the old value). The step size, h, is the length of time you jump forward in each step. Smaller steps are slower to compute but usually more accurate. Here is why the method works: over a short time the rate barely changes, so treating it as constant for one step gives a good estimate.

A common mistake is choosing a step size that is too large. For this equation, if k times h gets near or above 1, Euler's method overshoots. The computed temperature can leap past the outside temperature, which is physically impossible. If a bad result like that reached a dashboard, managers could make the wrong call on door times and risk spoiled food.

Validation means comparing a model's output to real measurements to see whether the model can be trusted. Error is the difference between the model's value and the measured value. A sensor test recorded 5.2 degrees after the door had been open for 2 minutes.

Finally, a written and oral presentation for a non-technical audience should lead with the answer and the recommendation. It should then explain the method briefly in plain words, show the evidence that the model is trustworthy, and state its limits honestly.

Your tasks:
1. Write a one-paragraph project statement. It should name the problem, the model, the computational technique, and a measurable success criterion.
2. Trace two Euler steps with h = 1 minute, starting from T = 2 at t = 0, and give T at t = 2. Then explain what goes wrong with h = 25 minutes by computing the first step.
3. Validate the model. Compare the Euler value and the exact-formula value at t = 2 with the 5.2 degree measurement. Then use the exact formula to find how many minutes it takes to reach 8 degrees.
4. Outline, in order, what your short talk to warehouse managers should contain. Include one limitation you must state.
modelAnswer: The project should say something like this: Brightwater needs to know how long a loading door can stay open before a chilled room starting at 2 degrees Celsius rises above the 8 degree policy limit on a 20 degree day. I will model room temperature with Newton's law of cooling, dT/dt = k(T_out - T), with k about 0.1 per minute taken from sensor logs. I will solve it numerically with Euler's method and check that result against the exact formula. Success means the model's predictions stay within about 0.5 degrees of measured sensor readings, and it produces a clear maximum door-open time that managers can use. A strong answer names all four parts: the problem, the model, the technique, and a measurable criterion.

Step 1: the rate at T = 2 is 0.1 x (20 - 2) = 1.8, so T at t = 1 is 2 + 1 x 1.8 = 3.8. Step 2: the rate at T = 3.8 is 0.1 x (20 - 3.8) = 1.62, so T at t = 2 is 3.8 + 1.62 = 5.42 degrees. With h = 25, the first step gives T = 2 + 25 x 0.1 x 18 = 2 + 45 = 47 degrees. That is far above the 20 degree outside air, which is physically impossible. It happens because k times h = 2.5, which is well above 1, so the method overshoots and becomes unreliable. The fix is a step small enough that k times h stays well below 1. Otherwise the dashboard could show nonsense and drive bad door-time decisions.

At t = 2, the exact formula gives T = 20 - 18e^(-0.2), which is about 20 - 18 x 0.819 = 5.26 degrees. Euler with h = 1 gives 5.42. Measured against the 5.2 degree reading, the error is about 0.22 degrees for Euler and about 0.06 degrees for the exact formula. Both are within the 0.5 degree criterion, so the model is supported. Time to reach 8 degrees: set 20 - 18e^(-0.1t) = 8. That gives e^(-0.1t) = 12/18, which is about 0.667. Taking logs, t = -10 x ln(0.667), which is about 10 x 0.405, or about 4.1 minutes. A sensible recommendation adds a safety margin, for example a limit of about 3 to 3.5 minutes.

The talk should go in this order. First, the answer and recommendation: on a 20 degree day the room reaches 8 degrees in about 4 minutes, so keep doors open no more than about 3 to 3.5 minutes. Second, the method in plain words: the room warms faster the bigger the gap from outside air, and the computer adds up small time steps to track the temperature. Third, the evidence: predictions at 2 minutes were within about 0.2 degrees of the sensor reading. Fourth, limitations and next steps: k was estimated from limited data and assumes a constant 20 degree outside temperature. It also ignores the cooling unit running and people or pallets moving through the door. On hotter days the safe time is shorter, so more sensor tests are needed. The talk should finish by inviting questions. Stating at least one honest limitation like these is required.

scenarios.title: Hollowbrook Supply: Fixing the Order Process Before Expanding
scenarios.scenario:
Hollowbrook Supply is a fictional company that sells flour, sugar, and packaging to about 60 local bakeries. The owner, Dana, wants to open in a second city next year, and she wants to cut order mistakes in half before then. Her office has only two staff members, and her budget is tight. She has asked you, the new junior IT analyst, to recommend a technology solution.

First, some terms. A business process is a repeatable set of steps a company follows to get a result, such as turning a customer's request into a delivered, billed order. Business process management (BPM) is the practice of writing down how a process works today, called the as-is process, finding its weak points, designing a better version, called the to-be process, and then checking whether the change actually helped. A bottleneck is a step that slows the whole process because work piles up there. Technology adds the most value where it removes repeated manual work, cuts errors, or clears a bottleneck. A common mistake is to automate a broken process exactly as it is. You just get the same mistakes, faster.

Here is Hollowbrook's as-is order process. Step 1: a customer phones or emails an order, and a sales rep writes it on a paper form, which takes about 5 minutes. Step 2: the rep retypes the paper form into a spreadsheet, which takes about 10 minutes. About 1 in 12 orders gets a typing error at this step. Step 3: the warehouse prints the spreadsheet only once a day, at 3 pm, and then picks the orders. Step 4: a billing clerk retypes the same order into an invoice, which takes about 8 minutes.

IT strategy alignment means choosing technology because it moves the organization toward its stated goals, not because it is new or impressive. Dana's goals are fewer errors, room to grow into a second city, and a limited budget. To compare options fairly, analysts often use a weighted scoring matrix. You list criteria and give each one a weight, meaning its share of importance, with all weights adding to 100%. You score each option from 1 (poor) to 5 (excellent) on each criterion. Then you multiply each score by its weight and add the results. One criterion is cost over three years, sometimes called total cost of ownership. This is the full cost of a solution over its life, including setup, subscriptions or licences, training, and upkeep, not just the purchase price.

Dana's weights are: fit to goals 40%, three-year cost 30%, ease of use 20%, and scalability 10%. Scalability means how well the solution keeps working as the business grows. There are three options. Option A is a custom ordering app built by a contractor. Its scores are fit 5, cost 1, ease 3, scalability 5. Option B is a subscription cloud order-management service, meaning software rented over the internet. It gives customers an online order form that sends each order straight to the warehouse and to invoicing. Its scores are fit 4, cost 4, ease 4, scalability 4. Option C is a better shared spreadsheet template. Its scores are fit 2, cost 5, ease 4, scalability 1.

Here is a worked example for Option C. Fit is 2 x 0.40 = 0.8. Cost is 5 x 0.30 = 1.5. Ease is 4 x 0.20 = 0.8. Scalability is 1 x 0.10 = 0.1. The total is 0.8 + 1.5 + 0.8 + 0.1 = 3.2. Notice that the cheapest option does not automatically win. Choosing on price alone is another common mistake.

Finally, technical writing for information systems documentation means writing instructions and records that a specific reader can follow without help. Good documentation states its purpose and its audience. It uses numbered steps that each begin with an action verb and contain one action. It uses the exact names of the screens and buttons the reader will see.

Your tasks:
1. Using the as-is process, name the two steps where technology would add the most value, and explain why for each.
2. Calculate the weighted scores for Options A and B, and rank all three options.
3. Recommend one option and explain how it aligns with Dana's three goals.
4. Write a short procedure, of 4 to 5 steps, telling sales reps how to enter a phone order into the new system. Include a one-line purpose and audience statement.
subParts: Write a short procedure for reps
modelAnswer: Step 2 is the first. Retyping the paper form into the spreadsheet is repeated manual work that takes 10 minutes per order, and it causes the 1-in-12 error rate. Having orders entered once, directly into a system, removes both the duplicate typing and the main source of errors. Step 3 is the second. The once-a-day 3 pm print is a bottleneck, because orders wait hours before the warehouse sees them. Sending orders to the warehouse as soon as they are entered clears that wait. Step 4 is also acceptable as a strong answer, since it is a second retyping of the same data. Its billing could be generated automatically from the entered order. A good answer ties each step to removing duplicate work, cutting errors, or clearing a bottleneck, and it does not simply suggest automating the paper form as it is.

Option A: 5 x 0.40 = 2.0, plus 1 x 0.30 = 0.3, plus 3 x 0.20 = 0.6, plus 5 x 0.10 = 0.5. The total is 3.4. Option B: 4 x 0.40 = 1.6, plus 4 x 0.30 = 1.2, plus 4 x 0.20 = 0.8, plus 4 x 0.10 = 0.4. The total is 4.0. Option C is 3.2, as given. The ranking is B first (4.0), A second (3.4), and C third (3.2).

Recommend Option B, the subscription cloud order-management service. For fewer errors, orders are entered once and flow straight to the warehouse and invoicing, which removes the two retyping steps where mistakes happen. For growth into a second city, it scored 4 on scalability: as rented online software, it can serve more customers and a second location without being rebuilt. Option C scored only 1 and would not keep up. For the tight budget, its three-year cost scored 4, far better than the custom app's 1, and its ease-of-use score of 4 suits a two-person office. A strong answer also notes that B had the highest weighted score, and that the cheapest option (C) and the best-fit-but-costly option (A) were each weaker overall.

Purpose: This procedure explains how to enter a customer's phone order into the order system so it reaches the warehouse and billing without retyping. Audience: Hollowbrook sales reps. Step 1: Open the order system and select New Order. Step 2: Search for the customer by business name and select the matching account. Step 3: Add each product and its quantity as the customer reads it out. Step 4: Read the full order back to the customer to confirm it. Step 5: Select Submit Order and tell the customer the order number shown on screen. A good answer states purpose and audience, uses numbered steps that each begin with an action verb, puts one action in each step, and does not include a step that copies the order onto paper.

scenarios.title: Bulk Order Checker at Tidewater Bakery Supply
scenarios.scenario:
You have just joined Tidewater Bakery Supply, a fictional wholesaler that sells flour and sugar to small bakeries, as a junior developer. Your lead hands you a short C++ console program, meaning a text-only program that reads from the keyboard and prints to the screen. It uses cin, the standard input stream that reads values typed by the user, and cout, the standard output stream that prints text. The program's job is to look at the bag quantities in a day's orders and report on the large ones.

Here is the main part of the code, written out in words and short pieces. It declares three whole-number variables (named storage spots in memory): int count = 0; int total = 0; int qty; Then it runs a loop, which is a block of code that repeats while a condition stays true: while (cin >> qty) { if (qty > 10) { total = total + qty; count++; } } The expression cin >> qty tries to read the next number into qty and counts as true only when a number was actually read, so the loop stops when the input runs out. Inside the loop is a conditional, an if statement that runs its block only when its test is true. The line count++ adds 1 to count. After the loop, the program runs cout << count << " " << total;

The program also calls a function, which is a named, reusable block of code that receives inputs called parameters and can send back one result called a return value. The function is: double averageQty(int total, int count) { return total / count; } Your lead says the average it prints "looks wrong sometimes" and that the program once crashed on a slow day with no large orders.

Finally, the team wants to start using object-oriented programming, a style where data and the actions on that data are bundled together. A class is the blueprint for that bundle, and an object is one actual item built from the blueprint. Members marked private can be used only by the class's own code; members marked public can be used by any code.

1. Trace the loop by hand for the typed input 4 12 10 25 (then the input ends). State the values of count and total after each number, and give the exact text the cout line prints.
2. Explain why averageQty gives a wrong answer for that same day, and why it can crash when count is 0. Write a corrected version of the function and explain each change.
3. Write a function named shippingFee that takes an order subtotal in dollars as a double and returns 0.0 when the subtotal is 100.00 or more, and 7.50 otherwise. Show what it returns for 99.99 and for 100.00.
4. Sketch a class named Order that stores a bag quantity and a price per bag as private data, has a constructor (a special function that runs when an object is created and sets its starting values), and has a public member function subtotal() that returns quantity times price. Explain why the data should be private.
modelAnswer: Start: count is 0 and total is 0. Read 4: the test 4 > 10 is false, so nothing changes; count 0, total 0. Read 12: 12 > 10 is true, so total becomes 0 + 12 = 12 and count becomes 1. Read 10: 10 > 10 is false, because greater-than does not include equal, so nothing changes; count 1, total 12. Read 25: 25 > 10 is true, so total becomes 12 + 25 = 37 and count becomes 2. The next read finds no number, cin >> qty becomes false, and the loop ends. The program prints 2 37 (the number 2, a space, then 37). A common mistake is counting the 10 as large; that would need qty >= 10, not qty > 10.

The wrong answer comes from integer division: when both sides of / are whole-number int values, C++ throws away the fractional part, so 37 / 2 gives 18 instead of 18.5. Returning it as a double does not help, because the fraction is already lost before the conversion happens. The crash comes from dividing a whole number by zero, which is not allowed and can stop the program on a day with no large orders. A corrected version: double averageQty(int total, int count) { if (count == 0) { return 0.0; } return static_cast<double>(total) / count; } The if statement checks for zero first and returns a safe value instead of dividing. Note it uses == (comparison), not = (assignment); writing count = 0 would set count to zero instead of testing it. static_cast<double>(total) converts total to a decimal type before dividing, so the division keeps the fraction and 37 and 2 give 18.5. Any equivalent fix, such as dividing by 2.0-style decimal conversion of either operand plus a zero check, earns full credit.

One correct version: double shippingFee(double subtotal) { if (subtotal >= 100.00) { return 0.0; } else { return 7.50; } } The parameter subtotal receives the value passed in, the if statement chooses a branch, and return sends the fee back to the caller. For 99.99 the test 99.99 >= 100.00 is false, so it returns 7.50. For 100.00 the test is true because >= includes equality, so it returns 0.0. A common mistake is writing > 100.00, which would wrongly charge 7.50 on an order of exactly 100.00. The caller could use it as cout << shippingFee(99.99); which prints 7.5.

One correct sketch: class Order { private: int quantity; double pricePerBag; public: Order(int q, double p) { quantity = q; pricePerBag = p; } double subtotal() { return quantity * pricePerBag; } }; Then an object is created and used like this: Order o(12, 18.50); cout << o.subtotal(); which prints 222 (12 times 18.50). The constructor has the same name as the class and no return type, and it runs once when the object o is created, giving the data its starting values. The data is private so that only the class's own code can change it; outside code cannot reach in and set quantity to something like -5 by accident. That keeps every Order object in a sensible state, and if a check is added later (for example, rejecting negative quantities in the constructor) it only has to be written in one place. A common mistake is forgetting the semicolon after the closing brace of the class, which causes a compile error. Answers that use a validation check in the constructor or separate getter functions are also acceptable.

scenarios.title: Fixing the Shipment Tracker at Driftwood Freight
scenarios.scenario:
You have just joined Driftwood Freight, a small fictional shipping company, as a junior developer. Your team keeps a C++ program that tracks packages in a warehouse. Your lead, Marisol, asks you to review four small pieces of it before tomorrow's release. She gives you a short refresher on each idea first.

Pointers. Every variable lives at a numbered spot in memory called its address. A pointer is a variable that stores an address instead of an ordinary value. In C++, writing &stock means the address of the variable stock. Writing int* p = &stock; makes p a pointer that holds that address. Writing *p is called dereferencing: it means go to the address stored in p and use the value there. So *p = 12; changes whatever variable p points to. A local variable is one created inside a function. It is destroyed when the function finishes. A pointer that still holds the address of a destroyed variable is called a dangling pointer. Using it reads or writes memory the program no longer owns. The result is unpredictable: wrong numbers or a crash.

Arrays and lists. An array is a fixed row of same-type values stored side by side in memory. Each value has a position number called an index, starting at 0. Because the values sit side by side, the program can jump straight to any index. But putting a new value at the front means shifting every existing value one place to the right. A linked list is a chain of separate pieces called nodes. Each node holds one value plus a pointer to the next node. The list keeps a pointer to its first node, called the head. To add at the front, you create one new node, point it at the old head, and make it the new head. No other node moves. The trade-off is reaching the 500th item. You cannot jump there. You must follow the pointers one node at a time from the head.

Recursion. A recursive function is one that calls itself on a smaller version of the same problem. It needs a base case, which is a condition where it returns an answer without calling itself again. Each call that has not yet finished takes up space on the call stack. The call stack is the area of memory where the program keeps track of unfinished function calls. If calls never stop, that space runs out. This crash is called a stack overflow. The team's function sumArray(arr, n) works like this. If n is 0, it returns 0. Otherwise it returns arr[n-1] + sumArray(arr, n-1). In words: the last item plus the sum of all the items before it.

Sorting and searching. Sorting means putting values in order. Selection sort is one simple sorting method. On each pass, it finds the smallest value in the part of the array that is not sorted yet. It then swaps that value into the first unsorted position. After each pass, the sorted part at the front grows by one. Searching means finding where a value is. Linear search checks items one by one from the start. Binary search only works on sorted data. It keeps two markers, low and high, around the part still being searched. It looks at the middle index, mid = (low + high) / 2, rounding down. If the middle value is the target, it is done. If the middle value is smaller than the target, it moves low to mid + 1. If larger, it moves high to mid - 1. Each check throws away about half of the remaining items. If the data is not sorted, throwing away a half can throw away the target, so binary search may wrongly report that the value is missing.

Your tasks:
1. The code contains int stock = 7; int* p = &stock; *p = 12; State the value of stock afterward and explain why. Then explain what is wrong with a function makeCounter that creates a local variable c inside itself and returns &c. Also say what could happen to the running program.
2. The warehouse keeps 10,000 shipment records. New urgent shipments must be added at the front many times per hour. Say whether an array or a linked list makes that front insertion cheaper, and explain why. Name one thing the other structure does better.
3. Trace sumArray on the array {4, 2, 5} with n = 3, showing each call and the value returned as the calls finish. Then explain what would happen if someone deleted the base case.
4. Sort the array {8, 5, 2, 6} with selection sort, showing the array after each pass. Then use binary search to find 6 in the sorted result, showing low, high and mid at each step. Say how many middle checks it took, and why binary search must not be run on the original unsorted array.
modelAnswer: stock becomes 12. The pointer p holds the address of stock, because p was set to &stock. Writing *p dereferences p, meaning go to the address p holds and use the value there. So *p = 12 writes 12 directly into stock's memory, even though the name stock never appears in that line. The problem with makeCounter is that c is a local variable, so it is destroyed when the function returns. The returned address therefore points to memory the program no longer owns. That makes it a dangling pointer. Reading or writing through it gives unpredictable results: garbage values, silently corrupted data, or a crash. This is a dangerous bug because it may appear to work during testing and then fail later.

A linked list makes front insertion cheaper. Adding at the front only means creating one new node, pointing it at the current head, and making it the new head. That is the same few steps whether the list holds 10 or 10,000 records. In an array, the values sit side by side, so inserting at index 0 means shifting all 10,000 existing values one place to the right first. That gets slower as the array grows. The array is better at reaching a record by its position: it can jump straight to any index. The linked list must follow pointers one node at a time from the head.

sumArray(arr, 3) returns arr[2] + sumArray(arr, 2), which is 5 + sumArray(arr, 2). sumArray(arr, 2) returns arr[1] + sumArray(arr, 1), which is 2 + sumArray(arr, 1). sumArray(arr, 1) returns arr[0] + sumArray(arr, 0), which is 4 + sumArray(arr, 0). sumArray(arr, 0) hits the base case and returns 0. As the calls finish, the values come back in reverse order. sumArray(arr, 1) returns 4 + 0 = 4. sumArray(arr, 2) returns 2 + 4 = 6. sumArray(arr, 3) returns 5 + 6 = 11. The final answer is 11. Without the base case, the function would keep calling itself with n = -1, -2, and so on, and never stop. It would also read outside the array. Each unfinished call takes space on the call stack, so the stack eventually runs out. The program then crashes with a stack overflow.

Selection sort on {8, 5, 2, 6}. Pass 1: the smallest value is 2, at index 2. Swap it with index 0, giving {2, 5, 8, 6}. Pass 2: the smallest of 5, 8, 6 is 5, already at index 1, so nothing moves: {2, 5, 8, 6}. Pass 3: the smallest of 8 and 6 is 6, at index 3. Swap it with index 2, giving {2, 5, 6, 8}. The array is now sorted. Binary search for 6. Step 1: low = 0, high = 3, mid = (0 + 3) / 2 = 1, rounding down. The value at index 1 is 5, which is less than 6, so low becomes 2. Step 2: low = 2, high = 3, mid = (2 + 3) / 2 = 2, rounding down. The value at index 2 is 6, so it is found at index 2. It took 2 middle checks. Binary search must not run on the unsorted array because it assumes everything left of the middle is smaller and everything right is larger. On unsorted data, discarding a half can discard the target, so the search may wrongly report that 6 is missing.

scenarios.title: Fixing the Order Tools at Bramblewood Parts
scenarios.scenario:
You have just joined Bramblewood Parts, a fictional company that sells replacement parts for farm machines. A small C++ program handles the warehouse's daily work, and your team lead has asked you to review four pieces of it. Every term below is defined so you can work from this page alone.

Piece one is the packing line. Orders arrive during the day and are packed in turn. A stack is a collection where the last item added is the first one removed (last in, first out). A queue is a collection where the first item added is the first one removed (first in, first out). The current code stores orders in a stack. This morning orders A, B, and C arrived in that order.

Piece two is the order line itself, written as a C++ class (a class is a programmer-defined type that bundles data with the functions allowed to work on it, so other code uses it only through those functions). Inside, the class uses a linked list. A linked list is a chain of small records called nodes, where each node holds one order plus a pointer (a variable that stores a memory address) to the next node. Each node is created with dynamic memory allocation. That means memory is requested while the program runs, using C++'s new, from an area called the heap, and it stays reserved until the program releases it with delete. This is different from static allocation, where the size is fixed before the program runs. The function that removes the front order does only this: head = head->next; It then returns the order.

Piece three is the part lookup. It uses a hash table. A hash table is an array of slots where a hash function turns a key, here a part number, into a slot number. This table has 7 slots, numbered 0 to 6, and the hash function is part number mod 7 (the remainder after dividing by 7). When two keys land in the same slot, that is called a collision. This table handles collisions with chaining: each slot holds a small linked list, and new keys are added to the end of that slot's list. Part numbers 15, 22, 9, and 29 were inserted in that order.

Piece four is a backup search over a sorted array of part numbers: [3, 8, 12, 19, 25, 31, 40], at positions 0 to 6. It uses binary search, which checks the middle position, then keeps only the half that could still hold the target. The search is written recursively. Recursion means a function solves a problem by calling itself on a smaller piece of the same problem. A base case is the condition where the function stops calling itself and returns an answer directly. The code computes mid = (low + high) / 2, rounding down. It returns mid if the value there matches. Otherwise it calls itself on the left half (high = mid - 1) or the right half (low = mid + 1). It has no other stopping check.

Your tasks:
1. Say in what order the stack would hand out orders A, B, and C. Then say which structure the packing line should use and why.
2. Explain what is wrong with the remove-front function in the linked-list class, what happens to a long-running program because of it, and how to fix it.
3. Show which slot each part number lands in, and draw the chains. Then count how many key comparisons it takes to look up 29, and to look up 36, which is not in the table.
4. Trace the recursive binary search for 31, giving low, high, and mid at each call. Then trace a search for 20, and explain what goes wrong and what base case is missing.
subParts: Recursive binary search and base case
modelAnswer: The stack hands out C first, then B, then A, because a stack is last in, first out. That makes the earliest customer wait longest. The packing line should use a queue, which is first in, first out, so orders come out as A, B, C, the order they arrived. That matches the fair rule of packing the oldest order first.

The function moves head to the next node but never frees the old front node. That node was created with new on the heap, and now no pointer refers to it, so the program can never release it. This is a memory leak: memory stays reserved but can no longer be used. In a program that runs all day and removes thousands of orders, memory use keeps growing until the program slows down or is killed for running out of memory. The fix is to save the old head in a temporary pointer, copy out its order, move head to head->next, and then call delete on the temporary pointer before returning the order. If the list becomes empty, also set any tail pointer to null.

15 mod 7 = 1, 22 mod 7 = 1, 9 mod 7 = 2, and 29 mod 7 = 1. Slot 1 holds the chain 15 -> 22 -> 29, slot 2 holds 9, and all other slots are empty. Looking up 29: 29 mod 7 = 1, so walk slot 1 comparing against 15, then 22, then 29, a match after 3 comparisons. Looking up 36: 36 mod 7 = 1, so compare against 15, 22, and 29, reach the end of the chain, and report not found after 3 comparisons. The collisions in slot 1 are what make these lookups slower than a single check.

Search for 31. Call 1: low = 0, high = 6, mid = 3, and the value is 19. Since 19 < 31, go right with low = 4. Call 2: low = 4, high = 6, mid = 5, and the value is 31, so it returns position 5.

Search for 20. Call 1: low = 0, high = 6, mid = 3, value 19 < 20, so low = 4. Call 2: low = 4, high = 6, mid = 5, value 31 > 20, so high = 4. Call 3: low = 4, high = 4, mid = 4, value 25 > 20, so high = 3. Now low = 4 is greater than high = 3, meaning no positions are left to check. The code has no check for this. It computes mid = (4 + 3) / 2 = 3, sees 19 < 20, and sets low = 4 again. This repeats forever. Each call uses more of the call stack until the program crashes with a stack overflow. The missing base case is: if low > high, return -1 (not found). It must be checked at the start of every call.

scenarios.title: Phished Password and a Fake Invoice at Maplewood Supply Co.
scenarios.scenario:
Maplewood Supply Co. is a fictional, 40-person company that sells baking ingredients to cafes. You have just joined its two-person IT team. On Monday, Dana, an accounts clerk, received an email that looked like it came from the company's email provider. It said her mailbox was full and gave her a link. The link opened a fake login page, a copy of the real one built by an attacker, and Dana typed in her username and password. Those two items together are her credentials, the secret details that prove who she is to a system. This trick is called phishing: a message that pretends to come from someone trusted so the reader hands over secrets or clicks something harmful.

The company's email accepts a password alone. It does not use multi-factor authentication (MFA), which means asking for a second, separate proof of identity, such as a code from a phone app, on top of the password. So the attacker logged in as Dana. From her real mailbox, they read past customer emails. Then they replied to a long-time customer with an invoice that changed Maplewood's bank account number to the attacker's own. The customer paid 18,000 dollars into the wrong account. Separately, the IT team learned that Dana, and every other staff member, signs in to the office computers with one shared administrator account. An administrator account is an account allowed to install software and change system settings. The attacker did not use that account this time, but it was in Dana's saved notes.

Your manager asks you to use four ideas from your security course. The CIA triad is the three goals of information security: confidentiality, meaning only the right people can see information; integrity, meaning information is not changed without permission and can be trusted; and availability, meaning information and systems work when needed. Least privilege means each person or account gets only the access its job needs, and nothing more. A security policy is a written rule set by the organisation that says what must or must not happen, who is responsible, and what happens when it is broken. Defense in depth means stacking several independent protections, so that when one fails, another still stops or limits the attack. Controls, meaning the safeguards themselves, come in three types. Preventive controls stop an attack before it succeeds. Detective controls notice an attack while it happens or afterwards. Corrective controls repair the damage and return things to normal.

1. For each of the three CIA goals, state whether it was harmed in this incident and give the specific evidence from the scenario.
2. Explain the attacker's tactic step by step, and why the password control was bypassed even though the password itself was never cracked or guessed.
3. Write two short security policy statements: one for changes to customer payment or bank details, and one for administrator accounts. Each must say what is required and who is responsible, and must apply least privilege where it fits.
4. Recommend a defense-in-depth set of at least three controls, with at least one preventive, one detective, and one corrective. For each, say which part of this attack it would stop, catch, or fix.
subParts: Apply the CIA triad to the incident
Explain the attack tactic and the control bypass
modelAnswer: Confidentiality was harmed. The attacker logged in as Dana and read past customer emails, so someone with no permission saw private business information. Integrity was harmed. The attacker sent an invoice with a changed bank account number, so the customer received altered information they had no reason to doubt, and paid 18,000 dollars to the attacker. Availability was not clearly harmed. Nothing in the scenario says email or systems stopped working, though the business may lose time and money handling the fallout. A strong answer names integrity as the cause of the money loss and confidentiality as the data exposure.

Step 1: the attacker sent a phishing email pretending to come from the email provider, using urgency (a full mailbox) to make Dana act fast. Step 2: the link went to a fake login page that looked real. Step 3: Dana typed her credentials, which went straight to the attacker. Step 4: the attacker signed in to the real email service with those valid credentials. Step 5: because the login was real, they could send emails customers trusted. The password control was bypassed, not broken. A password only proves someone knows a secret. Once the attacker knew it, the system had no way to tell them apart from Dana, because no second factor such as MFA was required. The weak point was tricking a person, not cracking the password. The lesson is that a single control that depends on one secret fails completely as soon as that secret is stolen.

Payment-detail policy (sample): Any request to change a customer's or supplier's bank or payment details must be confirmed by phone with a known contact, using a number already on file and never one given in the request. A second finance staff member must approve the change before it takes effect. The finance manager is responsible for enforcing this rule. Changes made without this check are treated as a policy violation. Administrator account policy (sample): Shared administrator accounts are not allowed. Staff use standard accounts for daily work. Only named IT staff who need administrator rights for their job receive a separate, personal administrator account, protected by MFA and used only for admin tasks. Passwords must never be stored in personal notes. The IT lead is responsible for reviewing administrator access every quarter and removing access that is no longer needed. Grading: each statement must say what is required and who is responsible. The admin policy must show least privilege (only those who need it, separate accounts, no sharing). The payment policy should include verification through a separate trusted channel.

Preventive: require MFA on email. Even with Dana's stolen password, the attacker could not log in without the second factor, which stops step 4 of the attack. Also preventive: the phone-verification payment policy, which would stop the fake bank change even if the email account were taken over. Another acceptable preventive control is email filtering that blocks or labels suspicious links and lookalike senders, along with phishing awareness training. Detective: alerts on unusual logins, such as sign-ins from a new location or device, and regular review of email login logs. Either would catch the account takeover while it is happening or soon after. Corrective: on discovery, reset Dana's password, end all her active sessions, remove any mail-forwarding rules the attacker created, contact the customer and the bank to try to recover the funds, and replace the shared administrator account with personal accounts. Grading: the answer needs at least one control of each type, each tied to a specific step of this attack, and should explain that the layers together mean one failure (such as a clicked link) does not lead to a full loss.
